data_protection.title: Material Context of Data Processing and Priority of the NDP Act
data_protection.description: (a) Every person, body or authority owes a duty of care to data subjects, to carefully examine the material context of personal data processing with a view to ascertaining whether the processing required in the said context is consistent with the constitutional right to privacy and the objectives set forth in section 1 of the NDP Act.  (d) Data controllers and data processors shall take into consideration the material character of data – particularly its value, volume, variety, velocity and veracity – as it flows within and beyond the Nigerian territory and put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures to mitigate associated risks.
data_protection.plain: (a). data_protection.title: Statutory Remedy for Multiple Regulation
data_protection.description: (1) In order to guarantee certainty, harmony and efficacy on the regulation of: a) Informational self-determination (fundamental right to privacy); b) Data sovereignty (the inherent right of an independent country to govern data processing pertaining to persons in her territory); c) National and cross-border data flows; and d) Treaty obligations (particularly in the material context highlighted in Article 2(b) of this GAID), it is imperative to uphold the provision of section 63 of the NDP Act in all proceedings and transactions pertaining to the processing of personal data. For ease of reference Section 63 of the NDP Act provides: “Where the provisions of any other law or enactment, in so far as they provide or relate directly or indirectly to the processing of personal data, are inconsistent with any of the provisions of this Act, the provisions of this Act shall prevail.”
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall ensure that in any matter relating to personal data, the provisions of the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDP Act) take precedence over any other conflicting laws, especially regarding privacy rights, data sovereignty, cross-border data flows, and treaty obligations.
data_protection.riskDescription: Continued reliance on obsolete NDPR policies may lead to non-compliance.
data_protection.primaryControl: Replace NDPR procedures with NDPA policies; staff retraining.
data_protection.additionalControl: Quarterly framework updates; sunset clause for NDPR documentation.

data_protection.title: Evaluation of Exemptions
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller, a data processor or an individual who relies on or intends to rely on any exemption pursuant to Section 3 of the NDP Act, shall abide by other provisions which are not exempted by the NDP Act.  (2) A data processing activity which falls within the exemptions under Section 3 of the NDP Act is at the minimum, bound by the following provisions of the NDP Act: a) S. 24 – Principles of personal data processing b) S. 25 – Lawful basis of personal data processing c) S. 32 - Designation of Data Protection Officers d) S. 40 – Personal data breaches notification e) Part VI - Data subjects’ rights
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. If relying on an exemption under Section 3 of the Nigerian Data Protection Act (NDPA), still comply with all other provisions of the NDPA that are not specifically exempted.  2. Ensure that even exempted data processing activities comply with the following mandatory NDPA provisions:  a) Section 24: Principles for processing personal data b) Section 25: Lawful basis for processing c) Section 32: Appointment of Data Protection Officers (DPOs) d) Section 40: Reporting personal data breaches e) Part VI: Data subjects’ rights
data_protection.riskDescription: Misuse or misunderstanding of exemptions leading to breach of principles or subject rights.

data_protection.title: General NDP Act Compliance Measures by Data Controllers and Data Processors
data_protection.description: a) Register with the Commission as a data controller or data processor of major importance as the Commission may determine in accordance with the NDP Act. d) Identify all its obligations under the NDP Act and prepare schedules of compliance; f) Prepare and follow Schedules on Monitoring Evaluation and Maintenance of Data Security System in order to guarantee data confidentiality, integrity and availability; g) Prepare and follow schedules on organisation-wide, internal sensitisation and training on data privacy and protection in order to foster a culture of compliance with the NDP Act and best practices; i) In the case of a data controller or data processor of major importance, designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO). Associate DPOs/Privacy Champions may be designated to support the DPO where the data controller or the data processor carries out data processing or interfaces with data subjects on multiple platforms and places; j) Develop or review its organisational privacy policies, the privacy policy shall be in compliance with the NDP Act; k) Publish its organisational privacy policies on its platforms with a view to sensitising data subjects on data processing activities as well as rights and duties in connection therewith;  l) Provide privacy and cookie notices at the homepage of its website. The cookie notice should give a data subject the opportunity to decline or accept the notice; A cookie notice must be displayed in such a way that it significantly obstructs the middle, the left or the right side of the home page of a website. Displaying a cookie notice at the bottom of a webpage where it may be ignored or be  unnoticed by a data subject is tantamount to lack of transparency in data processing. m) Ensure that the privacy policy and notice is transparent and appropriately provided on platforms/places where data processing is taking place; and without prejudice to the NDP Act, it shall also take into account specific directions on privacy by relevant Application Hosting Platforms through which a data subject may access its services; n) Develop and circulate an internal data protection strategy or policy and basic privacy checklist to help members of staff and other relevant persons (such as vendors, agents and contractors) understand the organisation’s direction in connection with the processing of personal data and outline the steps they are to take to ensure the organisation’s direction is maintained; o) Conduct a Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) when required under the NDP Act, or when directed by the Commission; q) Notify a data subject immediately after becoming aware of a personal data breach that may pose high risk to his or her privacy; r) Update agreements with third party processors to ensure compliance with the NDP Act; s) Design systems and processes to make data requests and access seamless for data subjects; t) Design systems and processes to enable data subjects to easily correct or update their personal data; u) Design systems and processes to enable data subjects easily transfer data to another platform or person (natural or artificial); v) At least within the six (6) months of commencement of business and then, at the minimum, on an annual basis, train its personnel on data protection law and practices; and  w) Clearly explain the complaints process to data subjects including the right to lodge a complaint with the Commission.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  (a) Register with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) if designated as a data controller or processor of major importance. (d) Identify all its compliance obligations under the NDPA and maintain clear schedules for meeting them. (f) Develop and implement schedules for monitoring, evaluating, and maintaining its data security systems to ensure data confidentiality, integrity, and availability. (g) Conduct regular organisation-wide sensitisation and training to promote a culture of data protection and compliance. (i) If the bank is of major importance, appoint a qualified Data Protection Officer (DPO), and optionally, assign Privacy Champions or Associate DPOs to support across various platforms or locations. (j) Develop or update the bank’s privacy policy to ensure compliance with the NDPA. (k) Publish the privacy policy prominently on the bank’s platforms to inform customers of data processing activities and their rights. (l) Display privacy and cookie notices clearly on the homepage (not hidden at the bottom), giving users the option to accept or decline cookies in a noticeable manner. (m) Ensure transparency of the privacy policy and display it appropriately wherever data is collected (including digital platforms and third-party apps), complying with both NDPA and relevant platform privacy requirements. (n) Develop and distribute an internal data protection strategy and checklist to staff, vendors, agents, and contractors to guide them in data protection practices. (o) Conduct Data Privacy Impact Assessments (DPIAs) where required by the NDPA or as directed by the NDPC. (q) Notify data subjects immediately of any personal data breach that may significantly affect their privacy. (r) Update all contracts with third-party processors to ensure they comply with the NDPA. (s) Create simple and accessible systems for data subjects to request and access their personal data. (t) Allow data subjects to easily correct or update their personal information. (u) Enable data subjects to transfer their personal data to another organisation or platform easily (data portability). (v) Provide mandatory training on data protection for all staff within six months of starting operations and then at least annually. (w) Clearly inform data subjects about how to file complaints, including their right to report to the NDPC.
data_protection.riskDescription: Lack of controls may result in data breach and reputational damage.
data_protection.primaryControl: Standard data protection program
data_protection.additionalControl: Annual self-assessment

data_protection.title: Designation of DCMIs
data_protection.description: (1) Section 65 of the NDP Act provides, “data controller or data processor of major importance” means a data controller or data processor that is domiciled, resident in, or operating in Nigeria and processes or intends to process personal data of more than such number of data subjects who are within Nigeria, as the Commission may prescribe, or such other class of data controller or data processor that is processing personal data of particular value or significance to the economy, society or security of Nigeria as the Commission may designate.  (2) “Operating in Nigeria” as stated in section 65 includes a data controller or a data processor who targets a data subject in Nigeria. Such data controller or processor may not be domiciled in or resident in Nigeria. This is taking into consideration the provision of section 2(2)(a) of the NDP Act on the Application of the Act as well as sections 24(3) and 44 on the need to hold accountable data controllers and processors whose processing activities significantly impact the economy, society or security of Nigeria.  (3) In carrying out an objective assessment of what is of value or significance to the economy, society or security of Nigeria, the Commission shall take into consideration all relevant factors – including but not limited to the following: a) The risks that the data processing by a data controller or a data processor poses to a data subject if such data controller or data processor is not under the obligation imposed by the NDP Act on a data controller or a data processor of major importance as contemplated by section 29(1)(a) of the NDP Act; ... i) The need for international standard certifications for people, processes and technologies involved in data confidentiality, integrity and availability.  (4) In order to ensure proportionality of obligations in relation to various levels of major data processing, the Commission classifies data controllers and data processors into 3 (three) levels or categories of major data processing, namely: (a) Ultra-High Level (UHL) (b) Extra-High Level (EHL) (c) Ordinary-High Level (OHL)
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Determine if it qualifies as a Data Controller or Data Processor of Major Importance (DCMI) by assessing whether it: – Processes personal data of a large number of Nigerians (as defined by NDPC); or – Handles data of particular value or importance to Nigeria’s economy, society, or national security.  2. Understand that it may still be classified as a DCMI even if not physically operating in Nigeria, if it targets or serves Nigerian data subjects.  3. Cooperate with NDPC assessments based on risk factors, including potential harm to individuals, type of data processed (e.g., sensitive or biometric), and relevance to national interests.  4. Be aware that the NDPC classifies DCMIs into: – Ultra-High Level (UHL) – Extra-High Level (EHL) – Ordinary-High Level (OHL)
data_protection.riskDescription: Failure to comply may trigger NDPC enforcement or penalties.
data_protection.primaryControl: Maintain status as DCMI with NDPC
data_protection.additionalControl: Periodic classification review

data_protection.title: Registration as DCMI
data_protection.description: 1) A data controller or a data processor of major importance as designated by the Commission shall register with the Commission in accordance with the Guidance Notice issued by the Commission and reproduced in this GAID as Schedule 7.   (4) A data controller or data processor of major importance shall notify the Commission of any significant change to the information submitted in its most recent registration submission within sixty (60) days after such change by providing any information required by the Commission through any electronic submission system provided by the Commission, or in the absence of which by email to an address provided by the Commission for such purpose.  (5) If a data controller or data processor no longer qualifies as a data controller or data processor of major importance, they may request removal from the register by providing the information required by the Commission through any electronic submission system provided by the Commission, or in the absence of which by email to an address that the Commission shall publish on its website.  (6) Notwithstanding its removal from the register, a former data controller or data processor of major importance shall remain responsible for payment of any outstanding fees from the then-current and any prior annual registration periods.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall : 1. Register with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) as a Data Controller or Data Processor of Major Importance, in line with the Guidance Notice in Schedule 7 of the GAID, if designated as such by the Commission. 2. Notify the NDPC within 60 days of any significant change to the information provided in its most recent registration, using the Commission’s electronic system or official email. 3. Request removal from the NDPC register if it no longer qualifies as a Data Controller or Data Processor of Major Importance, by providing the required information through the Commission’s specified submission channel. 4. Pay all outstanding registration fees due for the current and any previous annual periods, even after being removed from the NDPC register.

data_protection.title: Position of the DPO
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller or a data processor shall actively engage its DPO in all issues which relate to the processing of personal data.  (2) The data controller or data processor shall give appropriate support to the DPO in performing the data protection responsibilities as prescribed by the NDP Act or by the Commission. Accordingly, the data controller or data processor shall put in place the necessary organisational measures, namely: a) Provide necessary resources to the DPO to carry out data protection tasks; b) Ensure access to personal data processing activities and processing operations; and c) Make adequate provision for continuous training for the DPO.  (3) The data controller or data processor shall ensure that the DPO does not carry out his or her task under duress, coercion, covert or overt influence.  (4) He or she shall not be dismissed or penalised by the data controller or the data processor for performing his or her tasks.  (5) The DPO shall directly report to the management level of the controller or the processor.  (6) Data subjects may contact the DPO with regard to all issues relating to the processing of their personal data and to the exercise of their rights under the NDP Act.  (7) The DPO shall be bound by secrecy or confidentiality concerning the performance of his or her tasks, in accordance with relevant legislation.  (8) The DPO may fulfil other tasks and duties. The data controller or data processor shall ensure that any such tasks and duties do not result in a conflict of interest.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Actively involve the Data Protection Officer (DPO) in all matters related to personal data processing.  2. Support the DPO in fulfilling responsibilities under the NDPA and as directed by the Commission by:  a) Providing the necessary resources to perform data protection duties; b) Granting access to data processing operations; and c) Ensuring continuous training for the DPO.  3. Ensure the DPO operates independently, free from pressure, coercion, or improper influence.  4. Not dismiss or penalize the DPO for performing their data protection responsibilities.  5. Ensure the DPO reports directly to senior management.  6. Allow data subjects to contact the DPO about personal data processing and their rights under the NDPA.  7. Require the DPO to maintain confidentiality in line with relevant laws.  8. Ensure that any other roles assigned to the DPO do not create a conflict of interest.
data_protection.riskDescription: Undermining DPO’s independence could compromise regulatory confidence and data protection.
data_protection.primaryControl: Grant DPO autonomy, secure budget, and board-level access.
data_protection.additionalControl: Periodic review of DPO role effectiveness and organisational support.

data_protection.title: Submission of Internal Semi-Annual Reports
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller or a data processor shall ensure that a semi-annual data protection report is compiled by its DPO and submitted to its management.  (2) The report shall be submitted to an officer of the data controller or data processor who is authorised to receive a Record of Processing Activities (RoPA).  (3) The report shall be acknowledged by the receiving officer and shall form part of the ROPA by the data controller or data processor.  (4) The report shall be verified by a DPCO during the NDP Act compliance audit.  (5) The report to be submitted by the DPO shall among others, contain the compliance status of the data controller or data processor under the NDP Act – particularly taking into account: (a) Assessment of privacy notices – taking the requirements of the NDP Act into account.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Ensure the Data Protection Officer (DPO) compiles and submits a semi-annual data protection report to management.  2. Submit the report to an officer authorized to receive the Record of Processing Activities (RoPA).  3. Ensure the report is acknowledged by the receiving officer and included as part of the Bank’s RoPA.  4. Ensure the report is available for verification by a licensed Data Protection Compliance Organisation (DPCO) during the NDPA compliance audit.  5. Ensure the report includes, at a minimum, an assessment of the Bank’s compliance status with the NDPA, especially regarding the adequacy of privacy notices.
data_protection.riskDescription: Failure to monitor and escalate internal data issues timely can lead to privacy lapses or regulatory breaches.
data_protection.primaryControl: Establish a biannual internal reporting framework.
data_protection.additionalControl: Automate privacy metrics and embed them into enterprise compliance dashboards.

data_protection.title: Credential Assessment of the DPO
data_protection.description: (1) Considering that data privacy is a fundamental right to informational self-determination, it is prudent for a data controller to prioritise the interest of the data subject which may be effectively addressed through his or her informed consent.  (2) Where reliance on consent may effectively defeat the rule of law, another lawful basis may be considered.   (5) Reliance on any lawful bases of data processing which is not consent and not supported by any SRLI shall be strictly scrutinised during NDP Act compliance  audio and in any proceeding where the conduct of a data controller or processor is called into question.  (6)Whenever a data controller relies on consent, it shall keep a proper record that guarantees accountability in respect of the consent.  (7)In determining whether a data controller is accountable in the mode of obtaining consent, the data controller shall: 1. (a)Provide appropriate information to the data subject such that the data subject, on the basis of the information; may make an informed decision; 2. (b)Make the process of withdrawal of consent as easy as giving consent; and 3. (c)Ensure that refusal of consent is not detrimental to the rights and interests of the data subject.  (8)Nothing in this GAID shall prevent a data subject from giving a constructive or an implied consent to data processing in the following circumstances: 1. (a)A data subject's area of participation in a public event and the images taken in that event may be used for a report of that event - provided that such images shall not be used for profit or commerce-oriented advertisement without the express consent of the data subject. A data controller in this circumstance shall ensure that images captured do not portray data subjects in a bad light. In addition to other measures of duty of care, a data controller may put participants on notice that images captured may be used for reporting, journalistic or other purposes permitted by the NDP Act. 2. (b)Subject to the NDP Act and Article 18 of this GAID, a data subject's act of closing a privacy notice displayed on the centre of a webpage and which notice significantly obstructs the viewing of the webpage - provided that the data collected in such circumstances is limited to processing of personal data which is necessary to basic functionality of the website. Basic functionality means such functions that permit us website to respond to and analyse the interactions of the data subject with the website.  (9)At all times where consent is required, a data subject shall be provided with a clear and explicit option to accept or to decline.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Prioritize the data subject’s right to informational self-determination, especially by ensuring informed consent is obtained where appropriate.  2. Consider alternative lawful bases for data processing where relying on consent would undermine legal obligations or the rule of law.  3. Ensure that if the Bank relies on a lawful basis other than consent and that basis is not supported by any Statutory, Regulatory, Legal, or Institutional Instrument (SRLI), such reliance may be strictly reviewed during compliance audits and legal proceedings.  4. Keep proper and verifiable records of all instances where consent is relied upon to demonstrate accountability.  5. When relying on consent: a) Provide adequate and understandable information so that data subjects can make informed decisions. b) Make withdrawal of consent as simple as giving it. c) Ensure that refusal to give consent does not negatively affect the rights or interests of the data subject.  6. Recognize that constructive or implied consent may apply in certain situations, such as: a) Participation in public events where non-commercial image use is involved (e.g., event reporting), provided no harm or misrepresentation occurs. b) A data subject dismissing a central privacy notice on a webpage, as long as: i. It does not obstruct functionality; ii. Data collected is limited to what is necessary for basic website operation.  7. Always give data subjects a clear and explicit option to either accept or decline consent.
data_protection.riskDescription: Use of invalid consent or weak privacy controls can attract audit penalties or data subject complaints.
data_protection.primaryControl: Implement a DPO competency and continuous certification program.
data_protection.additionalControl: Conduct mock audits to assess DPO interpretation and documentation of lawful bases and SRLIs.

data_protection.title: Principles of Personal Data Protection
data_protection.description: (1) The entire principle of data protection are obligatory in any form of data processing.  The principles under section 24 of the NDP Act are:  a) Fairness, lawfulness and transparency of data processing,  b) Purpose limitation,  c) Data minimisation and ethics,  d) Storage limitation,  e) Data accuracy,  f) Data confidentiality, integrity and availability,  g) Accountability, and  h) Duty of care.  (2) The scope of the foregoing principles is more particularly described in Schedule 1 of this GAID.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Apply all principles of personal data protection in every data processing activity, without exception.  2. Ensure that all processing of personal data strictly follows the principles outlined in Section 24 of the NDPA, which include:  a) Process data in a way that is legal, fair, and clear to the data subject. b) Collect data only for specific, lawful purposes and not use it beyond those purposes. c) Collect only the data necessary for the intended purpose and handle it ethically. d) Do not keep personal data longer than necessary. e) Keep personal data accurate and up to date. f)  Protect data from unauthorized access, damage, or loss. g) Be able to demonstrate compliance with all data protection obligations. h) Always act in a way that protects the interests and rights of data subjects.  3. Refer to Schedule 1 of the Guidance Notice for further clarification on the scope and application of each principle.
data_protection.riskDescription: Breach of any of the 8 principles may lead to investigation, sanctions, or reputational harm.
data_protection.primaryControl: Embed principles in data lifecycle policies and staff SOPs.
data_protection.additionalControl: Regular audits and training to check principle adherence.

data_protection.title: Lawful Bases of Processing
data_protection.description: (1) In line with Section 25 of the NDP Act, it is important for a data controller to carefully assess the lawful bases of data processing before embarking on same.  (2) Subject to the provisions of the NDP Act and any regulatory instruments issued by  the Commission, a data controller shall carefully consider and choose the appropriate lawful bases of data processing in order to process personal data. The lawful bases  are:  a) Consent  b) Contractual Obligation  d) Legal Obligation  e) Valid Interest  f) Public Interest  g) Legitimate Interest.  (3) As the party who determines the purpose of data processing, the data controller is ultimately responsible for determining the lawful bases of data processing
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Carefully assess and select the appropriate lawful basis before processing any personal data, in line with Section 25 of the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA).  2. Ensure that the lawful basis chosen complies with the NDPA and any relevant regulatory instruments issued by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. Choose from the following lawful bases of processing:  a) Consent  b) Contractual Obligation  c) Legal Obligation  d) Valid Interest  e) Public Interest  f) Legitimate Interest  3. Acknowledge that, as the data controller, the Bank is fully responsible for determining and justifying the lawful basis used for each data processing activity.
data_protection.riskDescription: Unlawful processing due to unclear basis can lead to invalid operations or enforcement action.
data_protection.primaryControl: Map processing activities to lawful bases and maintain records.
data_protection.additionalControl: Review and update RoPA with basis for each category of processing.

data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Prioritize the data subject’s interest by ensuring that consent is informed, freely given, and clearly understood before collecting or processing personal data.  2. Not rely on consent if doing so would undermine the rule of law—in such cases, another lawful basis must be used.  3. Keep proper and verifiable records of all consents obtained, to demonstrate accountability.  4. When relying on consent: a) Provide the data subject with enough information to make an informed decision. b) Make it just as easy to withdraw consent as it is to give it. c) Ensure that refusal of consent does not negatively affect the data subject’s rights or interests. 5. Recognize that constructive or implied consent may apply in certain situations: a) If a data subject attends a public event, images may be used for reporting (but not for advertising or profit-making purposes without express consent). The Bank must ensure no harmful portrayal and may provide notice that images could be used for permitted purposes. b) If a data subject closes a prominently displayed privacy notice on a webpage, it may imply consent for basic website functions only (e.g., responding to or analyzing user interactions)—subject to Article 18 and the NDPA.  6. Always provide a clear and explicit option to either accept or decline consent wherever it is required.

data_protection.primaryControl: Implement standardised, explicit consent forms with logging.

data_protection.title: Data Processing Which Requires Consent
data_protection.description: (1) Without prejudice to the provisions of the NDP Act and in addition to other circumstances in which consent may be required under this GAID or by operation of law, consent is required: a) For any direct marketing activity; b) For the processing of sensitive personal data; c) For further processing that is incompatible with the original purpose of processing; d) For the processing of the personal data of a child; e) Before personal data may be transferred to a country in respect of which the Commission has not made an adequacy decision; and f) Before the data controller makes a decision based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects concerning or significantly affecting the data subject.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall obtain the data subject’s consent before:  (a) Engaging in any direct marketing activity; (b) Processing any sensitive personal data; (c) Performing further processing of personal data that is incompatible with the original purpose of collection; (d) Processing the personal data of a child; (e) Transferring personal data to a country without an adequacy decision by the Commission; (f) Making automated decisions that have legal or significant effects on the data subject.
data_protection.riskDescription: Failure to obtain valid consent may result in enforcement, fines, and reputational damage.
data_protection.primaryControl: Include consent management controls in all applicable systems.
data_protection.additionalControl: Train staff on consent obligations; audit periodically.

data_protection.title: Consent to Cookies and other Tracking Tools
data_protection.description: (1) Operation of cookies and other tracking tools shall comply with the principles of data protection under section 24 of the NDP Act.  (2) Except as otherwise provided by this GAID, the use of cookies on a website or other digital platforms requires consent.  (3) The consent shall be freely given, informed and specific.  (4) A Data Controller/Data Processor should display a cookie banner in a manner that is conspicuous and obvious to a user or site visitor.  (5) Necessary cookies which do not process sensitive data, financial data or any data stored privately by a data subject does not need the ticking of a box or similar methods;  (6) In this article "necessary cookies" means cookies that enable core functionality such as security, network stability management, and accessibility. All other forms of cookies require a specific selection of "yes or no" (alternatively: "except" or "reject") options presented to the data subject.  (7) In deploying cookies, website owners are required to:  a) Make cookies notice banner or display conspicuous. Accordingly, a data subject shall not be required to scroll to any part of a website before seeing the cookie banner. Similarly, every tracking tool shall be made known to the data subject at the section of the web page which appears first;  b) Make cookie listing onto clear and easy to understand;  c) Notify users of the presence and purpose of the cookies;  d) Identify the organisation responsible for the use of the cookies; and  e) Provide information on how to withdraw consent from the use of the cookies.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Ensure the use of cookies and tracking tools complies with the data protection principles in section 24 of the NDPA.  2. Obtain consent before using cookies on websites or digital platforms, unless otherwise exempted under the GAID.  3. Ensure the consent is freely given, informed, and specific.  4. Display a conspicuous and obvious cookie banner to users or site visitors—without requiring scrolling to locate it.  5. Use cookie banners that clearly list: a) The types and purposes of cookies, b) The identity of the organisation responsible for the cookies, c) How users can withdraw consent.  6. Distinguish necessary cookies (those enabling security, stability, or accessibility) which do not process sensitive or private data—these do not require opt-in.  7. Ensure that all non-essential cookies (including those involving sensitive, financial, or private data) require the user to explicitly accept or reject via clear “yes or no” options.
data_protection.riskDescription: Collecting data without valid cookie consent can lead to regulatory breach and user complaints.
data_protection.primaryControl: Deploy CMP tools; clearly differentiate between cookie types.
data_protection.additionalControl: Review third-party scripts and trackers regularly.

data_protection.title: Purpose Limitation
data_protection.description: (1) In addition to other obligations under the NDP Act and this GAID, every data processing shall only proceed from purposes that are: i. Lawful under the NDP Act; ii. Not in violation of other legislation for the time being in force in Nigeria, and iii. Not in violation of preemptory norms of general International Law.  (2) No consent shall be sought, given or accepted in any circumstance that may engender direct or indirect propagation of atrocities, hate, child rights violations and criminal acts.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Ensure that every data processing activity is for a specific purpose that is: a) Lawful under the NDPA, b) Not in conflict with any Nigerian law, and c) Not contrary to international legal norms.  2. Not request, give, or accept consent for any data processing that may directly or indirectly promote: a) Atrocities, b) Hate speech, c) Violations of child rights, or d) Criminal activities.
data_protection.riskDescription: Repurposing data unlawfully may trigger sanctions and loss of trust.
data_protection.primaryControl: Purpose must be documented in RoPA and Privacy Notices.
data_protection.additionalControl: Conduct DPIAs when changing data use purpose.

data_protection.title: Lawful Basis Clarifications
data_protection.description: (1) At the preliminary stage of a contract with a data subject, a data controller or data processor may carry out data processing on the data subject for the purpose of due diligence.  (2) Where the contract did not materialise, any personal data collected relating to the data subject shall be destroyed within six (6) months unless there is a justifiable ground to archive the data for the purposes of any future legal claim.  (3) A contract with a data subject involving data processing shall make provision for termination of the contract prior to the tenure of the contract.  (5) Pursuant to Section 46 of the 1999 Constitution and Section 34(1)(a)(v) of the NDP Act, a specific term of a contract on personal data processing that ousts or purports to oust the adjudicatory jurisdiction of Nigerian courts or the executive jurisdiction of the Commission shall be treated as void.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Only process personal data at the pre-contract stage (e.g., during due diligence) where it is necessary to evaluate a contract with the data subject.  2. If the contract does not go ahead, destroy any collected personal data within six (6) months, unless there is a lawful reason to retain it (e.g., for possible future legal claims).  3. Include a clause in contracts with data subjects that allows for early termination of the contract, especially when personal data is being processed.  4. Not include or rely on any contract term that removes or limits the legal rights of data subjects to: a) Seek redress from Nigerian courts, or b) Lodge complaints with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). Any such term is invalid and unenforceable.
data_protection.riskDescription: Illegal contract terms or extended retention beyond justification can lead to NDPC penalties.
data_protection.primaryControl: Standard contract templates; auto-deletion triggers for failed onboarding.
data_protection.additionalControl: Legal review of contracts for DP compliance.

data_protection.title: Reliance on Legal Obligation
data_protection.description: (1) A legal obligation means any one of the following: a) a specific duty imposed by law; b) an order of a court of competent jurisdiction; or c) a responsibility incidental to an obligation imposed by law to carry out an act which requires the processing of personal data.   (4) Data processing under legal obligation shall be strictly limited to the minimum requirement under a law in line with Sub-Article (3) above and shall not be used for a voyage of discovery into the privacy of a data subject or in circumstances of establishing a speculative claim.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Only rely on a legal obligation to process personal data if it is based on: a) A specific duty imposed by law; b) An order from a court of competent jurisdiction; or c) A responsibility that arises directly from a legal obligation requiring the processing of personal data.  2. Ensure that data processing based on legal obligation is: a) Strictly limited to what the law requires, b) Not used to unnecessarily intrude into a data subject’s privacy, or c) Not used to explore personal data for speculative or unjustified purposes.
data_protection.riskDescription: Applying conflicting data laws or outdated privacy standards could expose the bank to legal uncertainty, regulatory breaches, or data subject claims.
data_protection.primaryControl: Legal basis must be documented in RoPA; justify with applicable statutes.
data_protection.additionalControl: Periodic legal gap analysis between NDPA and other laws; NDPA training for legal and compliance staff

data_protection.title: Evaluation of Lawful Bases of Data Processing
data_protection.description: (a) The necessity of processing of personal data – taking into consideration the risks and the alternatives (agency; (b) The duty of care and the standard of care employed to mitigate unnecessary, disproportionate risks of data processing;  (d) The proportionality of the processing of personal data – taking into account: i. the scope of measures adopted or intended to be adopted for the processing of personal data in relation to the ii. the legitimate aim pursued. Duty of care shall be exercised in favour of the data subject and/or other data subjects whose fundamental rights and freedoms that may be affected. It is obligatory to avoid the setting of procedures which are prejudicial to fundamental rights and freedoms. It is prudent and obligatory to avoid any data processing that may undermine the adequacy of data protection which exists within the Federal Republic of Nigeria. (2) Nothing in the NDP Act, this GAID, any legislation, or any legal instrument shall be deemed as authorising any form of data processing without compliance with Sections 37 and 45 of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. For ease of reference, the sections provide:  Section 37 CERN 1999: The privacy of citizens, their homes, correspondences, telephone conversations and telegraphic communications is hereby guaranteed and protected.  Section 45(1) CERN 1999: Nothing in sections 37, 38, 39, 40 and 41 of this Constitution shall invalidate any law that is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society. (3) In the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health; or (4) for the purpose of protecting the rights and freedom or other persons.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Assess whether data processing is truly necessary, by weighing the risks to individuals against any alternatives (e.g., less intrusive methods).  2. Apply a strong duty of care when processing personal data, ensuring that risks—especially unnecessary or disproportionate ones—are identified and reduced through high data protection standards.  3. Ensure data processing is proportionate, meaning: a) The scope and extent of the data you collect or use must be clearly aligned with the legitimate purpose you are pursuing (e.g., fraud prevention, customer onboarding). b) Do not create procedures or systems that violate or reduce the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects.  4. Avoid any processing that undermines the standard of data protection recognized under Nigerian law.  5. Recognize that no law, regulation, or internal policy gives you the right to process personal data unless it complies with the Nigerian Constitution, especially: a) Section 37: which guarantees the privacy of individuals and their communications. b) Section 45(1): which allows restrictions on privacy rights only where the law is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society, such as for national security, public health, or protection of others’ rights.
data_protection.riskDescription: Failure to demonstrate proportionality or care may invalidate lawful basis and expose the bank to claims.
data_protection.primaryControl: Lawful basis review as part of DPIA and RoPA maintenance.
data_protection.additionalControl: Periodic reassessment of lawful basis and risk impact.

data_protection.title: Reliance on Vital Interest
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller may rely on vital interest as a lawful basis for the processing of personal data, particularly when circumstances do not permit the data subject to give consent to the processing.  (2) The vital interest referred to in Sub-Article (1) of this Article may be that of the data subject or of a third party and it shall meet the conditions stipulated below:  a) The processing is necessary for the preservation or protection of life or livelihood and failure or refusal to act may be harmful to the data subject or a third party;  b) There is a legitimate expectation based on relationship or connection, operation of law, convention or prevailing norms that personal data should be processed in such circumstances of vital interest; and  c) The data controller or data processor may be called into question as being negligent, unprofessional or reckless for failing to carry out the data processing in such adverse circumstances in which a vital interest is in jeopardy.  (3) The method of processing employed for the purposes of vital interest shall be necessary and proportionate.  (4) The data controller shall give an account of its processing to the affected data subject, his or her representative in interest, or to a competent authority upon request.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Rely on the "vital interest" basis for data processing only where it is not possible to obtain the data subject’s consent, and where such processing is necessary to protect life or livelihood.   2. Ensure that the processing is necessary, proportionate, and justified by imminent harm or risk to the data subject or another party.  3. Confirm that a legitimate expectation exists (due to law, relationship, or norms) that the Bank should process data in such situations.   4. Be able to justify its actions and provide an account of the processing to the data subject, their representative, or a competent authority upon request.
data_protection.riskDescription: Misuse of “vital interest” may be seen as unjustified intrusion.
data_protection.primaryControl: Policy for when to invoke “vital interest” basis; log justification.
data_protection.additionalControl: Internal approval before applying this basis.

data_protection.title: Reliance on Public Interest
data_protection.description: (1) Public interest may be relied upon as a lawful basis of data processing in circumstances where there is:  (a) a public health or humanitarian emergency; or  (b) there is a clear and present danger to public safety; or  (c) there is a need also address direction of destination or deprivation for the benefit of the data subject. In furtherance of the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy or Sustainable Development Goals.  (2) In addition to other obligations that may be imposed under the NDP Act, in any regulatory instrument issued by the Commission and any other legislation, a data controller shall take into account the safeguards in the provisions of Article 23 of this GAID when carrying out data processing on the ground of public interest.  (3) The method of processing employed for the purposes of public interest shall be necessary and proportionate.  (4) Article 23 of this GAID regarding the evaluation of legal obligation shall also apply to the evaluation of public interest when it is relied upon as a lawful basis of data processing.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Rely on public interest as a lawful basis for data processing only in cases of public health/humanitarian emergencies, public safety threats, or in pursuit of national policy goals (e.g., SDGs).   2. Apply all safeguards under Article 23 when processing on the basis of public interest.   3. Ensure that the processing is necessary and proportionate to the public interest objective.   4. Evaluate the basis for public interest using similar criteria as for legal obligation (Article 23).
data_protection.riskDescription: Overreliance or unjustified use of public interest can violate privacy rights and result in NDPC sanctions.
data_protection.primaryControl: Justify basis via DPIA; log reasoning and safeguards.
data_protection.additionalControl: Compliance review before invoking this basis.

data_protection.title: Reliance on Legitimate Interest
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller shall cautiously consider reliance on legitimate interest as a lawful basis for data processing and shall be required in a compliance audit to show the basis of its preference. A template of a Legitimate Interest Assessment is in Schedule 8.  (2) Section 25 (2) of the NDP Act makes compatibility with contract, vital interest, legal obligation or public interest, a basis for reliance on legitimate interest. Accordingly, it shall be mandatory for a data controller under the circumstances to: a) Carry out Legitimate Interest Assessment (as prescribed in Schedule 8) before embarking on data processing; b) Priorities privacy by design and by default – taking into consideration the suitability of anonymisation or pseudonymisation; c) Identify and document the lawful basis of processing which is compatible with the legitimate interest process; d) Identify and eliminate data processing that may overreach the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects – particularly such processing that may lead to behavioural monitoring or profiling, or lead to targeted advertisement by third parties or partners; e) Identify and eliminate data processing that may lead to a breach of data confidentiality, integrity and availability – taking into account vulnerable data subjects; f) Provide transparent information to data subjects in accordance with Section 27 of the NDP Act; g) Provide for prompt remediation of data subjects’ rights; and h) Priorities data ethics and utmost duty of care.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Be very careful before using “legitimate interest” as a reason for collecting or using someone’s personal data.  2. Be ready to explain and show why this reason was chosen, especially during audits. The bank must use the official Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) template to do this.  3. Only use legitimate interest if it clearly supports a contract, legal duty, public good, or protects someone’s life or safety.  4. Always carry out a Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) before using this reason for data processing.  5. Build privacy protections into its systems and processes right from the start (“privacy by design”) and use techniques like data masking (anonymisation or pseudonymisation) where possible.  6. Clearly write down the reason (lawful basis) for collecting or using personal data, and make sure it fits with the legitimate interest.  7. Stop any kind of data processing that: a) Tracks people’s behaviour or profiles them, b) Sends targeted ads through third parties, c) May harm vulnerable people or go against their basic rights.  8. Avoid anything that may weaken the security, accuracy, or availability of personal data.  9. Tell people clearly and openly how their data is being used, following the rules in Section 27 of the NDPA.  10. Fix any issues quickly if someone’s data rights are affected.  11. Always treat personal data with care, fairness, and high ethical standards.
data_protection.riskDescription: Failure to perform LIA may render processing unlawful, especially for profiling, advertising, or behavioural data.
data_protection.primaryControl: Standard LIA template (from Schedule 8); incorporate into data protection risk reviews.
data_protection.additionalControl: Annual audits of all legitimate interest-based processing.

data_protection.title: Consideration Regarding Information to Data Subjects
data_protection.description: (1) Provision of information to a data subject shall be in accordance with Section 27 of the NDP Act. The information shall be clear and shall take into consideration vulnerable data subjects.  (2) In circumstances of exclusive physical events, interviews or interactions where a data controller or data processor may not be able to provide data subjects with a privacy policy or if provided, the class of data subjects may not be able to understand the privacy policy without the aid of an interpreter, the data controller or data processor shall provide the information in the form that the data subject can understand.  (3) The information to be provided by the data controller or data processor includes but is not limited to the following:  a) The name of the data controller or data processor,  b) Lawful basis of data processing,  c) Types of personal data to be collected,  d) The purpose of the processing,  e) The means of processing,  f) Access to personal data by authorised third parties,  g) Purpose of access by third parties,  h) Data subject's rights,  i) Access to prompt internal remediation through contact to be supplied by the data controller or data processor, and  j) Right to lodge a complaint with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.  (4) Information to data subjects does not constitute a request for consent. Consent shall be specifically requested and obtained when it is required by law and on the ground that the information which may guide the data subject in making an informed decision has been duly provided prior to the processing of personal data.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Provide clear and understandable privacy information to data subjects, in line with Section 27 of the NDP Act, especially considering vulnerable groups.  2. Where events or interactions prevent traditional delivery of privacy notices (e.g., physical meetings or interviews), ensure information is given in a format that the data subject can understand, including using interpreters if needed.  3. Clearly disclose to data subjects:  a) The bank’s identity as data controller or processor;  b) The lawful basis for data collection and processing;  c) The types of personal data to be collected;  d) The specific purpose of the data processing;  e) The method or means of data processing;  f) Any authorised third parties with access to the data;  g) The reason such third parties need access;  h) The data subject’s rights under the Act;  i) Internal contact details for addressing data subject complaints and remediation; and  j) The right to lodge a complaint with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.  4. Ensure that the provision of this information does not amount to requesting consent unless the law requires consent, in which case separate and informed consent must be obtained.
data_protection.riskDescription: Omission or unclear communication may breach transparency obligations and reduce informed consent validity.
data_protection.primaryControl: Privacy notices on all forms, apps, websites; translated or simplified where necessary.
data_protection.additionalControl: Use layered privacy notices and automated acknowledgment.

data_protection.title: Data Privacy Impact Assessment
data_protection.description: (1) A Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) is mandated under Section 28 of the NDP Act when data processing may likely result in high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject by virtue of its nature, scope, context, and purposes.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall conduct a DPIA whenever data processing may result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals based on the nature, scope, context, or purpose of the processing.
data_protection.riskDescription: Failure to perform or submit DPIA can result in NDPC restriction on digital banking platforms.
data_protection.primaryControl: Conduct DPIA using certified DPO; follow Schedule 4; obtain NDPC acknowledgment.
data_protection.additionalControl: Use automated DPIA checklists during project launch reviews.

data_protection.description: (2) Introduction of new technologies or new processing techniques or directives mandating processing of personal data on a large scale requires a DPIA on the following grounds:  (a) Unintended, adverse consequences to the lives and livelihoods of data subjects may result from the data processing;  (b) Such adverse consequences are threats to fundamental rights and freedoms as well as to the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy - which Policy forms the basis of sustainable development, security and economic programmes of government; and  (c) In circumstances where data processing measures constitute a derogation from Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution, they shall comply with the safeguards under Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution. data_protection.title: Monitoring, Evaluation and Maintenance of Data Security System
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller or data processor shall have schedules for monitoring, evaluation and maintenance of data security systems.  (2) The schedules shall take into account people, processes and technologies involved in data security and each shall contain applicable technical and organisational measures including but not limited to: (a) Training; (b) Certifications; (c) Updates of software; (d) Vulnerability tests of databases; (e) Assessment of hardware for repairs or replacements; (f) Authentication checks; (g) Encryption reviews; and (h) Quality Assurance on products and services being used for data confidentiality, integrity and availability.  (3) A data controller or data processor shall assign relevant officers to carry out the tasks under the schedule and stipulate time to take appropriate technical and organisational measures under the schedule.  (4) The schedule shall be vetted and certified by a duly certified information security officer.  (5) Notwithstanding the schedule, a data controller or data processor shall carry out monitoring, evaluation and maintenance of data security systems as frequently as possible, taking into account the risks of data processing.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Develop and maintain formal schedules for monitoring, evaluating, and maintaining data security systems.  2. Ensure the schedules address the Bank’s people, processes, and technology, and include the following: (a) Staff training programs; (b) Obtaining and maintaining relevant data security certifications; (c) Regular updates to all software used for data processing or protection; (d) Conduct periodic vulnerability tests on all databases; (e) Assess and maintain hardware—repair or replace as needed; (f) Implement strong authentication checks for access control; (g) Conduct periodic reviews of encryption tools and practices; (h) Perform quality assurance on all systems and tools used for data confidentiality, integrity, and availability.  3. Assign specific officers to be responsible for each activity in the schedule and set timelines for completing the required security tasks.  4.Have the entire schedule reviewed and certified by a qualified and certified information security officer.  5. In addition to the schedule, carry out regular (and as-needed) monitoring, evaluation, and maintenance of data security systems based on the level of data processing risks.
data_protection.riskDescription: Security incidents, data breaches, or regulatory penalties due to poor maintenance or oversight of data protection systems.
data_protection.responsibility: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), IT Risk Team
data_protection.primaryControl: Existing IT audit plans, patch management protocols, training schedules
data_protection.additionalControl: Quarterly cybersecurity reviews; external audit of InfoSec plan; automated monitoring tools

data_protection.description: (1) A dats contlle rs data processor shall prepare and spent an organisational schedule fr inka seston sd ang on pvc.  (2) The schedule shall contain a mode of evaluating the level of compliance with the NDP Act, this GAID and other regulatory instruments issued by the Commission.  (3) In respect of people, a data controller or data processor may adopt the use of meetings, questionnaires and interviews.  (4) This schedule shall be used to identify: (a) Data processing practices to stop, (b) Data processing practices to start, and (c) Data processing practices to continue.  (5) A data controller or a data processor shall publish the schedule on appropriate communication mediums where employees and other relevant workers, agents, and contractors, who are engaged in relevant activities may see it.  (6) A data controller or data processor shall: (a) Review its data processing platforms, (b) Assign relevant officers to carry out the tasks under the schedule, and (c) Singulate time for implement appropriate technical and organisational measures.  (7) In order to enable persons engaged in data processing to understand their duties and responsibilities, a data controller or data processor shall develop a basic privacy checklist as a guide.  (8) A data controller or data processor shall develop and implement a written policy for routine checks on compliance practices which may be carried out without notice to employees. This policy may be part of a larger data governance policy of the data controller or data processor.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Develop and implement a structured internal training and sensitisation schedule on data privacy for staff and relevant parties.  2. Include in the schedule a clear method for evaluating how well employees comply with the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA), the GAID, and any other relevant data protection rules issued by regulators.  3. Use tools such as staff meetings, questionnaires, and interviews to assess knowledge and awareness among employees.  4. Use the results of sensitisation to identify: (a) Data practices that should be stopped; (b) New data practices to be adopted; (c) Existing data practices to be maintained  5. Publish the sensitisation and training schedule on internal platforms (e.g. intranet, notice boards, email bulletins) accessible to employees, contractors, and other relevant personnel.  6. (a) Review and assess current data processing systems and tools; (b) Assign designated officers to implement items in the schedule; (c) Set specific timelines for completing the required technical and organisational tasks.  7. Create a basic privacy checklist to help employees understand their roles and responsibilities regarding data protection.  8. Develop and enforce a written policy for routine, unannounced compliance checks. This can be part of a broader data governance policy.

data_protection.title: Deployment of a Data Processing Software by a Data Controller or Data Processor
data_protection.description: (1)A data controller or a data processor who (whether for itself or for other persons) deploy or intends to deploy data processing software for the purposes of tracking a data subject or enabling a communication link with a data subject and processing his or her personal data, is under an obligation to abide by the provisions of the NDP Act.  (2)For the purposes of complying with this GAID and in addition to other obligations imposed on a data controller or a data processor, it is mandatory for the data controller or data processor in the circumstances referred to in Article 31 (1) to: a) Carry out a DPIA before the deployment of the software; b) Ensure that the software is designed in accordance with the principles of privacy by design and by default; c) Without prejudice to any contrary provisions of the NDP Act or regulatory instruments issued immediately, ensure that the software follows data security guidelines or instructions provided in the stores where the software may be downloaded; d) Provide data privacy policy within the software; e) Provide a privacy statement to data subjects (prospective users) prior to installation -- expressly indicating the following: i. The types of personal data to be processed (types to be supplied by the data controller or data processor); ii. The lawful purpose for processing the personal data (lawful purpose to be supplied by the data controller or data processor); iii. data_protection.title: Measures Against Privacy Breach Abatement
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller or data processor shall put in place, appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent the use of its platform, facility, network or howsoever called, from being used to breach the privacy of a data subject. (2) When the Commission notifies a data controller or data processor that is platform, facility, network or howsoever called is being used by any person to commit an offence under the NDP Act or to carry out a breach of privacy, the data controller or data processor shall immediately restrict such person on its platform, facility or network, pending the outcome of an investigation by the Commission.  (4) Where a data controller or data processor fails, refuses or neglects to carry out the directive of the Commission to prevent further breach of privacy, the data controller or data processor shall be deemed as abetting a breach of privacy and shall be accountable for violations of the NDP Act as if it directly committed a breach of data privacy.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that its systems, platforms, and networks cannot be used to violate the privacy of any individual.  2. If the Commission notifies the Bank that its systems are being used to breach data privacy or commit an offence under the NDPA, the Bank must immediately restrict the person responsible from further access, while an investigation is ongoing.  3. If the Bank fails, refuses, or neglects to carry out the Commission’s directive to stop a privacy breach, it will be considered as if the Bank itself committed the breach and will be held accountable under the NDPA.
data_protection.riskDescription: Regulatory liability if platform used for breach and no action taken.
data_protection.primaryControl: Incident handling protocol; platform monitoring.
data_protection.additionalControl: Real-time alert system and NDPC response SOP.

data_protection.title: Data Breach Notification
data_protection.description: (1) The NDP Act under Section 40(2) provides that "a data controller shall, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach which is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, notify the Commission of the breach and, where feasible, describe the nature of the personal data breach including the categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and personal data records concerned."  (2) A breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals if, considering the nature of the breach, the personal data involved as well as the probability of accessing other personal data of the data subject through the breach, he/she subject may become a victim of fraud, identity theft or exposure of sensitive personal data.  (3) In line with Section 40(2) of the NDP Act, a data controller shall notify affected data subjects immediately after becoming aware of the breach in order to ensure that data subjects are not unlawfully targeted as a result of the breach. This is in furtherance of the principle of duty of care and accountability.  (4) Notwithstanding the time provided for the notification of a data breach, a data controller or data processor shall exercise a duty of care by providing immediate information on data breach to all relevant authorities including the Commission, if such immediate information may help in containing imminent data breaches on a national scale or when containment measures may be necessary at national, sectoral or at an individual level or where it may affect members of the general public.  (5) The content of a data breach notification to the Commission shall include the following among others: a) A description of the circumstances of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; b) The date or time period during which the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure occurred; c) A description of the personal information involved in the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; d) An assessment of the risk of harm to individuals as a result of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; e) An estimate of the number of individuals to whom there is a real risk of significant harm as a result of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; f) A description of steps the organisation has taken to reduce the risk of harm to individuals; g) A description of any steps the organisation has taken to notify individuals of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosures; and h) The time and contact information of a person who can answer on behalf of the organisation, the Commission's questions regarding the loss of unauthorised access or disclosure of personal data.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall: 1, Notify the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) within 72 hours of becoming aware of any personal data breach likely to pose a risk to data subjects’ rights and freedoms.   2. Assess if a breach poses high risk (e.g., risk of fraud, identity theft, or exposure of sensitive data) based on the breach nature and type of data involved.  3. Notify affected data subjects immediately after confirming a breach that puts their rights or freedoms at high risk.  4. Report a data breach immediately (not waiting for 72 hours) if early notice may help prevent or contain wider data breaches, especially those with national or sector-wide impact.  5. Notify the NDPC which include all required details (e.g., nature of breach, dates, affected data types, estimated affected individuals, harm risk, mitigation steps, contact person).
data_protection.deadlineType: Within 72 hours of breach detection, or immediately if national impact is possible
data_protection.riskDescription: Delay or failure in notifying data breaches can result in regulatory sanctions, loss of trust, lawsuits from affected data subjects, and reputational harm.
data_protection.primaryControl: - Incident response plan- Breach detection system- Pre-approved breach notification templates
data_protection.additionalControl: - Regular training on breach response- Breach response simulation drills- Escalation matrix for breach alerts

data_protection.title: Data Processing Agreement
data_protection.description: (1) In line with Section 29(2) of the NDP Act, a data processor is expected to rely on a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) with the data controller in order to carry out data processing on behalf of the data controller.  (2) In addition to other relevant terms and conditions as may be prescribed by law, a DPA shall include the following: a) Obligations of the data controller and data processor under Section 29 of the NDP Act; b) Name of parties; c) Addresses of parties; d) Recitals containing reference to any Principal Agreement or Service Level Agreement; e) Purpose of data processing; f) Location of data processing (taking into account the provisions of the NDP Act on cross-border data transfer); g) Scope of the processing; h) Lawful uses of data processing; i) Responsibilities of parties under the DPA; j) Technical and Organisational Measures for data protection (if highly technical or scientific, it should be expressly outlined in a schedule to the DPA); k) The outcome of a DPA where relevant; l) Potential risks; m) NDP Act compliance (evidence of registration with the Commission should be ascertained); n) Confidentiality; o) Tenure; p) Specific Restrictions; q) Indemnity; r) Insurance; s) Force Majeures; and t) Dispute Resolution.  (3)  A party to any DPA other than an individual data subject, shall take reasonable measures to ensure that the other party is compliant under the NDP Act, accountable to the Commission or, in the case of a foreign party, to a competent regulatory authority outside Nigeria; accordingly, every data controller or data processor shall  be accountable for the actions or inactions of third parties it engages or permits to carry out data processing.   (4) Where a party to an agreement operates as a sole proprietorship, an individual agent or a self-employed worker, by reason of which he or she may not be organised to fulfil  the obligations of corporate entities, such a person or individual shall for the purposes of his or her engagement in high-risk data processing, be required to be trained in data protection and privacy. Evidence of training and registration as a data processor of major importance shall be relied upon as a rebuttable proof of compliance with the NDP Act.
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Enter into a written Data Processing Agreement (DPA) with every third-party data processor it engages to process personal data on its behalf.  2. Ensure each DPA includes the following key terms: a) The legal obligations of both the bank (as data controller) and the processor under Section 29 of the NDPA. b) Names and addresses of both parties. c) A reference to any Principal Agreement or Service Level Agreement (if applicable). d) The purpose, scope, and lawful basis for the data processing. e) The location where processing will occur, especially for cross-border data transfers. f) Clear allocation of responsibilities between the bank and the processor. g) Detailed technical and organizational data protection measures, including a schedule if technical. h) Clear allocation of responsibilities between the bank and the processor. i) Detailed technical and organizational data protection measures, including a schedule if technical. j) Risk assessments and outcome expectations of the processing. k) Confirmation that the processor is registered with the NDPC. l) Confidentiality clauses. m) Duration of the agreement. n) Any restrictions, indemnity clauses, insurance coverage, force majeure provisions, and dispute resolution mechanisms.  3. Verify that any party it contracts with (local or foreign): a) Is compliant with the NDPA or its equivalent (if outside Nigeria), b) Is accountable to a competent authority, and c) That the bank remains accountable for any action or inaction of such processors.  4.  Ensure that individual or sole proprietor processors (e.g., freelancers or agents) involved in high-risk data processing: a) Have received data protection and privacy training, and b) Are registered as a data processor of major importance, with proof retained for NDPA compliance verification.
data_protection.deadlineType: Prior to engagement and periodic review (e.g., annually)
data_protection.riskDescription: Unlawful processing or regulatory sanctions from insufficient third-party control or missing DPA terms.
data_protection.primaryControl: Contract templates; Legal review; Processor onboarding policy
data_protection.additionalControl: Annual DPA reviews; Central processor registry with training/registration tracking; Legal/Compliance approval checklist

data_protection.title: Benchmarking with Interoperable Data Privacy Measures
data_protection.description: (1) A data controller or data processor shall be cognisant of the need to advance data protection and privacy rights and the measures meticulously designed for this purpose in the globally interconnected and constantly evolving data protection ecosystem.  (2) In the event that a data controller, data processor is to take a decision on an applicable technical and organisational measure for safeguarding data privacy rights, it is legally imperative to take into account the provisions of the extant Fundamental Rights Enforcement Procedure Rules in Nigeria on the importance of municipal, regional and international bill of rights.  (3) In furtherance of Article 56 (1), (2), a data controller or data processor may, subject to the approval of the Commission, benchmark its data processing with Interoperable Data Privacy Measures (IDPMs) in circumstances where a specific directive is required by the Commission under the NDP Act.  (4) Where a data controller or data processor intends to benchmark with an IDPM which expressly requires directives of the Commission under the NDP Act, it shall seek the approval of the Commission through an application stating the following:  a) The name and address of the data controller or data processor,  b) The nature of business  c) The purpose and lawful bases of data processing,  d) The nature of data processing in which an IDPM is required,  e) The author and the jurisdiction of the IDPM being proposed for approval,  f) The benefit of the IDPM in data processing value chain,  g) The benefit of the IDPM to the ecosystem,  h) Three (3) use cases of the IDPM,  i) Any disadvantage of the IDPM, and  j) The name and contact details of its certified DPO.  ( (6) For the purposes of Article 15 (1) - (5), IDPM means best practice templates which are not limited by jurisdictional procedures and are particularly in finitenance of the NDP Act. Accordingly, instances where IDPM may be used include but are not limited  b) Automated Decision Making,  c) Child Online Protection,  d) Data Preliability,  e) Data Subject-Access Request,  f) Data Privacy Impact Assessment,  g) Deployment of Artificial Intelligence,  h) Encryption,  i) Promise Data Security Audit,  j) Legitimate Interest Assessment,  k) Pseudonymisation, and  l) Record of Processing Activities.  (7) Without prejudice to the provisions of the NDP Act and any regulatory instrument issued by the Commission a DPO is required to consider suitable IDPMs which maybe used by a data controller or a data processor as part of global best practices in data processing. Accordingly, it is appropriate for a DPO to proactively review IDPMs prior to when the need for them arises. The Commission shall continuously provide
data_protection.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Be aware of the evolving nature of global data privacy rights and adopt measures that reflect current global best practices in safeguarding personal data.  2. When choosing technical and organisational data protection measures, consider the Fundamental Rights Enforcement Procedure Rules in Nigeria, as well as applicable local, regional, and international bills of rights.  3.  IDPMs	With CBN/NITDA approval, the bank may benchmark its practices with Interoperable Data Privacy Measures (IDPMs) when the NDP Act requires specific regulatory direction.  4. If the bank wants to use an IDPM that requires Commission approval, it must submit a formal application including: a) Bank's name and address; b) Business nature; c) Purpose and lawful basis for processing; d) Description of processing where IDPM is required; e) Origin and jurisdiction of the proposed IDPM; f) Benefits to processing and the broader ecosystem; g) Three use cases of the IDPM; h) Any known disadvantages; i) Contact details of a certified DPO.  5. Be aware that IDPMs may be applicable to a range of activities, including but not limited to: • Automated decision-making • Child online protection • Data subject access requests • Data reliability • Data Privacy Impact Assessments (DPIA) • AI deployment • Encryption • Security audits • Legitimate interest assessments • Pseudonymisation • Records of processing activities  6. Ensure the DPO proactively reviews suitable IDPMs as part of global best practice in data protection, even before a need for them arises. The Commission will provide ongoing guidance in this regard.
data_protection.riskDescription: Non-compliance with regulatory expectations on global best practices and rights-based data protection may lead to reputational damage, fines, or legal challenges.
data_protection.primaryControl: Existing privacy frameworks; awareness of international best practices
data_protection.additionalControl: IDPM review log maintained by DPO; Regular engagement with Commission on evolving IDPMs; Legal approval of IDPM-related applications
