crmp.title: Recording Identification Evidence
crmp.description: 36.—(1) Records of the supporting evidence and methods used to verify identity shall be retained for a minimum period of five years after the account is closed or the business relationship has ended.  (2) Where the supporting evidence cannot be copied at the time it was presented, the reference numbers and other relevant details of the identification evidence shall be recorded to enable the documents to be obtained later.  (3) Confirmation of evidence in sub-regulation (2) of this regulation shall be acceptable provided that the original documents were seen by certifying either on the photocopies or on the record that the details were taken down as evidence.  (4) Where checks are made electronically, a record of the actual information obtained or where it can be re-obtained shall be retained as part of the identification evidence.  (5) The record in sub-regulation (4) of this regulation shall make the production of the actual information that would have been obtained before, less cumbersome.
crmp.plain: 1.The Bank shall keep records of the documents and methods used to verify a customer’s identity for at least five years after the account is closed or the business relationship ends.  2.If the documents cannot be copied at the time they are presented, the Bank should record key details such as reference numbers and other identifying information so the documents can be obtained later.  3.It is acceptable to rely on these records if the original documents were seen and this was confirmed in writing—either on the copies or in the record itself.  4. If electronic checks are used, the Bank must keep a record of the actual information obtained or of where the information can be retrieved.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to retain proper records of customer identity verification may result in non-compliance with regulatory requirements, hinder investigations, and expose the Bank to legal penalties, reputational damage, and increased risk of financial crime.

crmp.title: Attention on Complex and Unusual Large Transactions
crmp.description: (1) Financial Institutions shall pay special attention to all complex, unusually large transactions or unusual patterns of transactions that have no visible economic or lawful purpose. (2) Financial Institutions shall investigate suspicious transactions and report its findings to the NFIU immediately, in compliance with the relevant provisions of the MLPPA. (3) For the purpose of sub-regulation (1) of this regulation, “complex or unusually large transactions” or “unusual pattern of transactions” include significant transactions relating to a relationship or transactions that exceed certain limits, very high account turnover inconsistent with the size of the balance or transactions which fall outside the regular pattern of the account’s activity.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Watch out for complex or unusually large transactions and any transaction patterns that seem abnormal or have no clear legal or economic reason. (2) Investigate these suspicious transactions thoroughly. (3) Report findings immediately to the Nigeria Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU). (4) Examples of such transactions include: – Transactions significantly larger than normal for that account. – High account turnover that doesn't match the account’s usual balance. – Any unusual activity that doesn’t align with the account’s known use.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to detect and report suspicious or abnormal transactions can result in aiding money laundering or terrorist financing and lead to regulatory penalties or reputational damage.
crmp.owner: Transaction Monitoring Unit, Compliance Department, Relationship Managers
crmp.primaryControl: - Deploy automated transaction monitoring systems with risk flags - Set account-specific transaction thresholds and alerts - Conduct manual reviews of flagged transactions - Maintain a suspicious transaction review log - Ensure prompt reporting to NFIU

crmp.title: Evidence of Suspicious Transaction Monitoring
crmp.description: 38.—(1) Where a transaction— (a) involves a frequency which is unjustifiable or unreasonable; (b) is surrounded by conditions of unusual or unjustified complexity; (c) appears to have no economic justification or lawful objective; or (d) in the opinion of the Financial Institution involves proceeds of criminal activity, unlawful act, ML, TF, PF or is inconsistent with the known transaction pattern of the account or business relationship; the transaction shall be deemed to be suspicious, regardless of the amount, and the Financial Institution shall seek information from the customer as to the origin and destination of the funds, the purpose of the transaction and the identity of the beneficiary. (2) Where a Financial Institution suspects that the funds mentioned under sub-regulation (1) of this regulation— (a) are derived from legal or illegal sources but are intended to be used for an act of terrorism; (b) are proceeds of a crime related to terrorism financing; (c) belong to a person, entity or organization considered as terrorists; or (d) are intended for financing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, it shall immediately and without delay report the matter to the NFIU and shall not be liable for violation of the confidentiality rules and banking secrecy obligations for any lawful action taken in furtherance of this obligation.  (3) Financial Institutions shall immediately and without delay; but not later than 24 hours— (a) draw up a written report containing all relevant information on the transaction, together with the identity of the principal and where applicable, of the beneficiary or beneficiaries; (b) take appropriate action to prevent the laundering of the proceeds of a crime, an illegal act or financing of terrorism; and (c) report to the NFIU any suspicious transaction, stating clearly the reasons for the suspicion and actions taken.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1)If a transaction: Happens more often than what is reasonable or normal; -Is unusually complicated without a clear reason; -Doesn’t seem to have a valid business or legal purpose; or -Appears to involve criminal activity, money laundering (ML), terrorism financing (TF), proliferation financing (PF), or doesn’t match the customer’s usual transaction pattern, then the Bank must treat it as suspicious, no matter how much money is involved. The Bank must also ask the customer for more details about the source and destination of the funds, the purpose of the transaction, and who the beneficiary is. (2) Immediately report to the NFIU (no delay) if it suspects that funds:  1. Are from any source (legal/illegal) but meant for terrorism;  2. Are proceeds of a crime related to terrorism financing;  3. Belong to a terrorist person, group, or entity;  4. Are meant for proliferation financing. The bank is protected from confidentiality or banking secrecy violation if reporting such suspicions. (3) Within 24 hours, the bank shall:  1. Prepare a written report with full transaction details and identities of involved persons;  2. Take steps to stop laundering, crime, or terrorism financing;  3. Report to the NFIU stating the reasons for suspicion and what was done.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to detect or report terrorism financing or proliferation transactions could lead to legal breaches, reputational damage, fines, and facilitation of terrorism.
crmp.owner: AML/CFT Compliance Officer, Transaction Monitoring Unit, IT Surveillance Team
crmp.primaryControl: - Automated monitoring system - Manual alert triggers - Escalation flow to Compliance - Immediate STR filing procedures - Staff whistleblowing protocol

crmp.title: Procedure for the Monitoring and Reporting of Suspicious Transactions
crmp.description: (1) Financial Institutions shall have a written Policy Framework that guides and enables its staff to monitor, recognize and respond appropriately to suspicious transactions in addition to the guidance issued by competent authorities. (2) Financial Institutions shall have ML, TF and PF monitoring systems in place which may be manual or automated and the monitoring system shall be documented, reviewed and updated regularly. (3) A Financial Institution shall appropriately designate an officer as the AML, CFT and CPF Compliance Officer to supervise the monitoring and reporting of terrorism financing and suspicious transactions, among other duties. (4) Financial Institutions shall be alert to the various patterns of conduct that are known to be suggestive of ML, TF and PF and shall maintain and disseminate a checklist of such transactions to the relevant staff. (5) When any staff of a Financial Institution detects any “red flag” or suspicious ML, TF and PF activity, the institution shall promptly institute a “Review Panel” under the supervision of the Compliance Officer and every action taken shall be recorded. (6) Financial Institutions and their staff shall maintain confidentiality in respect of any investigation conducted in pursuance of these Regulations and any suspicious transaction report that may be filed with the NFIU consistent with the provision of the MLPPA and TPPA and shall not say anything that might “tip off” any person or entity that is under suspicion of ML, TF or PF. (7) A Financial Institution that suspects or has reason to suspect that funds are the proceeds of a criminal activity or are related to terrorism financing shall promptly report its suspicions to the NFIU. (8) All suspicious transactions, including attempted transactions are to be reported regardless of the amount involved. (9) The requirement to report suspicious transactions applies regardless of whether they are considered to involve tax matters or other matters. (10) Financial Institutions, their directors, officers and employees whether permanent or temporary, are prohibited from disclosing the fact that a report of a transaction shall be or has been filed with the competent authorities. (11) In compliance with the TPPA, Financial Institutions shall forward to the NFIU without delay but not later than 24 hours, reports of suspicious transactions relating to— (a) funds derived from illegal or legal sources that are intended to be used for any act of terrorism; (b) proceeds of a crime related to terrorism financing; or (c) proceeds belonging to a terrorist, terrorist entity or organization.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall:  1.Have a written policy that helps staff detect, monitor, and respond to suspicious transactions, in line with regulatory guidance. 2.Put in place systems—manual or automated—to monitor for money laundering (ML), terrorism financing (TF), and proliferation financing (PF); and ensure these systems are regularly reviewed and updated. 3.Appoint a Compliance Officer responsible for overseeing AML/CFT/CPF monitoring, reporting suspicious activity, and related duties. 4.Educate staff on known warning signs of ML, TF, and PF by maintaining and sharing a checklist of suspicious patterns. 5.Immediately set up a Review Panel, led by the Compliance Officer, when any staff detects a red flag or suspicious activity, and document every step taken. 6.Keep all investigations and reports confidential and ensure no one “tips off” a person or group under suspicion. 7.Promptly report any suspicion that funds are linked to crime or terrorism financing to the NFIU. 8.Report all suspicious transactions—including attempted ones—no matter the amount. 9.Submit suspicious transaction reports even if the matter relates to tax or other non-terrorism issues. 10.Ensure no staff, whether permanent or temporary, reveals that a suspicious transaction report has been or will be filed. 11.In line with the Terrorism Prevention laws, send suspicious transaction reports to the NFIU within 24 hours when: a)The funds are linked to any planned or actual terrorist act (even if the source is legal), b)The money is the result of crime tied to terrorism, or c)The funds belong to a terrorist, terrorist group, or organization.
crmp.riskDescription: If the bank fails to monitor or report suspicious activity, criminals may exploit the system to launder money or finance terrorism, which can result in regulatory sanctions, legal consequences, and reputational damage.
crmp.owner: Compliance Department, Operations Team, Frontline Staff, Chief Compliance Officer
crmp.primaryControl: - Written suspicious transaction monitoring and reporting policy - Automated transaction monitoring tools - Checklist of known red flags and typologies - Prompt review and escalation by Compliance Officer - STR reporting workflow integrated into core systems - Staff confidentiality agreement and awareness

crmp.title: Other Forms of Reporting
crmp.description: (1) Financial Institutions shall report in writing any single transaction, lodgment or transfer of funds in excess of N5,000,000 and N10,000,000 or their equivalent made by an individual and corporate body respectively to the NFIU in accordance with the MLPPA.  (2) Financial Institutions shall render reports in writing on transfers to or from a foreign country of funds or securities by a person or body corporate, of a sum exceeding US$10,000 or its equivalent to CBN, and the NFIU within 7 days from the date of the transaction.  (3) Money Service Business shall render reports in writing on transfers to or from a foreign country of funds or securities by a person or body corporate, of a sum exceeding US$5,000 or its equivalent to CBN and the NFIU within 7 days from the date of the transaction.  (4) Financial Institutions shall render reports in writing on domestic transfers involving foreign currencies by a person or body corporate, of a sum exceeding US$10,000 or its equivalent to CBN, and the NFIU within 7 days from the date of the transaction.  (5) Details of a report sent by a Financial Institution to the NFIU shall not be disclosed by the Financial Institution or any of its officers to any other person including the principal and beneficiaries of the transaction.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Report in writing to the NFIU any single transaction, deposit, or fund transfer exceeding:  - ₦5,000,000 for individuals  - ₦10,000,000 for corporate entities.  (2) Report to the CBN and NFIU within 7 days any transfer of funds or securities exceeding US$10,000 (or equivalent) to/from a foreign country by an individual or company.  (3) Ensure Money Service Businesses must report within 7 days to CBN and NFIU any transfer to/from a foreign country exceeding US$5,000 (or equivalent).  (4) Report within 7 days to CBN and NFIU any domestic transfer involving foreign currency exceeding US$10,000 (or equivalent).  (5) Not disclose details of any report sent to the NFIU to anyone, including the person who conducted or benefited from the transaction.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to report large or foreign-linked transactions could lead to non-compliance with statutory obligations, regulatory sanctions, and exposure to money laundering or terrorism financing activities.

crmp.title: AML, CFT and CPF Employee Awareness and Training Programme
crmp.description: (1) Financial Institutions shall design comprehensive training programmes for board members, management and staff to establish full awareness of their obligations and also to equip them with relevant skills required for the effective discharge of their AML, CFT and CPF tasks. (2) The timing, coverage and content of the employee training programme shall be tailored to meet the needs of the Financial Institution to ensure compliance with the requirements and provisions of these Regulations. (3) Financial Institutions shall provide comprehensive training programmes for staff covering compliance officers and as part of the orientation programmes for new staff and those posted to the front office, banking operations and branch office staff, particularly cashiers, account opening, mandate, and marketing staff, internal control and audit staff. (4) Financial Institutions shall render quarterly returns on their level of compliance on its education and training programmes to the CBN. (5) An AML, CFT and CPF training programme shall be developed under the guidance of the Compliance Officer in collaboration with top Management.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Develop full training programs for board members, management, and staff to help them understand and perform their AML/CFT/CPF duties effectively. (2) Tailor the training content, schedule, and scope to fit the bank’s specific needs. (3) Include training for Compliance Officers and ensure it is part of onboarding for new staff, especially frontline roles (e.g., cashiers, account opening, marketing, internal control, audit). (4) Submit quarterly reports to the CBN on how well training programs are being implemented. (5) Ensure the AML/CFT/CPF training plan is devel/oped by the Compliance Officer in collaboration with senior management.
crmp.riskDescription: Without ongoing training, staff may fail to detect or properly handle suspicious activity, leading to regulatory breaches, missed red flags, and increased ML/TF/PF exposure.
crmp.owner: Compliance Officer, Human Resources (HR), Training Department, Departmental Heads
crmp.primaryControl: - Documented AML/CFT/CPF training policy - Scheduled onboarding and refresher trainings - Training attendance records - Role-specific training modules - Quarterly compliance reporting to CBN - Management review of training effectiveness

crmp.title: Monitoring of Employee Conduct
crmp.description: (1) Financial Institutions shall monitor the conduct of their employees to ensure compliance with AML, CFT and CPF policies and procedures. (2) Financial Institutions shall establish mechanisms to detect and report any suspicious activities or breaches of internal controls by employees. (3) Any employee found to be in violation of AML, CFT and CPF regulations shall be subject to disciplinary actions, including termination and reporting to relevant authorities where necessary.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Monitor how staff behave to make sure they are following AML policies and procedures. (2) Set up systems to detect and report any suspicious staff activities or policy violations. (3) Discipline any employee who breaks AML/CFT/CPF rules. This may include termination and reporting them to authorities.
crmp.riskDescription: If staff are not monitored, they may aid or overlook money laundering or terrorist financing, risking internal fraud, regulatory breaches, and reputational damage.
crmp.owner: Compliance Department, Internal Control/Audit, HR, Line Managers
crmp.primaryControl: - Whistleblowing policy and reporting channels - Internal control mechanisms - Surveillance systems/log review - Disciplinary procedures - Regular staff conduct reviews - Monitoring logs

crmp.title: Protection of Staff Who Report Violation
crmp.description: (1) Financial Institutions shall ensure that employees who report violations or suspicious activities in good faith are protected from retaliation, discrimination, or any form of victimization. (2) Confidentiality shall be maintained regarding the identity of the reporting employee, except where disclosure is required by law. (3) Employees shall not be liable for any civil or criminal proceedings arising from their reports made in compliance with these Regulations.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Protect staff who report violations or suspicious activities in good faith from retaliation or victimization. (2) Keep the identity of whistleblowers confidential unless the law requires disclosure. (3) Ensure such employees are not punished or held liable for reporting in line with AML/CFT/CPF rules.
crmp.riskDescription: If whistleblowers are not protected, staff may fear reporting suspicious activities, increasing the risk of undetected ML/TF/PF activities.

crmp.title: Client Accounts Opened by Professional Intermediaries
crmp.description: 51.—(1) Stockbrokers, fund managers, solicitors, accountants, estate agents and other intermediaries frequently hold funds on behalf of their clients in “client accounts” opened with Financial Institutions.  (2) Accounts in sub-regulation (1) of this regulation may be general omnibus accounts holding the funds of many clients or they may be opened specifically for a single client.  (3) In each case, it is the professional intermediary who is the Financial Institution’s customer and this situation shall be distinguished from those where an intermediary introduces a client who himself becomes a customer of the Financial Institution.  (4) Where a professional intermediary is covered or supervised for compliance to AML, CFT or CPF, identification may be waived on production of evidence.  (5) Notwithstanding sub-regulation (4) of this regulation, where the professional intermediary is not supervised for AML, CFT or CPF and does not have measures for compliance with CDD and record-keeping requirements, the Financial Institution shall verify the identities of the professional intermediary and the person on whose behalf it is acting.  (6) Where it is impossible for Financial Institutions to establish the identity of the person for whom a solicitor or accountant is acting, it shall take a commercial decision based on its knowledge of the intermediary, as to the nature and extent of business that they are prepared to conduct where the professional firm is not itself covered by these Regulations.  (7) Financial Institutions shall make reasonable enquiries about transactions passing through client-accounts that give cause for concern and shall report any suspicion to the NFIU.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall:  1.Recognize that professionals like stockbrokers, fund managers, lawyers, accountants, estate agents, and others often hold money for their clients in “client accounts” opened at the Bank.  2.Understand that these accounts may either hold funds for multiple clients (omnibus accounts) or be dedicated to one client.  3.Treat the professional intermediary (e.g., the lawyer or accountant) as the Bank’s customer, unless the client they introduce becomes a direct customer of the Bank.  4.Accept valid proof of identity from intermediaries who are supervised for AML/CFT/CPF compliance and allow for simplified identification in such cases.  5.When the intermediary is not supervised for AML/CFT/CPF or lacks proper customer due diligence and record-keeping systems, the Bank must verify the identities of both the intermediary and the actual client they are representing.  6.If it is not possible to confirm the identity of the person on whose behalf the intermediary is acting, the Bank must make a careful business decision based on its knowledge of the intermediary and the type of transactions they typically handle.  7.Monitor transactions in these client accounts, investigate anything unusual, and report any suspicious activity to the NFIU without delay.

crmp.title: Unincorporated Business or Partnership
crmp.description: (1) For unincorporated businesses or partnerships, Financial Institutions shall verify the identity of all partners or owners and obtain evidence of the business’s legal existence. (2) Evidence of the address of a business or partnership shall be obtained and where a current account is being opened, a visit to the place of business may be made to confirm the true nature of the business activities and a copy of the latest report or audited accounts shall be obtained. (3) The nature of the business or partnership shall be verified to ensure that it has a legitimate purpose. (4) Where a formal partnership arrangement exists, a mandate from the partnership authorizing the opening of an account or undertaking of the transaction shall be obtained.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Verify identities of all owners/partners and confirm legal existence of the business. (2) Get the business address and possibly visit the location; obtain latest report or audited accounts if opening a current account. (3) Confirm the business has a legitimate purpose. (4) Get a mandate from the partnership if it is formally structured.
crmp.riskDescription: Unverified unincorporated entities may be used for money laundering or shell operations due to poor ownership transparency.
crmp.owner: Account Opening Team, Compliance Officer, Relationship Managers
crmp.primaryControl: - Mandatory KYC forms for each partner - Verification of business location - Review of audited accounts - Mandate authorization for partnership accounts

crmp.title: Pure Corporate Customers
crmp.description: 54.—(1) The legal existence of an applicant-company shall be verified from official documents or sources to ensure that persons purporting to act on its behalf are fully authorized.  (2) Where the controlling principals cannot be identified, enquiries shall be made to confirm that the legal person is not merely a “brass-plate company”.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Confirm that a company applying to open an account is legally registered by checking official documents or sources, and ensure that the people claiming to represent the company are properly authorized. (2) If the individuals who control the company cannot be clearly identified, the Bank shall investigate further to ensure the company is real and not just a shell company with no actual business activity.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to verify the legal existence and controlling individuals of an applicant-company may expose the Bank to the risk of dealing with shell companies used for money laundering, fraud, or other illicit activities, resulting in regulatory breaches and reputational harm.
crmp.primaryControl: Current corporate account onboarding checklist; CAC search; beneficial ownership registry checks

crmp.title: The Identity of  corporate company
crmp.description: 55.—(1) The identity of a corporate company shall comprise of—  (a) CAC registration number; (b) registered corporate name and any trading names used; (c) registered address and any separate principal trading addresses; (d) directors (including their BVN); (e) owners and shareholders; (f) the nature of the company’s business. (g) Tax Identification Number (TIN); and (h) Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering (SCUML) registration (number, certificate or approval) for DNFBPs.  (2) The extent of identification measures required to validate the information or the documentary evidence to be obtained in this regulation depends on the nature of the business or service that the company requires from the Financial Institution and a risk-based approach shall be taken.  (3) Information as to the nature of the normal business activities that the company expects to undertake with the Financial Institution shall be obtained.  (4) Before a business relationship is established, measures shall be taken by way of company search at the CAC and other commercial enquiries undertaken to check that the applicant-company’s legal existence has not been or is not in the process of being dissolved, struck off, wound up or terminated.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Collect and verify key details to confirm the identity of any corporate customer. This includes:     * CAC registration number    * Registered and trading names    * Business and trading addresses    * Names and BVNs of directors    * Names of owners and shareholders    * Nature of the company’s business    * Tax Identification Number (TIN)    * SCUML registration (if applicable, for DNFBPs)  2. Apply a risk-based approach to decide how much verification is needed, depending on the type of services the company wants from the Bank.  3. Obtain information about the company’s usual or expected business activities with the Bank.  4. Before starting any business relationship, check with the CAC and other relevant sources to confirm that the company is legally active and not dissolved, closed down, or under termination.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to properly verify the identity and legal status of a corporate customer exposes the Bank to significant risks, including onboarding shell companies or entities involved in money laundering, terrorism financing, or other illicit activities. Inadequate due diligence may result in regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, and financial loss.
crmp.primaryControl: Corporate account KYC checklist; CAC search process; beneficial ownership verification; SCUML validation

crmp.title: Non Face -to Face  Business
crmp.description: (1) Additional procedures shall be undertaken to ensure that the applicant’s business, company or society exists at the address provided and it is for a legitimate purpose because of the risks with non-face-to-face business, as with the requirements for private individuals.  (2) Where the characteristics of the product or service permit, steps shall be taken to ensure that relevant evidence is obtained to confirm that any individual representing the company has the necessary authority to do so.  (3) Where the principal owners, controllers or signatories need to be identified within the relationship, the relevant requirements for the identification of personal customers shall be followed.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Take extra steps to confirm that the applicant’s business, company, or society actually exists at the address provided and is being used for a genuine purpose—especially when the relationship is not established face-to-face.  2. Where the product or service allows, obtain evidence that any person acting on behalf of the company is properly authorised to do so.  3. Apply the same identity verification requirements used for individual customers to identify the main owners, controllers, or signatories of the company.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to verify the existence, purpose, and authorized representatives of non-face-to-face or corporate applicants increases the risk of onboarding shell companies, fraudulent entities, or unauthorized individuals. This exposes the Bank to potential misuse for money laundering, terrorism financing, or other financial crimes, leading to regulatory breaches and reputational damage.
crmp.owner: Compliance, Account Opening Unit, E-Business Operations, Legal
crmp.primaryControl: Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) policy; remote verification procedures; customer onboarding checklist

crmp.title: Public Registered Companies
crmp.description: (1) Corporate customers that are listed on the stock exchange are considered to be publicly-owned and generally accountable and there is no need to verify the identity of the individual shareholders.  (2) A Financial Institution shall make appropriate arrangements to ensure that an officer or employee, past or present, is not using the name of the company or its relationship with the Financial Institution for a criminal purpose.  (3) The Board resolution or other authority for a representative to act on behalf of the company in its dealings with the Financial Institution shall be obtained.  (4) Phone calls may be made to the Chief Executive Officer of a company in sub-regulation (3) of this regulation to intimate him of the application to open the account in the Financial Institution.  (5) The Identity of the directors of a quoted company may be verified.  (6) Due diligence shall be conducted where the account or service required falls within the category of higher risk business.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Treat listed companies as publicly-owned and generally transparent, with no need to verify individual shareholders. (2) Ensure that company employees are not using the company’s name for illegal purposes. (3) Obtain a Board resolution or formal authorization for anyone acting on the company’s behalf. (4) Optionally call the CEO to confirm the account opening. (5) May verify identities of the company’s directors. (6) Apply enhanced due diligence if the account is high-risk.
crmp.riskDescription: Public companies may be exploited by insiders or used as a front by individuals acting without proper authorization.
crmp.owner: Corporate Banking Team, Compliance Officer, KYC/Onboarding Unit
crmp.primaryControl: - board resolution/authorization for representatives - confirmation call to CEO (where applicable) - risk-based due diligence on services requested - screening of company and directors against watchlists

crmp.title: Higher Risk Business Applicant
crmp.description: Where a higher-risk business applicant is seeking to enter into a full banking relationship or any other business relationship where third party funding and transactions are permitted, the following evidence shall be obtained either in documentary or electronic form— (a) for established companies that are incorporated for 18 months or more, a set of the latest report and audited accounts shall be produced; (b) a search report at the CAC or an enquiry through a business information service or an undertaking from a firm of lawyers or accountants confirming the documents submitted to the CAC; (c) a certified copy of the resolution of the Board of Directors addressed to the Financial Institution to open an account and conferring authority on those who will operate it; (d) the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the company; and (e) any other document that the Financial Institution shall deem necessary.
crmp.plain: For high-risk companies applying to open an account, the bank shall collect the following documents (physically or electronically): (a) For companies older than 18 months, submit latest audited financials; (b) Conduct a CAC search, use a business info service, or obtain verification from lawyers/accountants; (c) Obtain a certified Board resolution authorizing account opening and operators; (d) Submit the Memorandum and Articles of Association; (e) Provide any other documents the bank may require.
crmp.riskDescription: High-risk businesses may use banking relationships for laundering proceeds, hiding beneficial owners, or funding illegal transactions.

crmp.title: Higher Risk Business Relating to Private Companies
crmp.description: (1) Where a private company is undertaking a higher risk business, in addition to verifying the legal existence of the business, the principal requirement is to look behind the corporate entity to identify those who have ultimate control over the business and the company’s assets. (2) What constitutes significant shareholding or control for the purpose of this regulation depends on the nature of the company and identification evidence shall be obtained for shareholders with interests of 5% or more. (3) Identification evidence shall be obtained for the principal-beneficial owner of the company and any other person with principal control over the company’s assets. (4) Where the principal owner is another corporate entity or trust, the Financial Institution shall take measures that look behind that company or vehicle and verify the identity of the beneficial-owner or settlers and where the Financial Institution is aware that the principal-beneficial owners or controllers have changed, they are required to verify the identities of the new owners. (5) A Financial Institution shall— (a) identify directors who are not principal controllers and signatories to an account for risk based approach purposes. (b) visit the place of business to confirm the existence of such business premises and the nature of the business conducted. (6) Where suspicions are aroused by a change in the nature of the business transacted or the profile of payment through a bank or investment account, further checks shall be made to ascertain the reason for the changes. (7) In full banking relationships, periodic enquiries shall be made to establish changes to controllers, shareholders or the original nature of the business or activity. (8) Particular care shall be taken to ensure that full identification and KYC requirements are met where the company is an International Business Company (IBC) registered in an offshore jurisdiction and operating out of a different jurisdiction.
crmp.plain: For private companies involved in high-risk businesses, the Bank shall: (1) Verify the company’s legal existence and identify those who ultimately control the company and its assets. (2) Identify and verify any shareholder with 5% or more interest. (3) Identify and verify the principal beneficial owner(s) and anyone with major control over assets. (4) Verify the actual beneficial owners or settlers behind them If another company or trust is a principal owner. (5) Identify directors and account signatories for risk-based purposes, and visit the business location. (6) Conduct further investigations if suspicious changes occur in business activity or payment profile. (7) Periodically check for changes in shareholders, controllers, or business nature for full banking relationships. (8) Exercise extra caution and full KYC for offshore International Business Companies (IBCs) operating from different jurisdictions.
crmp.riskDescription: Private companies in higher risk sectors may conceal true ownership, facilitate illicit flows, or use offshore entities to obscure beneficial control.
crmp.owner: Corporate Banking Team, Relationship Managers, Compliance Unit, KYC Officers
crmp.primaryControl: - Mandatory identification of 5%+ shareholders and beneficial owners - Corporate structure and trust transparency checks - Periodic updates and site verification - Risk-based screening of directors and signatories - Enhanced monitoring of account activity and changes

crmp.title: Foreign Financial Institutions
crmp.description: (1) For a foreign Financial Institution, the confirmation of existence and regulated status shall be checked by— (a) checking with the home country’s Central Bank or relevant supervisory body; (b) checking with another office, subsidiary, branch, or correspondent bank in the same country; (c) checking with Nigerian regulated correspondent bank of the overseas institution; or (d) obtaining evidence of its license or authorization to conduct financial and banking business from the institution itself.  (2) Additional information on banks all over the world may be obtained from various international publications and directories or any of the international business information services such as Swift KYC Registry and Banker’s Almanac.  (3) The publications referred to in sub-regulation (2) of this regulation shall not replace the confirmation evidence requirements under these Regulations.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall:  Confirm that a foreign financial institution is properly licensed and regulated by:  (a) Checking with the Central Bank or regulator in the institution’s home country;  (b) Verifying with another office, branch, subsidiary, or correspondent bank in that country;  (c) Contacting a Nigerian-regulated correspondent bank that deals with the foreign institution; or  (d) Obtaining direct proof (e.g., license or authorization) from the institution itself.  Use trusted international sources like the Swift KYC Registry or Banker’s Almanac for additional background information on foreign banks.  Understand that while international directories and databases are helpful, they do not replace the need for formal evidence of licensing and regulation.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to verify the licensing and regulatory status of foreign financial institutions exposes the Bank to significant risks, including dealing with unregulated or shell banks, facilitating money laundering or terrorism financing, and breaching cross-border regulatory requirements. This may result in legal penalties, reputational damage, and regulatory sanctions.

crmp.title: Bureau De Change
crmp.description: (1) A Bureau De Change (“BDC”) is subject to the provisions of these Regulations and shall be verified in accordance with the procedures for Financial Institution, and satisfactory evidence of identity, ownership structure, source of funds and a certified copy of the applicant’s operating license shall be obtained.  (2) A Financial Institution shall consider the risks associated with doing business with BDCs before entering into a business relationship with them.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Verify any Bureau De Change (BDC) it deals with using the same procedures as for other financial institutions. This includes confirming the BDC’s identity, ownership, source of funds, and obtaining a certified copy of its operating license. (2) Consider the risks involved in doing business with BDCs before starting any relationship with them.
crmp.riskDescription: Engaging with BDCs without proper verification may expose the Bank to high risks of money laundering, terrorism financing, and regulatory breaches due to the cash-intensive nature of their operations and potential lack of transparency.          Ask ChatGPT

crmp.title: Designated Non-financial Businesses and Professions(DNFBs)
crmp.description: (1) As part of KYC documentation for designated non-financial businesses and professions, the certificate of registration with SCUML or a certificate from a self-regulatory organization shall be obtained. (2) Where an application is made on behalf of a club or society, Financial Institution shall take reasonable steps to satisfy itself as to the legitimate purpose of the organization by sighting its constitution and the identity of at least two of the principal contact persons or signatories which shall be verified in line with the requirements for private individuals and where signatories are changed, Financial Institutions shall verify the identity of at least two of the new signatories. (3) Where the purpose of a club or a society is to purchase the shares of a regulated investment company or where all the members are regarded as individual clients, all the members in such cases shall be identified in line with the requirements for personal customers on a case-by-case basis.
crmp.plain: 1.The Bank shall obtain a certificate of registration with SCUML or from a recognized self-regulatory organization for all designated non-financial businesses and professions as part of KYC checks.  2.The Bank shall verify the legitimacy of any club or society applying for services by reviewing its constitution and confirming the identity of at least two key contact persons or signatories. If there is any change in signatories, the Bank shall verify the identity of at least two new signatories.  3.If a club or society exists to buy shares in an investment company or its members are treated as individual clients, the Bank shall identify all members individually, using personal customer requirements and a case-by-case approach.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to conduct proper KYC on clubs, societies, or designated non-financial businesses may expose the Bank to the risk of onboarding shell entities or fronts for illegal activities, including money laundering or terrorist financing.

crmp.title: Occupational Pension Schemes
crmp.description: (1) Where transactions carried out on behalf of an Occupational Pension Scheme, where the transaction is not in relation to a long term policy of insurance, the identities of both the principal employer and the Trust shall be verified. (2) In addition to the identity of the principal employer, the source of funding shall be verified and recorded to ensure that a complete audit trail exists if the employer is dissolved or wound up. (3) For the Trustees of Occupational Pension Schemes, satisfactory identification evidence shall be based on the inspection of formal documents concerning the Trust which confirm the names of the current Trustees and their addresses for correspondence and in addition to the documents, confirming that the Trust identification shall be based on extracts from Public Registers or references from Professional Advisers or Investment Managers. (4) Any payment of benefits by or on behalf of the Trustees of an Occupational Pension Scheme will not require verification of identity of the recipient. (5) Where individual members of an Occupational Pension Scheme are to be given personal investment advice, their identities shall be verified but where the Trustees and principal employer have been satisfactorily identified, and the information is still current, it will be appropriate for the employer to provide confirmation of the identity of individual employees.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall verify the identities of both the main employer and the Trust when handling transactions for an Occupational Pension Scheme, except for insurance-related transactions.  The Bank shall confirm and record the source of the employer’s funds to ensure traceability in case the employer is dissolved.  The Bank shall confirm the identity of pension scheme Trustees by reviewing formal trust documents that include their names and contact details, and additional verification may come from public registers or references from professional advisers.  The Bank shall not require identity checks for individuals receiving benefit payments from the Trustees of a pension scheme.  Where employees under a pension scheme are to receive personal investment advice, their identity shall be verified. However, if the Trustees and employer have already been identified and their information is up to date, the employer may confirm the identities of those individual employees.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to verify the identities of occupational pension scheme Trustees, employers, or funding sources may expose the Bank to misuse of pension funds or involvement with dissolved or shell entities, increasing the risk of money laundering or financial fraud.
crmp.primaryControl: Corporate customer KYC procedures

crmp.title: Registered Charity Organizations
crmp.description: (1) Financial Institutions shall adhere to the identification procedures requirements for opening of accounts on behalf of charity organizations; and the confirmation of the authority to act in the name of the organization. (2) The opening of accounts on behalf of charity or non-governmental organizations in Nigeria shall be carried out by a minimum of two signatories, duly verified and documentation evidence shall thereupon be obtained. (3) When dealing with an application from a registered charity organization, Financial Institutions shall obtain and confirm the name and address of the organization concerned. (4) Where a person making an application or undertaking a transaction is not the official correspondent or the recorded alternate, Financial Institutions shall send a letter to the official correspondent, informing him of the charity organizations’ application before it and the official correspondent shall respond as a matter of urgency where there is any reason to suggest that the application has been made without authority. (5) An application on behalf of un-registered charity organization shall be made in accordance with the procedures for clubs and societies as set out in these Regulations. (6) Where a charity organization is opening a current account, the identity of all signatories shall be verified and where the signatories change, identities of the new signatories shall be verified.
crmp.plain: The bank shall: 1. Follow standard customer identification procedures and confirm the authority of individuals acting on behalf of the charity organization. 2. Ensure that accounts are opened with a minimum of two duly verified signatories, and obtain appropriate documentation. 3. Confirm the name and address of the charity organization during the account opening process. 4. If the applicant is not the official correspondent or alternate, send a notification letter to the official correspondent and act based on the response. 5. For unregistered charities, apply the account opening procedures applicable to clubs and societies. 6. Verify the identity of all signatories for current accounts and re-verify any new signatories in the event of changes.
crmp.riskDescription: Charity organizations may be misused for money laundering or terrorist financing, especially if their source of funds, activities, or authorized representatives are not properly verified.
crmp.owner: Account Opening Officers, Relationship Managers, Compliance Officers
crmp.primaryControl: - Mandatory verification of registration and address of the charity - Minimum of two signatories required and verified - Notification to and confirmation from official correspondent when necessary - Use of club/society procedures for unregistered organizations - KYC review upon any change in signatory

crmp.title: Religious Organizations
crmp.description: A Religious Organization (“RO”) shall have a CAC and SCUML registered numbers and its identity may be verified by reference to the CAC, appropriate headquarters or regional area of denomination, and the identity of at least two signatories to its account shall be verified.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall ensure that a Religious Organization (RO) provides its Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) and SCUML registration numbers. crmp.title: Three-Tiers of Government and Parastatals
crmp.description: (1) Where the applicant for business relationship is one of the tiers of government or parastatals, Financial Institutions shall verify the legal standing of the applicant, including its principal ownership and address. (2) A certified copy of the resolution, letter of authority or other documents which authorize an official representing the body to open an account or undertake any transaction shall be obtained. (3) Financial Institutions may telephone the Chief Executive Officer of the organization or parastatal concerned, to verify and confirm the application for opening an account with the Financial Institution. (4) An authorization from the Federal or State Accountant-General shall be obtained before any of the three tiers of government or parastatals can open accounts with Financial Institutions in Nigeria.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Verify the legal status of the government entity or parastatal, including its principal ownership and registered address. 2. Obtain a certified resolution, letter of authority, or official documentation authorizing the representative to open an account or conduct transactions. 3. Call the Chief Executive Officer of the applying entity to confirm the authenticity of the account opening request. 4. Ensure that an authorization from the Federal or State Accountant-General is obtained before opening any account for any tier of government or parastatal.
crmp.riskDescription: Accounts opened for government entities and parastatals may be vulnerable to political misuse, misappropriation of public funds, or unauthorized transactions without proper verification.

crmp.description: The authenticity of an applicant who requested to open accounts or undertake transactions in the name of Nigerian-resident foreign consulates and any document of authorization presented in support of the application shall be checked with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the relevant authorities in the Consulate’s home country or as confirmed by the Head of Mission of that country in Nigeria.

crmp.riskDescription: Failure to verify the authenticity of foreign consulate-related transactions could expose the Bank to diplomatic fraud, reputational damage, and misuse of accounts for unauthorized or illicit activities under the cover of diplomatic immunity.

crmp.title: Intermediaries or other third parties to verify identity or to introduce business
crmp.description: (1) Whilst the responsibility to obtain satisfactory identification evidence rests with the Financial Institution that is entering into a relationship with a client, it is reasonable, in a number of circumstances, for reliance to be placed on another Financial Institution to— (a) undertake the identification procedure when introducing a customer and to obtain any additional KYC information from the client; (b) confirm the identification details where the customer is not resident in Nigeria; or (c) confirm that the verification of identity has been carried out where an agent is acting for a principal.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Remain responsible for collecting proper identification from customers it is doing business with.  2. However, in some cases, the Bank may rely on another financial institution to:  - Carry out customer identification and collect required KYC details when introducing a new customer;  - Confirm the identity details for customers who live outside Nigeria;  - Confirm that identity checks have been done when an agent is acting on someone else's behalf.
crmp.riskDescription: Relying on third-party financial institutions to conduct customer identification and KYC checks without adequate verification may expose the Bank to identity fraud, onboarding of high-risk or sanctioned clients, and non-compliance with KYC/AML regulations.
crmp.primaryControl: Interbank KYC reliance agreements; AML/CFT policy

crmp.title: Duty to report international transfer or transportation of funds, securities and cash
crmp.description: (1) A transfer to or from a foreign country of funds or securities by a person or body corporate including a money service business of a sum exceeding US$10,000 or its equivalent shall be reported to the Unit, Central Bank of Nigeria and Securities and Exchange Commission in writing within one day from the date of the transaction.  (2) A report made under subsection (1) shall indicate the nature and amount of the transfer, the names and addresses of the sender and the receiver of the funds or securities.  (3) Transportation of cash or negotiable instruments in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent by individuals in or out of Nigeria shall be declared to the Nigerian Customs Service.  (4) The Nigerian Customs Service shall report any declaration made under subsection (3) to the Central Bank and the Unit.  (5) Any person who falsely declares or fails to make a declaration to the Nigerian Customs Service under section 12 of the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, commits an offence and is liable on conviction to forfeit the undeclared funds or negotiable instrument or to imprisonment for a term of at least two years or both.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Report to the NFIU, CBN, and SEC in writing within 1 day for any transfer of funds/securities exceeding US$10,000 or equivalent. (2) Ensure that the report contains: nature, amount, sender and receiver names and addresses. (3) Inform customers that individuals transporting cash/negotiable instruments over US$10,000 must declare to Nigerian Customs. (4) Recognize that Nigerian Customs must report all such declarations to CBN and NFIU. (5) Warn customers that false declarations or failure to declare can lead to forfeiture or imprisonment (minimum of 2 years), or both.
crmp.riskDescription: Non-compliance may result in severe regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, exposure to ML/TF activities, criminal liability, or disconnection from international financial systems.

crmp.primaryControl: - Threshold-based automated alerts for US$10,000+ transfers - Mandatory review by Compliance before processing international transactions - Record-keeping of reports sent to regulators - Standard operating procedures (SOPs) for reporting timelines

crmp.title: Identification of customers
crmp.description: (1) A financial institution and a designated non-financial business and profession shall— (a) identify a customer, whether permanent or occasional, natural or legal person or any other form of legal arrangements, using identification documents as may be prescribed in any relevant regulation; (b) verify the identity of that customer using reliable, independent source documents, data or information; (c) identify the beneficial owner using relevant information or data obtained from a reliable source such that the financial institution or the designated non-financial business and profession is satisfied that it knows who the beneficial owner is; and (d) take reasonable measures to verify that any person purporting to act on behalf of the customer is so authorised, identified and verify the identity of that person. (2) Financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions shall undertake customer due diligence measures when— (a) establishing business relationships; (b) carrying out occasional transactions above the applicable designated threshold prescribed by relevant regulations, including transactions carried out in a single operation or in several operations that appear to be linked; (c) carrying out occasional transactions that are wire transfers; (d) there is a suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing, regardless of any exemptions or thresholds; or (e) the financial institution or designated non-financial business and profession has doubts about the veracity or adequacy of previously obtained customer identification data. (3) Financial institutions or designated non-financial businesses and professions shall— (a) conduct ongoing due diligence on a business relationship; (b) scrutinise transactions undertaken during the course of the relationship to ensure that the transactions are consistent with the institution’s knowledge of the customer, their business and risk profile and where necessary, the source of funds; and (c) ensure that documents, data or information collected under the customer due diligence process is kept up-to-date and relevant by undertaking reviews of existing records, particularly for higher risk categories of customers or business relationships. (4) Financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions shall take appropriate measures to manage and mitigate the risks and— (a) where higher risks are identified, apply enhanced measures to manage and mitigate the risk; (b) where lower risks are identified, take simplified measures to manage and mitigate the risks, provided that simplified customer due diligent measures are not permitted whenever there is suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing; and (c) in the case of cross-border correspondent banking and other similar relationships and in addition to carrying out customer due diligence measures— (i) gather sufficient information about a respondent institution, (ii) assess the respondent institution’s anti-money laundering and combating the financing of terrorism controls, (iii) document respective responsibilities of each institution in this regard, and (iv) obtain management approval before establishing new correspondent relationships. (5) A casual customer shall comply with the provisions of subsection (2) for any number or manner of transactions including wire transfer involving a sum exceeding US$1,000 or its equivalent if the total amount is known at the commencement of the transaction or as soon as it is known to exceed the sum of US$1,000 or its equivalent. (6) Where a financial institution or designated non-financial business and profession suspects or has reasonable grounds to suspect that the amount involved in a transaction is the proceeds of a crime or an illegal act, it shall require identification of the customer notwithstanding that the amount involved in the transaction is less than US$1,000 or its equivalent. (7) Financial institutions or designated non-financial business and profession shall put in place appropriate risk management systems and procedures to determine whether a customer or the beneficial owner of a customer is a politically exposed person. (8) In relation to a foreign politically exposed person, the financial institution or designated non-financial institution shall in addition to the requirements of subsections (1) and (2)— (a) obtain senior management approval before establishing (or continuing, for existing customers) such business relationships; (b) take reasonable measures to establish the source of wealth and the source of funds of customers and beneficial owners identified as politically exposed persons; and (c) conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring on that relationship. (9) In relation to a domestic politically exposed persons or person who has been entrusted with a prominent function by an international organisation, the financial institution or designated non-financial institution shall in addition to the requirements of subsections (1) and (2), adopt the measures referred to in subsection (8) in managing the business relationship.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1)(a) Identify all customers (individuals or entities, permanent or occasional) using officially prescribed ID documents. (b) Verify identity using reliable, independent sources. (c) Identify the beneficial owner using reliable sources and ensure clarity on ownership. (d) Verify identity and authority of anyone acting on behalf of the customer. (2) Perform CDD in the following situations: - (a) When establishing a business relationship. - (b) For occasional transactions above prescribed thresholds. - (c) When executing occasional wire transfers. - (d) Where there is suspicion of ML/TF regardless of thresholds. - (e) When prior customer identification data is inadequate or doubtful. (3).1.Keep checking the customer’s information regularly during the business relationship;    2.Review transactions to ensure they match what the Bank knows about the customer, their business, and source of funds;    3.Make sure all customer information is kept up to date, especially for high-risk customers. (4).The Bank shall take steps to reduce risks by: 1.Applying stricter checks where the risk is high; 2.Using simplified checks only for low-risk cases, unless there's suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing; 3.For cross-border banking partners, the Bank shall: -Collect information about the partner bank; -Check the partner bank’s controls against money laundering and terrorist financing; - Clearly document who is responsible for what; - Get management approval before starting the relationship. (5).The Bank shall identify a casual customer if they are doing any type of transaction (like wire transfers) of $1,000 or more, at the start or as soon as it becomes clear the total will reach that amount. (6).The Bank shall still verify the customer’s identity if there is suspicion the funds come from crime, even if the amount is below $1,000. (7).The Bank shall put systems in place to find out if a customer or their owner is a politically exposed person (PEP). (8). If the customer is a foreign PEP, the Bank shall: Get approval from senior management before starting or continuing business; Take extra steps to find out where the customer’s money came from; Monitor the customer’s activities closely. 9. If the customer is a local PEP or linked to one, the Bank shall also follow the requirements under (1) and (2) and treat the relationship as high-risk.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to carry out proper due diligence, especially for high-risk customers or politically exposed persons, exposes the Bank to increased risks of money laundering, terrorist financing, and reputational damage. Inadequate identification and monitoring of customers may result in regulatory breaches, financial penalties, or being used as a conduit for illicit activities

crmp.title: Suspicious transaction reporting
crmp.description: (1) Where a transaction— (a) involves a frequency which is unjustifiable or unreasonable, (b) is surrounded by conditions of unusual or unjustified complexity, (c) appears to have no economic justification or lawful objective, (d) is inconsistent with the known transaction pattern of the account or business relationship, or (e) in the opinion of the financial institution or non-financial business and profession involves the proceeds of a criminal activity, unlawful act, money laundering or terrorist financing, that transaction shall be deemed to be suspicious and the financial institution and designated non-financial business and profession involved in the transaction shall report to the Unit as the case may be immediately. (2) A financial institution or designated non-financial business and profession shall within 24 hours after the transaction referred to in subsection (1)— (a) draw up a written report containing all relevant information on the matters mentioned in subsection (1) together with the reasons and identity of the principal and, where applicable, of the beneficiary or beneficiaries; (b) take appropriate action to prevent the laundering of the proceeds of a crime or an illegal act; and (c) report the suspicious transaction and actions taken to the Unit.
crmp.plain: 1)The Bank shall treat any transaction as suspicious and report it immediately to the appropriate authority if it: happens too frequently or without a clear reason, is unusually complicated or lacks justification, seems to have no clear legal or economic purpose, does not match the customer’s typical transaction pattern, or appears to involve money from crime, unlawful activity, money laundering, or terrorist financing.  2)The bank must within 24 hours of identifying a suspicious transaction:  (a) Prepare a written report with all relevant details of the transaction, including the reasons for suspicion and the identities of the principal and beneficiaries.  (b) Take necessary preventive actions to stop possible laundering of criminal proceeds.  (c) Report the suspicious transaction and actions taken to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU).
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to detect and report suspicious transactions may result in:  - Regulatory sanctions by CBN or NFIU  - Legal liability  - The bank being used for money laundering or terrorist financing  - Loss of reputation and trust
crmp.owner: Compliance Officer, Transaction Monitoring Team, Branch/Operations Staff
crmp.primaryControl: - Automated suspicious transaction monitoring systems (rules/AI-based) - Internal STR checklist and red flag indicators - Escalation protocol to compliance unit - Centralized STR logging and approval workflow

crmp.title: Preservation of Records
crmp.description: (1) Financial institution and designated non-financial business and profession shall preserve and keep at the disposal of the authorities specified in section 9 of this Act— (a) all necessary records on transactions, both domestic and international, for at least five years following completion of the transaction; and (b) all records obtained under section 4 of this Act, including account files and business correspondence, and results of any analysis undertaken, for at least five years following the termination of the business relationship or after the date of the occasional transaction.  (2) The records referred to in subsection (1) shall be— (a) sufficient to permit individual transactions to be readily reconstructed at any time by the competent authorities; and (b) made swiftly available to the competent authorities.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: 1(a) Keep all transaction records (domestic and international) for at least 5 years after the transaction is completed. (b) Retain customer identification records, account files, business correspondence, and results of analysis for 5 years after the end of the business relationship or occasional transaction. (2) These records must be: (a) Detailed enough to allow authorities to reconstruct the transaction. (b) Swiftly retrievable when requested by competent authorities.
crmp.riskDescription: Inadequate record preservation may lead to: - Failure to support investigations by law enforcement - Regulatory breaches and sanctions - Inability to trace transaction trails or confirm customer due diligence - Loss of credibility and trust with regulators

crmp.title: Coomunication of Information
crmp.description: The records referred to in section 8 of this Act shall be communicated on demand to a competent authority and such other regulatory authorities or judicial persons as the Unit or Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering may specify by order published in the Federal Government Gazette.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall promptly communicate any customer or transaction records (as specified in Section 8) upon request to: - Any competent authority (e.g., CBN, NFIU) - Regulatory/judicial authorities designated by the Unit (SCUML or NFIU), as published in the Federal Government Gazette.
crmp.riskDescription: - Regulatory penalties for failure to share requested records. - Obstruction of justice or Regulatory investigation. - Reputational damage and legal liabilities. - Potential suspicion of collusion or concealment.

crmp.title: Internal procedures, policies and controls
crmp.description: (1) Every financial institution and designated non-financial business and profession shall develop programmes to combat the laundering of the proceeds of a crime or other unlawful acts, and these shall include— (a) the designation of compliance officers at management level at its headquarters and at every branch and local office; (b) regular training programmes for its employees; (c) the centralisation of the information collected; and (d) the establishment of an internal audit unit to ensure compliance with and effectiveness of the measures taken to enforce the provisions of this Act.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (a) Appoint Compliance Officers at management level at both the headquarters and all branches/local offices. (b) Provide regular AML/CFT/CPF training to all employees. (c) Ensure centralized data and information collection related to AML/CFT/CPF efforts. (d) Establish an Internal Audit Unit to monitor and verify the effectiveness and enforcement of AML/CFT/CPF measures.
crmp.riskDescription: - Risk of regulatory breach due to poor internal controls. - Operational risk from fragmented compliance oversight. - Failure to detect/report suspicious activity. - High exposure to money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing.
crmp.owner: Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), Head of HR (for training), Head of Internal Audit, Branch Managers
crmp.primaryControl: - Appoint trained compliance officers across all operational units. - Maintain a centralized AML system for data/information. - Schedule regular and role-specific AML/CFT training. - Set up and empower internal audit with AML-specific scope.

crmp.title: Mandatory disclosure by financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions
crmp.description: (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law or regulation, a financial institution or designated non-financial business and profession shall report to the Unit in the case of a financial institution and to Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering in the case of a designated non-financial business and profession in writing within seven days, any single transaction, lodgment or transfer of funds in excess of— (a) N5,000,000 or its equivalent, in the case of an individual; or (b) N10,000,000 or its equivalent, in the case of a body corporate.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall report in writing to the NFIU within 7 days any single transaction, lodgment, or transfer exceeding: (a) ₦5,000,000 (for individuals); or (b) ₦10,000,000 (for corporate entities).
crmp.riskDescription: - Regulatory breach for non-disclosure of high-value transactions. - Potential reputational damage or sanctions. - Opportunity for criminals to launder money through large, unreported transactions.
crmp.owner: Compliance Officer, Transaction Monitoring Unit, Operations Manager
crmp.primaryControl: - Automated transaction monitoring system with value thresholds. - Daily exception reports for high-value transactions. - Internal escalation and approval workflow for report submission.

crmp.title: Prohibition of numbered or anonymous accounts, accounts in fictitious names and shell banks
crmp.description: (1) The opening or maintaining of numbered or anonymous accounts by any person, financial institution or body corporate is prohibited. (2) A person shall not establish or operate a shell bank in Nigeria. (3) A financial institution shall— (a) not enter into or continue correspondent banking relationships with shell banks; and (b) satisfy itself that a respondent financial institution in a foreign country does not permit its accounts to be used by shell banks.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall:  1.Not allow the opening or use of anonymous or numbered accounts. 2.Not set up or operate any shell bank in Nigeria. 3.Not do business with shell banks, and must also confirm that any foreign bank it works with does not allow shell banks to use its accounts.
crmp.riskDescription: Allowing anonymous accounts or doing business with shell banks may expose the Bank to serious financial crime risks, including money laundering, regulatory violations, and reputational damage. Strict adherence to these rules protects the Bank from facilitating illicit activities.
crmp.owner: Chief Compliance Officer, Head of International Banking, Legal & Risk Unit
crmp.primaryControl: - Perform Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) on all correspondent banking relationships. - Require written confirmation from foreign respondent banks that they do not deal with shell banks. - Periodic audits of international correspondent relationships.

crmp.title: New products, business practices and technologies
crmp.description: (1) Financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions shall identify and assess the money laundering and terrorism financing risks that may arise in relation to the development of new products and new business practices, including new delivery mechanisms, and the use of new or developing technologies for both new and pre-existing products in accordance with the requirements specified by the regulatory authorities.  (2) Pursuant to the provisions of subsection (1), financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions shall— (a) undertake the risk assessments prior to the launch or use of such products, business practices and technologies; and (b) take appropriate measures to manage and mitigate the risks.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Identify and assess ML/TF risks linked to new products, services, delivery channels, and technologies (whether new or existing). (2) Conduct risk assessments before launching or using such products or technologies. (3) Implement appropriate risk mitigation measures.
crmp.riskDescription: - New delivery channels (e.g., mobile apps, online banking) may facilitate undetected money laundering or terrorism financing. - Failure to assess or mitigate such risks could result in regulatory sanctions, customer fraud, and reputational harm.
crmp.owner: Chief Risk Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, Product Development/Innovation Teams
crmp.primaryControl: - Conduct pre-launch ML/TF risk assessment on all new products/technologies. - Use risk-based controls, including enhanced due diligence and transaction monitoring for tech-driven products. - Maintain a risk register for new technology-enabled services.

crmp.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
crmp.title: CUSTOMER IDENTIFICATION AND VERIFICATION PROCEDURES FOR PEPS
crmp.description: FIs are required to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) for the purpose of establishing that a customer is a PEP, as provided by the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations. FIs are expected to identify and verify the identities of PEPs before providing them with financial services, or as soon as possible afterwards. The identification should also cover legal persons and legal arrangements that have at least one beneficial owner who is a PEP.  3.1 New Customers 3.1.1 Self-declaration by customers of their PEP status will guide the FIs in determining whether a customer is a PEP (i.e. by disclosing present or former employment or principal occupation clearly recognizable as a PEP). FIs may obtain verbal or written declarations from customers. 3.1.2 Information may be obtained directly from the customer in response to questions posed in the application or on-boarding form. FIs may also develop questionnaires with specific reference to criteria that identify PEPs, including family members and persons known to be their close associates. Such questionnaire would be required to be completed and signed by the customer and the beneficial owner, where applicable. 3.1.3 FIs should apply risk-based procedures in determining whether a customer is a PEP, either before the relationship is established or shortly thereafter. Once a new customer is established to be a PEP the FI should assess the risk on the customer and apply appropriate due diligence measures in a timely manner.  3.2 Existing Customers: where the FI becomes aware that an individual or beneficial owner has become a PEP it should re-classify the customer as such and apply risk-based due diligence and controls.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Conduct CDD to determine if a customer or beneficial owner is a PEP, both at onboarding and during ongoing relationships. (2) Obtain PEP status through self-declaration, questionnaires, and onboarding forms. (3) Apply risk-based due diligence to PEPs, both new and existing. (4) Reclassify existing customers as PEPs if new information surfaces.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to properly identify PEPs can expose the bank to money laundering, corruption-related offenses, and regulatory sanctions. It may also lead to relationships with high-risk clients without proper controls.
crmp.owner: Compliance Officer, Onboarding/KYC Teams, Relationship Managers
crmp.primaryControl: - Embed PEP screening in onboarding forms. - Use PEP identification checklists/questionnaires. - Automate screening with PEP databases. - Implement enhanced due diligence (EDD) for confirmed PEPs. - Periodically re-screen existing customers.
