crmp.title: Reliance on Consent
crmp.description: 1) Considering that data privacy is a fundamental right to informational self-determination, it is prudent for a data controller to prioritize the interest of the data subject which may be effectively addressed through his or her informed consent.  (2) Where reliance on consent may effectively defeat the rule of law, another lawful basis may be considered.  (3) In any complaint to the Commission as to whether consent was not obtained before data processing, and the Commission is to make a determination whether reliance on consent would effectively defeat the rule of law, the Commission shall take into account: a) The clear and present risk to fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject and third parties; b) The security implication; c) Public welfare; d) The need for efficacy in the administration of justice - taking into account the need to: i. Uphold equality before the law, ii. Submit to the neutrality and impartiality of courts of competent jurisdiction; e) Sustainable development; f) Prior relationship between the data controller and the data subject; and g) Proportionality and necessity of the scope of the processing.  (4) The items listed in sub (3) above are hereafter referred to collectively as Special Rule of Law Indexes (SRLI).  (5) Reliance on any lawful bases of data processing which is not consent and not supported by any SRLI shall be strictly scrutinized during NDP Act compliance audits and in any proceeding where the conduct of a data controller or processor is called into question.  (6) Whenever a data controller relies on consent, it shall keep a proper record that guarantees accountability in respect of the consent.  (7) In determining whether a data controller is accountable in the mode of obtaining consent, the data controller shall: a) Provide appropriate information to the data subject such that the data subject, on the basis of the information, may make an informed decision; b) Make the process of withdrawal of consent as easy as giving consent; and c) Ensure that refusal of consent is not detrimental to the rights and interests of the data subject.
crmp.plain: The Bank must prioritize obtaining informed consent from data subjects as a fundamental right, ensuring individuals clearly understand and agree to how their personal data is processed. However, if relying on consent conflicts with the rule of law, The Bank may use another lawful basis for data processing.  If there is a complaint regarding the absence of consent, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) will evaluate whether consent is necessary by considering factors collectively called the Special Rule of Law Indexes (SRLI). These factors include:  - Risks to fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects and third parties  - Security implications  - Public welfare  - Fair administration of justice  - Sustainable development  - The prior relationship between The Bank and the data subject  - Proportionality and necessity of the data processing  If The Bank relies on a lawful basis other than consent without support from any SRLI, this reliance will be strictly scrutinized during compliance audits and enforcement actions. Whenever The Bank relies on consent, it must keep proper records to demonstrate that valid consent was obtained, ensuring accountability.  To uphold accountability in obtaining consent, The Bank must:  - Provide clear and appropriate information to data subjects enabling informed decisions  - Make withdrawing consent as easy as giving consent  - Ensure refusal of consent does not negatively affect the rights or interests of data subjects
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to obtain or demonstrate valid consent, or improper use of alternative lawful bases, may result in enforcement action, reputational harm, or invalidation of data processing.
crmp.primaryControl: Consent Management System; Privacy Notice with clear consent terms; Consent withdrawal process; Documentation of lawful basis with SRLI assessment

crmp.title: Reliance on Consent
crmp.description: (8) Nothing in this GAID shall prevent a data subject from giving a constructive or an implied consent to data processing in the following circumstances: a) A data subject’s acts of participation in a public event and the images taken in that event may be used for a report of that event – provided that such images shall not be used for profit or commerce-oriented advertisement without the express consent of the data subject. A data controller in this circumstance shall ensure that images captured do not portray data subjects in a bad light. In addition to other measures of duty of care, a data controller may put participants on notice that images captured may be used for reporting, journalistic or other purposes permitted by the NDP Act.
crmp.plain: The Bank recognizes that a data subject may give constructive or implied consent in certain situations. For example, if a data subject participates in a public event where images are taken, those images may be used for event reporting provided they are not used for profit or commercial advertising without explicit consent. The Bank must ensure such images do not portray data subjects negatively and should, where applicable, notify participants that images may be used for reporting, journalism, or other lawful purposes under the NDPA.
crmp.riskDescription: Misuse of images without proper consent can lead to privacy violations, reputational damage, or regulatory penalties.
crmp.primaryControl: Public event notices; Image-use disclaimers; Non-commercial use policy; Pre-event DPO review

crmp.title: Data Processing Which Requires Consent
crmp.description: (1) Without prejudice to the provisions of the NDP Act and in addition to other circumstances in which consent may be required under this GAID or by operation of law, consent is required: a) For any direct marketing activity; b) For the processing of sensitive personal data; c) For further processing that is incompatible with the original purpose of processing; d) For the processing of the personal data of a child; e) Before personal data may be transferred to a country in respect of which the Commission has not made an adequacy decision; and f) Before the data controller makes a decision based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects concerning or significantly affecting the data subject.
crmp.plain: The Bank must obtain explicit consent in the following data processing cases, in addition to other situations required by law or GAID:  (a) Any direct marketing activity; (b) Processing of sensitive personal data; (c) Any further processing incompatible with the original purpose; (d) Processing personal data of a child; (e) Before transferring personal data to a country without an adequacy decision by the Commission; (f) Before making any automated decisions that have legal effects or significantly affect the data subject.
crmp.riskDescription: Non-compliance with consent obligations can result in privacy violations, regulatory fines, reputational harm, or data subject complaints — especially in cases involving minors, cross-border data transfers, sensitive data, or automated decisions.
crmp.primaryControl: Consent management systems, parental consent tools, data flow checks, automated processing reviews, and legal adequacy assessments

crmp.title: Consent to Cookies and other Tracking Tools
crmp.description: (1) Operation of cookies and other tracking tools shall comply with the principles of data protection under section 24 of the NDP Act.  (2) Except as otherwise provided by this GAID, the use of cookies on a website or other digital platforms requires consent.  (3) The consent shall be freely given, informed and specific.

crmp.title: Lawfulness of Purpose, Reliance on Consent, and Other Lawful Bases
crmp.description: (1) In addition to other obligations under the NDP Act and this GAID, every data processing shall only proceed from purposes that are: i. Lawful under the NDP Act; ii. Not in violation of other legislation for the time being in force in Nigeria, and iii. Not in violation of preemptory norms of general International Law.  (2) No consent shall be sought, given or accepted in any circumstance that may engender direct or indirect propagation of atrocities, hate, child rights violations and criminal acts.
crmp.plain: (1) All personal data processing by The Bank must: - Be lawful under the NDPA; - Not violate any Nigerian laws; - Not breach established international legal norms.  (2) The Bank must never seek, accept, or rely on consent to process data in ways that promote atrocities, hate, child rights violations, or criminal acts.

crmp.title: Lawful Basis Clarifications
crmp.description: (1) At the preliminary stage of a contract with a data subject, a data controller or data processor may carry out data processing on the data subject for the purpose of due diligence.  (2) Where the contract did not materialise, any personal data collected relating to the data subject shall be destroyed within six (6) months unless there is a justifiable ground to archive the data for the purposes of any future legal claim.  (3) A contract with a data subject involving data processing shall make provision for termination of the contract prior to the tenure of the contract.  (5) Pursuant to Section 46 of the 1999 Constitution and Section 34(1)(a)(v) of the NDP Act, a specific term of a contract on personal data processing that ousts or purports to oust the adjudicatory jurisdiction of Nigerian courts or the executive jurisdiction of the Commission shall be treated as void.
crmp.plain: (1) The Bank may process personal data during contract negotiations with a data subject for due diligence purposes.  (2) If no contract results, any collected data must be destroyed within six months, unless there is a legitimate reason to keep it for future legal claims.  (3) Contracts involving data processing should include provisions for early termination of the contract.  (5) Any contract clause that tries to exclude Nigerian courts or NDPC jurisdiction over data protection matters is void and unenforceable.
crmp.riskDescription: Legal risk from retaining personal data beyond lawful period; invalid contract clauses could lead to regulatory penalties or nullity.
crmp.primaryControl: Contract templates reviewed by Legal; pre-contract data retention policy with auto-delete; legal clause approval checklist

crmp.title: Reliance on Legal Obligation
crmp.description: (1) A legal obligation means any one of the following: a) a specific duty imposed by law; b) an order of a court of competent jurisdiction; or c) a responsibility incidental to an obligation imposed by law to carry out an act which requires the processing of personal data.  (2) Where a legal obligation derogates from the general safeguards of the NDP Act, it shall be treated as a derogation from the right to privacy as enshrined under Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution, and accordingly, Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution applies.  (3) In line with Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution, data processing shall only take place in such circumstances of derogation as stipulated in Sub-Article (2) of this Article if the enabling law for the said legal obligation is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society attd: i. it is in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health; or ii. for the purpose of protecting the rights and freedom of other persons; accordingly, account shall be taken of practices in a democratic society where the rule of law is firmly entrenched.  (4) Data processing under legal obligation shall be strictly limited to the minimum requirement under a law in line with Sub-Article (3) above and shall not be used for a voyage of discovery into the privacy of a data subject or in circumstances of establishing a speculative claim.
crmp.plain: (1) The Bank may process personal data where it has a legal obligation, such as: - A specific duty imposed by law, - A court order, or - A responsibility tied to a legal obligation.  (2–3) Such processing is a derogation from the right to privacy and must be:  - Justifiable in a democratic society, serving public safety, defense, public order, morality, health, or protecting others’ rights;  - Consistent with constitutional safeguards.  (4) The Bank must ensure that data processing under legal obligation is strictly limited to what is necessary and not used for speculative or intrusive purposes.
crmp.riskDescription: Unlawful data processing under the guise of legal obligation may violate constitutional rights and expose The Bank to sanctions.
crmp.primaryControl: Legal review and documentation of all legal obligations requiring data processing; obtain court orders in writing and file justification memos.

crmp.title: Evaluation of Lawful Bases of Data Processing
crmp.description: (1) In all adjudicatory or administrative proceedings pertaining to personal data processing, it shall be essential to the character of a democratic society to meticulously evaluate: (a) The necessity of processing of personal data – taking into consideration the risks and the alternatives (agency; (b) The duty of care and the standard of care employed to mitigate unnecessary, disproportionate risks of data processing; (c) The functional opportunity of redness accessible to an aggrieved person in accordance with Part 10 of the NDP Act and the Fundamental Rights Enforcement Procedure Rules for the time being in force; (d) The proportionality of the processing of personal data – taking into account: i. the scope of measures adopted or intended to be adopted for the processing of personal data in relation to the ii. the legitimate aim pursued. Duty of care shall be exercised in favour of the data subject and/or other data subjects whose fundamental rights and freedoms that may be affected. It is obligatory to avoid the setting of procedures which are prejudicial to fundamental rights and freedoms. It is prudent and obligatory to avoid any data processing that may undermine the adequacy of data protection which exists within the Federal Republic of Nigeria.
crmp.plain: The bank must ensure that personal data is processed only when necessary, with care and proportionality, and that affected individuals have access to redress. These factors must guide data protection policies, DPIAs, and legal justifications.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to justify data processing on grounds of necessity and proportionality may result in legal challenges, enforcement actions, or reputational damage.
crmp.primaryControl: Integrate necessity and proportionality reviews into Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs); ensure procedures for redress are in place and accessible.

crmp.title: Reliance on Vital Interest
crmp.description: (1) A data controller may rely on vital interest as a lawful basis for the processing of personal data, particularly when circumstances do not permit the data subject to give consent to the processing.  (2) The vital interest referred to in Sub-Article (1) of this Article may be that of the data subject or of a third party and it shall meet the conditions stipulated below:  a) The processing is necessary for the preservation or protection of life or livelihood and failure or refusal to act may be harmful to the data subject or a third party;  b) There is a legitimate expectation based on relationship or connection, operation of law, convention or prevailing norms that personal data should be processed in such circumstances of vital interest; and  c) The data controller or data processor may be called into question as being negligent, unprofessional or reckless for failing to carry out the data processing in such adverse circumstances in which a vital interest is in jeopardy.  (3) The method of processing employed for the purposes of vital interest shall be necessary and proportionate.  (4) The data controller shall give an account of its processing to the affected data subject, his or her representative in interest, or to a competent authority upon request.
crmp.plain: (1) The Bank may process personal data based on vital interest when the data subject cannot give consent, particularly during emergencies.  (2) This vital interest may relate to the data subject or a third party. It must meet the following criteria:  Processing is necessary to preserve life or livelihood and inaction may be harmful.  There is a legitimate expectation (from relationship, law, norms, etc.) that processing should occur in such a situation.  The Bank could be considered negligent for failing to act.  (3) The processing must be necessary and proportionate to the situation.  (4) The Bank must be able to justify and explain the processing to the data subject, their representative, or a competent authority upon request.
crmp.riskDescription: Unjustified or excessive reliance on vital interest may result in unlawful data processing, legal liability, and regulatory sanctions.
crmp.primaryControl: Include "vital interest" scenarios in data processing policy. Apply strict review criteria before relying on this lawful basis. Maintain documentation.

crmp.description: (1) Public interest may be relied upon as a lawful basis of data processing in circumstances where there is:  (a) a public health or humanitarian emergency; or  (b) there is a clear and present danger to public safety; or  (c) there is a need also address direction of destination or deprivation for the benefit of the data subject. In furtherance of the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy or Sustainable Development Goals.  (2) In addition to other obligations that may be imposed under the NDP Act, in any regulatory instrument issued by the Commission and any other legislation, a data controller shall take into account the safeguards in the provisions of Article 23 of this GAID when carrying out data processing on the ground of public interest.  (3) The method of processing employed for the purposes of public interest shall be necessary and proportionate.  (4) Article 23 of this GAID regarding the evaluation of legal obligation shall also apply to the evaluation of public interest when it is relied upon as a lawful basis of data processing.
crmp.plain: (1) The Bank may process personal data based on public interest when:  - There's a public health or humanitarian emergency,  - There’s a danger to public safety, or  - The data processing addresses issues of deprivation, aligns with national development goals, or supports the Fundamental Objectives of the Nigerian Constitution.  (2–4) When relying on public interest:  - The Bank must implement safeguards (as outlined in Article 23) to protect rights.  - The processing must be necessary and proportionate.  - Legal obligation safeguards under Article 23 also apply here.
crmp.riskDescription: Improper or unjustified reliance on public interest may result in rights violations, regulatory breaches, or reputational damage.
crmp.primaryControl: Document clear justification for invoking public interest. Ensure all Article 23 safeguards are reviewed and implemented in such cases.

crmp.title: Reliance on Legitimate Interest
crmp.description: (1) A data controller shall cautiously consider reliance on legitimate interest as a lawful basis for data processing and shall be required in a compliance audit to show the basis of its preference. A template of a Legitimate Interest Assessment is in Schedule 8.  (2) Section 25 (2) of the NDP Act makes compatibility with contract, vital interest, legal obligation or public interest, a basis for reliance on legitimate interest. Accordingly, it shall be mandatory for a data controller under the circumstances to: a) Carry out Legitimate Interest Assessment (as prescribed in Schedule 8) before embarking on data processing; b) Priorities privacy by design and by default – taking into consideration the suitability of anonymisation or pseudonymisation; c) Identify and document the lawful basis of processing which is compatible with the legitimate interest process; d) Identify and eliminate data processing that may overreach the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects – particularly such processing that may lead to behavioural monitoring or profiling, or lead to targeted advertisement by third parties or partners; e) Identify and eliminate data processing that may lead to a breach of data confidentiality, integrity and availability – taking into account vulnerable data subjects; f) Provide transparent information to data subjects in accordance with Section 27 of the NDP Act; g) Provide for prompt remediation of data subjects’ rights; and h) Priorities data ethics and utmost duty of care.
crmp.plain: (1) The Bank must carefully consider using legitimate interest as a lawful basis. It will be required to justify its decision during audits.  (2) To rely on legitimate interest, The Bank must:  - Complete a Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) as per Schedule 8.  - Apply privacy by design and default (e.g., anonymisation/pseudonymisation).  - Identify and document compatible lawful bases (e.g., contract, vital interest).  - Avoid processing that overreaches rights (e.g., profiling or targeted ads).  - Avoid processing that compromises confidentiality, integrity, or availability, especially for vulnerable individuals.  - Provide clear information to data subjects (per Section 27 of NDPA).  - Ensure remediation options for data subjects are available.  - Uphold data ethics and a high duty of care.
crmp.riskDescription: Relying on legitimate interest without proper LIA may result in unlawful data processing, breaches of data subjects’ rights, regulatory penalties, or reputational harm.
crmp.primaryControl: Mandatory Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) using Schedule 8 template; embed privacy by design; exclude profiling or sensitive targeting unless justified; provide data subject transparency and rights mechanisms.

crmp.title: Consideration Regarding Information to Data Subjects
crmp.description: (1) Provision of information to a data subject shall be in accordance with Section 27 of the NDP Act. The information shall be clear and shall take into consideration vulnerable data subjects.  (2) In circumstances of exclusive physical events, interviews or interactions where a data controller or data processor may not be able to provide data subjects with a privacy policy or if provided, the class of data subjects may not be able to understand the privacy policy without the aid of an interpreter, the data controller or data processor shall provide the information in the form that the data subject can understand.  (3) The information to be provided by the data controller or data processor includes but is not limited to the following:  a) The name of the data controller or data processor,  b) Lawful basis of data processing,  c) Types of personal data to be collected,  d) The purpose of the processing,  e) The means of processing,  f) Access to personal data by authorised third parties,  g) Purpose of access by third parties,  h) Data subject's rights,  i) Access to prompt internal remediation through contact to be supplied by the data controller or data processor, and  j) Right to lodge a complaint with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.  (4) Information to data subjects does not constitute a request for consent. Consent shall be specifically requested and obtained when it is required by law and on the ground that the information which may guide the data subject in making an informed decision has been duly provided prior to the processing of personal data.
crmp.plain: (1–2) The Bank must provide clear, accessible information to data subjects in line with Section 27 of the NDPA. This includes formats understandable to vulnerable or non-literate persons.  (3) The Bank must inform data subjects about:  - Its name (as controller or processor),  - The lawful basis for processing,  - The types of personal data collected,  - The purpose and means of processing,  - Third-party access, its purpose, and those authorised,  - Rights of the data subject,  - Internal complaint and remediation channels, and the right to lodge a complaint with the NDPC.  (4) Providing information is not the same as requesting consent. Consent must still be specifically obtained when required.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to properly inform data subjects can result in non-compliance with the NDPA, especially where vulnerable individuals are involved. This may lead to sanctions, reputational damage, and inability to lawfully process data.
crmp.primaryControl: Prepare standardised, accessible privacy notices in various formats; ensure field officers, agents, or event facilitators are trained to communicate these notices clearly to vulnerable audiences; separate consent process when required.

crmp.title: Data Privacy Impact Assessment
crmp.description: (1) A Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) is mandated under Section 28 of the NDP Act when data processing may likely result in high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject by virtue of its nature, scope, context, and purposes.  (2) Introduction of new technologies or new processing techniques or directives mandating processing of personal data on a large scale requires a DPIA on the following grounds:  (a) Unintended, adverse consequences to the lives and livelihoods of data subjects may result from the data processing;  (b) Such adverse consequences are threats to fundamental rights and freedoms as well as to the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy - which Policy forms the basis of sustainable development, security and economic programmes of government; and  (c) In circumstances where data processing measures constitute a derogation from Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution, they shall comply with the safeguards under Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution. In this regard, the need to fulfil the conditions of necessity and proportionality and other safeguards stipulated under Article 29 of this GAID is obligatory.
crmp.plain: The bank must conduct a Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA) before initiating any data processing activity that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. This obligation applies when: - The bank introduces new technologies or new processing techniques. - The bank processes personal data on a large scale (e.g., automated profiling, credit scoring, biometrics).  The bank must particularly conduct a DPIA when: 1. The data processing could lead to unintended, adverse consequences to individuals’ lives or livelihoods.  2. These adverse outcomes could threaten fundamental rights and freedoms, or conflict with national development, economic, or security objectives.  3. The processing involves a derogation from the right to privacy under Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution—in such cases, the bank must ensure that: - The processing is necessary and proportionate, and - It includes safeguards required under Section 45 of the Constitution and Article 29 of this Directive.
crmp.riskDescription: Failing to conduct a DPIA for high-risk processing may lead to serious privacy breaches, regulatory action, reputational damage, or constitutional violations.
crmp.primaryControl: Embed DPIA requirement into internal project initiation processes; Train relevant teams (e.g., IT, legal, compliance) on DPIA triggers; Use standard DPIA templates approved by the DPCO; Review all tech or process changes for DPIA necessity.

crmp.title: Monitoring, Evaluation and Maintenance of Data Security System
crmp.description: (1) A data controller or data processor shall have schedules for monitoring, evaluation and maintenance of data security systems.  (2) The schedules shall take into account people, processes and technologies involved in data security and each shall contain applicable technical and organisational measures including but not limited to: (a) Training; (b) Certifications; (c) Updates of software; (d) Vulnerability tests of databases; (e) Assessment of hardware for repairs or replacements; (f) Authentication checks; (g) Encryption reviews; and (h) Quality Assurance on products and services being used for data confidentiality, integrity and availability.  (3) A data controller or data processor shall assign relevant officers to carry out the tasks under the schedule and stipulate time to take appropriate technical and organisational measures under the schedule.  (4) The schedule shall be vetted and certified by a duly certified information security officer.  (5) Notwithstanding the schedule, a data controller or data processor shall carry out monitoring, evaluation and maintenance of data security systems as frequently as possible, taking into account the risks of data processing.
crmp.plain: 1 The bank must create and maintain a formal schedule for regularly monitoring, evaluating, and maintaining its data security systems.L235  2) The bank’s schedule must include people, processes, and technologies, and contain specific controls, such as: (a) Staff training, (b) Security certifications, (c) Regular software updates, (d) Vulnerability testing of databases, (e) Hardware assessment and replacement, (f) Authentication checks, (g) Encryption review, and (h) Quality assurance for tools used to ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data.  (3)  The bank must assign qualified officers to carry out each task in the schedule and must set timelines for applying technical and organisational security measures.  29(4)  The bank must ensure that the schedule is reviewed and certified by a certified information security officer (CISO).  29(5)   The bank must perform data security monitoring and maintenance as frequently as possible, especially in high-risk data processing environments — regardless of the fixed schedule.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to proactively maintain security systems may result in data breaches, loss of customer trust, or non-compliance with NDPA.
crmp.owner: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Head of IT Security
crmp.primaryControl: Formal maintenance schedule with documented controls and timelines; Roles and responsibilities clearly assigned; CISO approval required

crmp.description: (1)A data controller or a data processor who (whether for itself or for other persons) deploy or intends to deploy data processing software for the purposes of tracking a data subject or enabling a communication link with a data subject and processing his or her personal data, is under an obligation to abide by the provisions of the NDP Act.   (3) Examples of software referred to in this GAID are: (a) Operating System (b) Mobile Applications (c) Device Driver (d) Firmware (e) Programming Language Translator (f) Utilities

Self-service measures which may disable, uninstall or restrict the software is available (link shall be supplied by the data controller); ix. crmp.title: Measures Against Privacy Breach Abatement
crmp.description: (1) A data controller or data processor shall put in place, appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent the use of its platform, facility, network or howsoever called, from being used to breach the privacy of a data subject.
crmp.plain: The Bank must establish and maintain appropriate technical and organizational measures (such as access controls, monitoring tools, and data protection protocols) to ensure that its platforms, systems, or networks are not used to violate customers’ data privacy.
crmp.riskDescription: Unauthorized system use may lead to privacy breaches and NDPA violations.

crmp.description: (5) The content of a data breach notification to the Commission shall include the following among others: a) A description of the circumstances of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; b) The date or time period during which the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure occurred; c) A description of the personal information involved in the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; d) An assessment of the risk of harm to individuals as a result of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; e) An estimate of the number of individuals to whom there is a real risk of significant harm as a result of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosure; f) A description of steps the organisation has taken to reduce the risk of harm to individuals; g) A description of any steps the organisation has taken to notify individuals of the loss or unauthorised access or disclosures; and h) The time and contact information of a person who can answer on behalf of the organisation, the Commission's questions regarding the loss of unauthorised access or disclosure of personal data.
crmp.plain: When reporting a data breach to the NDPC, the Bank must include key details such as: what happened, when it occurred, what type of personal data was involved, how individuals might be harmed, how many people were affected, actions taken to reduce the harm, how individuals were notified, and a contact person for follow-up by the Commission.
crmp.riskDescription: Incomplete or inaccurate breach reporting may lead to regulatory penalties or harm to affected individuals.

crmp.title: Data Processing Agreement
crmp.description: (1) In line with Section 29(2) of the NDP Act, a data processor is expected to rely on a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) with the data controller in order to carry out data processing on behalf of the data controller.  (2) In addition to other relevant terms and conditions as may be prescribed by law, a DPA shall include the following: a) Obligations of the data controller and data processor under Section 29 of the NDP Act; b) Name of parties; c) Addresses of parties; d) Recitals containing reference to any Principal Agreement or Service Level Agreement; e) Purpose of data processing; f) Location of data processing (taking into account the provisions of the NDP Act on cross-border data transfer); g) Scope of the processing; h) Lawful uses of data processing; i) Responsibilities of parties under the DPA; j) Technical and Organisational Measures for data protection (if highly technical or scientific, it should be expressly outlined in a schedule to the DPA); k) The outcome of a DPA where relevant; l) Potential risks; m) NDP Act compliance (evidence of registration with the Commission should be ascertained); n) Confidentiality; o) Tenure; p) Specific Restrictions; q) Indemnity; r) Insurance; s) Force Majeures; and t) Dispute Resolution.  (3) A party to any DPA other than an individual data subject, shall take reasonable measures to ensure that the other party is compliant under the NDP Act, accountable to receive complaints by any reasonable means through which it may be contacted by a complainant (including but not limited to hard copies at its known offices and emails).
crmp.plain: If the Bank engages any external party (a data processor) to process personal data on its behalf, it must ensure there is a valid and signed Data Processing Agreement (DPA) in place before data processing begins. The DPA must contain all mandatory elements outlined in Article 34(2), and the Bank must also confirm that the third party is compliant with the NDPA and reachable by complainants through reasonable means.

crmp.title: Right to Data Portability
crmp.description: (1) A data subject has a right to data portability.  (2) The right to data portability shall apply where the data subject provided the personal data on the basis of his or her consent or the processing is necessary for the performance of a contract. It may not apply where processing is based on a legal ground other than consent or contract.  (3) The right to data portability may not apply against a data controller or data processor in the performance of its public duties; unless there is a compelling legitimate interest or right of a data subject that may be abridged by reason of denying the data subject's right of data portability.  (4) Where, in a certain set of personal data, more than one data subject is concerned, the right to receive the personal data should be without prejudice to the rights and freedoms of other data subjects in accordance with the NDP Act or any regulatory instrument issued by the Commission.  (5) The right to data portability shall not prejudice the right of the data subject to obtain the erasure of personal data and the limitations of that right as prescribed under the NDP Act.  (6) Nothing in this Article shall imply the erasure of personal data concerning the data subject which has been provided by him or her for the performance of a contract to the extent that and for as long as are necessary for the performance of that contract.
crmp.plain: The bank must enable customers (data subjects) to obtain and reuse their personal data, where data was collected based on consent or contract. This data must be provided in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format. The bank must ensure the right is exercised without harming others’ data rights and must not refuse portability where required. crmp.title: Data Subject's Standard Notice to Address Grievance
crmp.description: (2) An aggrieved data subject may cause SNAG to a data controller or a data processor where the data subject reasonably believes that the data controller or data processor violated his or her right to data privacy.  (3) SNAG shall not be regarded as a condition precedent for lodging a direct complaint with the Commission or for instituting an action, rather it shall be regarded as a standardised template for demanding internal remediation in an organisation which may be acting in violation of a data subject's privacy.  (4) SNAG may be served directly by a data subject or by a person acting under his or her authority or by a civil society organisation acting in the public interest.  (6) Upon receipt of a SNAG, a data controller or a data processor shall communicate its decision on the SNAG to the Commission through the designated electronic platform.  (8)A SNAG may be served on a data controller or a data processor via its physical sources, telephone messaging medium, e-mail address, courier service or other reasonable means of correspondence.
crmp.plain: 1. The bank must be prepared to receive a Standard Notice to Address Grievance (SNAG) from any individual (data subject) who reasonably believes that the bank has violated their right to data privacy.  2. The bank must recognise that a SNAG is a standard internal grievance tool—even though it is not mandatory before a complaint is made to the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), the bank is still required to treat it seriously and provide internal remediation.  3. The bank must accept SNAGs served by:  - The data subject, - A person authorized by the data subject (e.g., lawyer or agent), or - A civil society organization acting in the public interest.  4. The bank must acknowledge and receive SNAGs via any of the following channels: - Physical delivery (e.g., front desk), - SMS or telephone messaging, - Email, - Courier service, - Any other reasonable means of communication.  5. Once a SNAG is received, the bank must communicate its decision or response to the Commission through the designated electronic platform provided by the NDPC.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to acknowledge or respond to SNAGs may breach privacy obligations, harm customer trust, and result in regulatory scrutiny from NDPC.

crmp.primaryControl: Grievance handling policy; Multiple accessible complaint channels (physical, SMS, email, courier); Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for SNAG responses

crmp.title: Parameters for Assessing Privacy and Public Interest in Emerging Technologies
crmp.description: (1) In line with Section 5(a) of the NDP Act, the Commission shall foster the development of personal data protection technologies, in accordance with recognised international best practices and applicable international law; accordingly, the Commission shall accord priority to ETs which strengthen data privacy.  (2) In furtherance of Section 1(b) of the NDP Act towards strengthening the legal foundations of the national digital economy and guaranteeing the participation of Nigeria in the regional and global economies through the beneficial and trusted use of personal data, the Commission shall take into account the utilitarian value of ETs in achieving sustainable development through lawful processing of personal data.  (3) A data controller or data processor who intends to process personal data in the circumstances contemplated by Article 44 (2), may benchmark with global consensus on ETs such as the United Nations Resolution on Artificial Intelligence. Accordingly, data controllers and data processors shall, among other self-correcting measures, remain from or cease the use of ET systems that are impossible to operate in compliance with international human rights law or that pose undue risks to the enjoyment of human rights.
crmp.plain: If the bank plans to adopt emerging technologies (ETs)—such as AI, automated decision systems, advanced analytics, biometrics, etc.—it must ensure those technologies protect personal data privacy and comply with international human rights standards. The bank must avoid or stop using any technology that violates privacy laws or poses undue risks to individuals’ rights. It should also benchmark with global frameworks (e.g., the UN AI Resolution) to ensure its systems meet global ethical standards in personal data use.
crmp.riskDescription: Use of ETs without benchmarking to human rights or data protection standards can result in data breaches, regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, or civil liability.
crmp.primaryControl: Pre-deployment risk assessments; Human rights and DPIA screening; Global standards benchmarking (e.g., UN, OECD)

crmp.title: Capacity Building in Data Protection and Continuous Professional Development Credits
crmp.description: (1) Capacity building is mandatory as an organizational measure of data privacy and protection.  (2) In furtherance of Section 5(e)-(f) of the NDP Act and taking into account the high technical skill required, the Commission shall foster capacity building and professional development in data protection and privacy.  (3) All employees and other persons who are engaged by the data controller or data processor shall be trained and sensitized periodically on emerging developments in data processing and to such an extent that is reasonably relevant to their job descriptions respectively.  (4) The Commission may develop a mechanism in place for the training, and the award of certifications on Data Privacy and Protection.
crmp.plain: The bank must ensure that all employees and persons it engages (e.g., contractors, consultants) are regularly trained on data protection, privacy rules, and new developments in data processing. Training must be relevant to their job roles, and the bank must treat capacity building as a mandatory internal control for data protection compliance.
crmp.riskDescription: Lack of continuous training may result in non-compliance, human error, data breaches, and enforcement penalties.
crmp.primaryControl: Training schedules, role-specific content, attendance records, CPD credits, NDPC-approved certifications

crmp.title: Evidence of Compliance with the NDP Act
crmp.description: (1) Evidence by a data controller or a data processor relating to compliance with the NDP Act or any regulatory instrument issued by the Commission shall be evaluated in the context they directly relate to.  (2) Compliance in relation to registration, filing of annual CAE, submission of DPIA or cross-border transfer instruments approved by the Commission shows commitment to accountability and prima facie good faith in data processing. It does not replace the need to provide concrete evidence in defence of any complaint of violation relating to other provisions of the NDP Act.  (3) The Commission, in furtherance of Section 486(R) of the NDP Act shall take compliance in terms of accountability as a partial fulfillment of cooperation.
crmp.plain: The bank must maintain documented proof of compliance with data protection obligations (e.g., registration with the Commission, DPIAs, CAEs, cross-border transfer documents). This evidence must be specific, contextually relevant, and available when required, especially in the event of any investigation or complaint. Such documentation also shows that the bank is acting in good faith and is accountable under the NDPA.
crmp.riskDescription: Inability to provide documentary proof during audits or complaints can imply non-compliance and result in reputational or regulatory penalties.

crmp.title: Objectives of the Regulation
crmp.description: The objectives of this Regulation are as follows:  a) to safeguard the rights of natural persons to data privacy;  b) to foster safe conduct for transactions involving the exchange of Personal Data;  c) to prevent manipulation of Personal Data; and  d) to ensure that Nigerian businesses remain competitive in international trade through the safe-guards afforded by a just and equitable legal regulatory framework on data protection and which is in tune with best practice.
crmp.plain: The Bank must implement data protection practices that: - Respect and protect individuals’ privacy rights; - Ensure that all transactions involving personal data are conducted safely; - Prevent unauthorized access, alteration, or misuse of personal data; - Align with international best practices in data protection, so that Nigerian banks can compete globally.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to align with NDPR goals may lead to privacy breaches, loss of trust, legal risk, and reputational damage.
crmp.primaryControl: Establish a Data Protection Policy aligned with NDPR goals; embed privacy in transaction processing and staff training programs.

crmp.title: Privacy Policy
crmp.description: Notwithstanding anything contrary in this Regulation or any instrument for the time being in force, any medium through which Personal Data is being collected or processed shall display a simple and conspicuous privacy policy that the class of Data Subject being targeted can understand. The privacy policy shall in addition to any other relevant information contain the following:  a) what constitutes the Data Subject's consent;  b) description of collectable personal information;  c) purpose of collection of Personal Data;  d) technical methods used to collect and store personal information, cookies, JWT, web tokens etc.;  e) access (if any) of third parties to Personal Data and purpose of access;  f) a highlight of the principles stated in Part 2;  g) available remedies in the event of violation of the privacy policy;  h) the time frame for remedy; and  i) provided that no limitation clause shall avail any Data Controller who acts in breach of the principles set out in this Regulation.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall publish a simple, conspicuous, and understandable privacy policy wherever it collects or processes personal data. The policy must include: what consent means, what data is collected, its purpose, methods (e.g. cookies), third-party access, rights, remedies, and response timelines. No clause shall override these principles.
crmp.riskDescription: Legal, reputational, and regulatory risks from non-transparent data collection or inadequate privacy disclosures.
crmp.primaryControl: Implement uniform privacy policy templates for all channels; include required disclosures and periodic review for updates.

crmp.title: Data Security
crmp.description: Anyone involved in data processing or the control of data shall develop security measures to protect data; such measures include but not limited to protecting systems from hackers, setting up firewalls, storing data securely with access to specific authorized individuals, employing data encryption technologies, developing organizational policy for handling Personal Data (and other sensitive or confidential data), protection of emailing systems and continuous capacity building for staff.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall implement technical and organizational security measures to protect data from unauthorized access. These include firewalls, encryption, access control, email security, and regular staff training.
crmp.riskDescription: Data breach, cyberattack, legal non-compliance.
crmp.primaryControl: Firewall setup, access-level permissions, encryption protocols, email filters, quarterly staff training.

crmp.plain: The Bank shall ensure that any data processing by a third party is covered by a written contract and is fully compliant with the Regulation.

crmp.title: Advancement of Right to Privacy
crmp.description: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Regulation, the privacy right of a Data Subject shall be interpreted for the purpose of advancing and never for the purpose of restricting the safeguards Data Subject is entitled to under any data protection instrument made in furtherance of fundamental rights and the Nigerian laws.

crmp.description: (11) The Data Subject shall have the right to obtain from the Controller restriction of processing where one of the following applies: a) The accuracy of the Personal Data is contested by the Data Subject for a period enabling the Controller to verify the accuracy of the Personal Data; b) The processing is unlawful, and the Data Subject opposes the erasure of the Personal Data and requests the restriction of their use instead; c) The Controller no longer needs the Personal Data for the purposes of the processing, but they are required by the Data Subject for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims; and d) The Data Subject has objected to processing pending the verification whether the legitimate grounds of the Controller override those of the Data Subject.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall restrict processing of a Data Subject’s personal data where any of the following apply: the accuracy is disputed; the Data Subject prefers restriction to deletion; the Bank no longer needs the data but the Data Subject does for legal purposes; or the Data Subject has objected while a decision is pending.

crmp.description: (12) Where processing has been restricted such Personal Data shall, except for storage, only be processed with the Data Subject's consent or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims or for the protection of the rights of another natural or legal person or for reasons of important public interest in Nigeria.

crmp.description: (13) The Controller shall communicate any rectification or erasure of Personal Data or restriction to each recipient to whom the Personal Data have been disclosed, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort. crmp.description: (14) The Data Subject shall have the right to receive the Personal Data concerning him or her, which he or she has provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and have the right to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance from the controller to which the Personal Data have been provided, where: (a) The processing is based on consent, or (b) On a contract, and (c) The processing is carried out by automated means.
crmp.plain: The Bank shall, upon request, provide personal data (originally supplied by the customer) in a structured, machine-readable format if processing is based on consent or contract and is automated.

crmp.title: Administrative Redress Panel
crmp.description: (1) Without prejudice to the right of a Data Subject to seek redress in a court of competent jurisdiction, the Agency shall set up an Administrative Redress Panel under the following terms of reference;  (2) Investigation of allegations of any breach of the provisions of this Regulation;  (3) Invitation of any party to respond to allegations made against it within seven days;  (4) Issuance of Administrative orders to protect the subject-matter of the allegation pending the outcome of investigation;  (5) Conclusion of investigation and determination of appropriate redress within twenty-eight (28) working days; and  (6) Any breach of this Regulation shall be construed as a breach of the provisions of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) Act of 2007.
crmp.plain: (1) The Bank must be aware that data subjects can file complaints before an Administrative Panel, and not only in court.  (2)  The Bank must be prepared for investigations by the Administrative Panel following any complaints.   (3) The Bank must be prepared to respond to NDPR complaints within 7 days of notice.  (4) The Bank must comply with temporary measures issued by the Panel during investigations.  (5) The Bank must cooperate and provide necessary documentation within investigation timelines.  (6) The Bank must treat any NDPR breach as a legal breach with serious regulatory consequences.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to respond promptly or cooperate with the Panel could lead to sanctions or reputational damage.
crmp.primaryControl: Establish internal NDPR complaint handling SOPs, designate responsible officer, track timelines, and maintain open communication with the Panel.

crmp.title: Application
crmp.description: (1) This Act shall apply to the processing of personal data, whether by automated means or not.
crmp.plain: The bank must comply with the Act whenever it handles personal data—whether using digital systems (automated) or manually (e.g., paper records, physical forms).
crmp.riskDescription: Non-compliance may lead to regulatory sanctions, fines, and reputational damage.
crmp.primaryControl: Implement policies covering all personal data processing, including manual and automated systems.

crmp.title: Application
crmp.description: (2) This Act shall apply, where the— (a) data controller or the data processor is domiciled in, resident in, or operating in Nigeria; (b) processing of personal data occurs within Nigeria; or (c) the data controller or the data processor is not domiciled in, resident in, or operating in Nigeria, but is processing personal data of a data subject in Nigeria.
crmp.plain: The bank must comply with this Act if it is based in Nigeria, operating in Nigeria, or processing personal data within Nigeria. Even if the bank is outside Nigeria, it must still comply if it handles the personal data of anyone located in Nigeria.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of violating jurisdictional data protection requirements, potential cross-border legal exposure.
crmp.primaryControl: Maintain a register of data processing activities and locations; monitor cross-border data flows.

crmp.title: Data Protection Officers
crmp.description: (1) A data controller of major importance shall designate a Data Protection Officer or expert knowledge of data protection law and practices, and the ability to carry out the tasks prescribed under this Act and subsidiary legislation made under it.  (2) The Data Protection Officer may be an employee of a data controller or engaged by a service contract. (3) The Data Protection Officer shall— (a) advise the data controller or the data processor, and their employees, who carry out processing made under this Act; (b) monitor compliance with this Act and related policies of the data controller or data processor; and (c) act as the contact point for the Commission on issues relating to data processing.
crmp.plain: If the bank is classified as a “data controller of major importance” (i.e., handling significant volumes or sensitive data), it must appoint a qualified Data Protection Officer (DPO) either as an employee or via contract. crmp.title: Withdrawal of Consent
crmp.description: (1) A data subject shall have the right to withdraw, at any time, consent to the processing of personal data under this Act. (2) The data controller shall ensure that it is as easy for the data subject to withdraw, as to give consent.
crmp.plain: The bank must allow individuals to withdraw their consent to data processing at any time and make this withdrawal process as easy as giving consent.

crmp.title: Right to Object
crmp.description: 1) A data subject shall have the right to object to the processing of personal data relating to the data subject.
crmp.plain: The bank must respect and act on an individual’s right to object to the processing of their personal data, stopping the processing unless there are overriding legitimate grounds.
crmp.riskDescription: Continuing processing after objection is unlawful.
crmp.primaryControl: Enable processing flag to block activity after objection.

crmp.title: Right to Object
crmp.description: (2) A data controller shall discontinue the processing of personal data, unless the data controller demonstrates a compelling public interest or other lawful grounds, which overrides the fundamental rights and freedoms, and the interests of the data subject.
crmp.plain: If an individual objects to the processing of their personal data, the bank must stop processing it unless the bank can prove there is a compelling public interest or another lawful reason that outweighs the individual’s rights and freedoms.
crmp.riskDescription: Weak justification may be rejected by NDPC.
crmp.primaryControl: Require Legal review before overriding objection.

crmp.title: Security, Integrity, and Confidentiality
crmp.description: (1) A data controller and data processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security, integrity and confidentiality of personal data in its possession or under its control, including protection against accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, misuse, alteration, unauthorised disclosure, or access, taking into account—  (a) the amount and sensitivity of the personal data; (b) the nature, degree and likelihood of harm to a data subject that could result from the loss, disclosure, or other misuse of the personal data; (c) the extent of the processing; (d) the period of data retention; and (e) the availability and cost of any technologies, tools, or other measures to be implemented relative to the size of the data controller or data processor.
crmp.plain: The bank must implement appropriate technical and organizational controls to protect personal data from unauthorized access, loss, or damage. The measures should consider: - The sensitivity and volume of data; - Potential harm to individuals if data is mishandled; - The scale and duration of data processing; - Available and cost-effective security technologies.
crmp.riskDescription: Weak security framework increases exposure to data breaches
crmp.primaryControl: Risk-based technical and organisational measures

crmp.description: (2) Measures implemented under subsection (1) may include— (a) pseudonymisation or other methods of de-identification of personal data; (b) encryption of personal data; (c) processes to ensure security, integrity, confidentiality, availability and resilience of processing systems and services; (d) processes to restore availability of and access to personal data in a timely manner, in the event of a physical or technical incident; (e) periodic assessment of risks to processing systems and services, including where the processing involves the transmission of data over an electronic communications network; (f) regular testing, assessing, and evaluation of the effectiveness of the measures implemented against current and evolving risks identified; (g) regular updating of the measures and introduction of new measures to address shortcomings in effectiveness, and accommodate evolving risks.

crmp.title: Personal Data Breaches
crmp.description: (1) Where personal data breach has occurred with respect to personal data being stored or processed by a data controller or data processor, the data processor shall, on becoming aware of a breach—  (a) notify the data controller or data processor that engaged it, describing the nature of the personal data breach including, where possible, the categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and personal data records concerned; and (b) respond to all information requests from the data controller or data processor that engaged it, as they may require to comply with their obligations under this section.
crmp.plain: When a data processor becomes aware of a data breach, it must promptly notify the bank (data controller) and provide details about the breach, including affected data categories and numbers, and assist the bank in fulfilling its legal obligations.
crmp.riskDescription: Processor fails to notify the bank about breach
crmp.primaryControl: Contractual obligation for processors to notify bank

crmp.title: Personal Data Breaches
crmp.description: (2) A data controller shall, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach which is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, notify the Commission of the breach and, where feasible, describe the nature of the personal data breach including, where possible, the categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and personal data records concerned.
crmp.plain: If the bank becomes aware of a data breach likely to harm individuals’ rights or freedoms, it must notify the data protection Commission within 72 hours, describing the breach and affected data as fully as possible.

crmp.title: Adequacy of Protection
crmp.description: (2) The adequacy of protection referred to in subsection (1) shall be assessed taking into account the— (a) availability of enforceable data subject rights, the ability of a data subject to enforce such rights through administrative or judicial redress, and the rule of law; (b) existence of any appropriate instrument between the Commission and a competent authority in the recipient jurisdiction that ensures adequate data protection; (c) access of a public authority to personal data; (d) existence of an effective data protection law; (e) existence and functioning of an independent, competent data protection, or similar supervisory authority with adequate enforcement powers; and (f) international commitments and conventions binding on the relevant country and its membership of any multilateral or regional organisations.

crmp.title: Customer identification
crmp.description: FIs shall identify their customer (whether permanent or occasional,and whether natural or legal persons or legal arrangements) and obtain the following information — (a) for Individuals — (i) legal name and any other names used (such as maiden name), (ii) permanent address (full physical address), (iii) residential address (where the customer can be located), (iv) telephone number, e-mail address and social media handle, (v) date and place of birth, (vi) Bank Verification Number (BVN), (vii) Tax Identification Number (TIN), (viii) nationality, (ix) occupation, public position held and name of employer, (x) an official personal identification number or other unique identifier contained in an unexpired document issued by a government agency, that bears a name, photograph and signature of the customer such as a passport, national identification card, residence permit, social security records or drivers’ license, (xi) type of account and nature of the banking relationship, and (xii) signature, and (xiii) politically exposed persons (PEPs) status ;
crmp.plain: The Bank must collect and verify full identification information for every individual customer, whether they are permanent or occasional. This applies to all natural persons opening an account or conducting transactions. The required information includes: 1. Full legal name and any other names used (e.g., maiden name) 2. Permanent and residential address 3. Telephone number, email address, and social media handle 4. Date and place of birth 5. Bank Verification Number (BVN) 6. Tax Identification Number (TIN) 7. Nationality 8. Occupation, public position held, and employer name 9. A valid government-issued ID with photo, name, and signature (e.g., passport, driver’s license, national ID) 10. Type of account and purpose of the banking relationship 11. Customer’s signature 12. Politically Exposed Person (PEP) status  The Bank must ensure that all the above information is properly documented and verified during account opening or onboarding, in compliance with KYC and AML/CFT requirements
crmp.riskDescription: Incomplete or unverified identity data could lead to onboarding of high-risk or illicit customers, facilitating ML/TF/PF.
crmp.primaryControl: KYC checklist with mandatory fields, ID validation tools, BVN/TIN verification portals

crmp.plain: The Bank must collect and verify detailed information before opening an account for any legal entity or legal arrangement (e.g., companies, partnerships, NGOs, trusts). The following information must be obtained and documented: 1. Name of the institution or entity 2. Mailing address 3. Email address and social media handle 4. Phone numbers 5. Corporate registration number 6. Registered address 7. Business/operational address 8. Valid legal identifier, such as a Tax Identification Number (TIN) 9. Nature and purpose of the business or legal activity 10. Certified true copy of incorporation documents (e.g., certificate of incorporation) 11. Certified true copy of the memorandum and articles of association (or similar founding documents) 12. Certified true copy of the list of directors and shareholders (or similar documentation) 13. Board resolution authorizing the opening of the account 14. Identification of authorized signatories (those allowed to operate the account) 15. Legal documents identifying persons who control or influence the entity’s assets (e.g., beneficial owners, trustees) 16. Valid ID documents for those individuals identified in item 15 17. Names and valid ID documents of all individuals in senior management positions 18. The Bank must sight and retain the original versions of all documents listed in items 10–14.  All this information must be collected, verified, and securely documented to establish the legitimacy, control structure, and risk profile of the legal entity. This ensures compliance with CBN’s Know Your Customer (KYC), AML, and CFT requirements.

crmp.description: (1) FIs shall understand and obtain sufficient information on the nature and purpose of the business that its customer intends to undertake, including expected or predictable patterns of transactions.

crmp.title: Ongoing Due Diligence
crmp.description: (1) FIs shall conduct ongoing due diligence on a business relationship and scrutinize transactions undertaken throughout the course of the relationship to ensure that the transactions being conducted are consistent with the — (a) FI’s knowledge of the customer ; (b) customer’s business and risk profile ; and (c) source of funds.
crmp.plain: The bank must continuously monitor customer transactions to ensure they match what it knows about the customer’s identity, business, risk profile, and the source of their funds.
crmp.riskDescription: Undetected suspicious activity; outdated customer data
crmp.primaryControl: Ongoing monitoring using automated systems; periodic KYC reviews

crmp.plain: The bank must apply customer due diligence (CDD) to existing customers based on the risk level and continue to monitor the relationship as necessary.

crmp.title: Reliance on identification and verification already performed
crmp.description: (1) FIs may rely on the identification and verification steps that it had previously undertaken, unless it has doubts about the veracity of that information or where there is a material change in the circumstances or profile of the customer.
crmp.plain: The bank can rely on customer identification and verification already completed unless: - There is a reason to doubt the accuracy of the information; or - The customer’s situation or profile has significantly changed.

crmp.riskDescription: Risk of tipping off a suspect, interfering with an investigation
crmp.primaryControl: Employee STR decision-making training and escalation protocol

crmp.title: Record-Keeping
crmp.description: In addition to the provisions of regulation 35 of the CBN AML, CFT and CPF Regulations, FIs shall — (a) keep all records obtained through CDD measures, account files and business correspondence, and results of any analysis undertaken, either in electronic or written form for at least five years following the termination or cessation of the business relationship or after the date of the occasional transaction ; and
crmp.plain: The Bank must retain all customer due diligence (CDD) records, account files, correspondence, and analysis (in physical or digital format) for at least five (5) years after the account is closed or after any one-off transaction.
crmp.riskDescription: Non-compliance could lead to sanctions and loss of historical audit trail.
crmp.primaryControl: Automated archiving system with date stamps; periodic backup to secure servers.

crmp.title: External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts

crmp.plain: The bank must ensure that the customer truly lives permanently outside Nigeria before opening an account for them.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of opening external accounts for ineligible or misrepresented individuals.
crmp.primaryControl: Review of valid foreign residential documentation; verification through embassy or other reputable institution.

crmp.title: External and Non-Resident Non-Nigerians Accounts
crmp.description: (9) Where approvals are granted for individuals (including directors of legal persons) that are non-Nigerian and non-resident, the requirements of regulations 6 and 7 of these Regulations shall apply and the appropriate category of BVN as relates to non-resident individuals shall apply.
crmp.plain: When non-Nigerian, non-resident individuals (including directors of companies) are approved for accounts, The Bank must follow Regulations 6 and 7 (general CDD/KYC obligations) and apply the appropriate BVN category for non-resident individuals.
crmp.riskDescription: Inadequate due diligence on non-resident individuals could lead to ML/TF exposure, regulatory breaches, or reputational harm.
crmp.primaryControl: Use of onboarding checklist for non-resident individuals; ensure proper CDD under Regs 6 & 7; validate BVN as per non-resident classification.

crmp.title: Non-Resident Nigerians
crmp.description: (1) FIs shall obtain and verify applicant’s name, date of birth and permanent residential address (in host country) directly through a reputable Credit Institution or FI in the applicant’s country of residence or a correspondent bank, provided that particular care shall be taken when relying on identification evidence obtained from other countries.
crmp.plain: The Bank must obtain and verify the name, date of birth, and permanent residential address (in the host country) of non-resident Nigerian applicants.  This should be done through a reputable Credit Institution, financial institution, or correspondent bank in the applicant's country of residence.  The Bank must exercise extra caution when using foreign-sourced identification evidence.
crmp.riskDescription: Weak verification of identity or source of funds may enable fraud, ML/TF, or misuse of the banking system.
crmp.primaryControl: Onboarding procedure includes mandatory verification with reputable foreign FI or correspondent bank and mandatory documentation of source of funds as per the regulation.

crmp.title: Non-Resident Nigerians
crmp.description: (2) FIs shall validate the source of funds by obtaining identification issued by employer, payslips or statements of accounts from a bank in the country of residence.
crmp.plain: The bank must confirm where the applicant’s money is coming from by collecting: - A valid ID issued by the applicant’s employer, - Recent payslips, or - Bank statements from the applicant’s financial institution in their country of residence.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of onboarding individuals with illicit or unverifiable income.
crmp.primaryControl: Require one or more of the listed documents for validation of source of funds.

crmp.title: Resident Non-Nigerians
crmp.description: (1) FIs shall, as part of CDD measures, obtain and verify the valid Resident Permit of resident non-Nigerians.
crmp.plain: The bank must collect and verify a valid Resident Permit from any non-Nigerian applying to open an account or use banking services in Nigeria.
crmp.riskDescription: Failure to verify residency or identity may result in onboarding illegal migrants or impersonators.
crmp.primaryControl: Include Resident Permit verification in onboarding checklist. Require notarized home country address for new arrivals.

crmp.title: Resident Non-Nigerians
crmp.description: (2) Where a foreign national has recently arrived in Nigeria, the residential address in the applicant’s home country shall be notarized.

crmp.riskDescription: Risk of false identity or unverifiable residential information being used for account creation.
