crmp.title: Correspondent Banking Relationship
crmp.description: (1) Transactions conducted through correspondent relationships shall be managed in accordance with a risk-based approach.
crmp.plain: The bank must manage all correspondent banking relationships using a risk-based approach to identify and respond to potential money laundering or terrorism financing risks.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of exposure to money laundering, terrorist financing, or dealing with shell banks through unregulated or high-risk correspondent relationships.
crmp.primaryControl: - Risk-based due diligence - Verification of AML regulation status - Internal AML/KYC policy checks - Recordkeeping - Staff training - STR reporting - Termination of risky relationships

points.text: The bank must manage all correspondent banking relationships using a risk-based approach to identify and respond to potential money laundering or terrorism financing risks.
points.content: The bank must manage all correspondent banking relationships using a risk-based approach to identify and respond to potential money laundering or terrorism financing risks.

crmp.title: Correspondent Banking Relationship
crmp.description: (2) Due diligence procedures shall be established to ascertain whether or not the correspondent bank or the counter-party is itself regulated for prevention of ML, TF or PF, and where regulated, the correspondent respondent shall verify the identity of its customers in accordance with FATF standards.
crmp.plain: Before entering into a correspondent banking relationship, the bank must confirm that the correspondent bank is regulated for AML/CFT, and ensure it verifies the identity of its own customers using FATF standards.
crmp.riskDescription: Entering into a relationship with an unregulated or non-compliant correspondent bank may expose the bank to ML/TF/PF risks, enforcement penalties, or reputational damage.
crmp.primaryControl: Perform and document AML/CFT checks on counterparties; require CDD/EDD reports from correspondents; review FATF alignment

points.text: Before entering into a correspondent banking relationship, the bank must confirm that the correspondent bank is regulated for AML/CFT, and ensure it verifies the identity of its own customers using FATF standards.
points.content: Before entering into a correspondent banking relationship, the bank must confirm that the correspondent bank is regulated for AML/CFT, and ensure it verifies the identity of its own customers using FATF standards.

crmp.title: Correspondent Banking Relationship
crmp.description: (3) Where the correspondent bank or the counter-party is itself unregulated, additional due diligence shall be required to ascertain and assess the correspondent or respondent’s internal policy for prevention of ML, TF or PF and KYC procedures.
crmp.plain: If the correspondent bank is unregulated, the bank must carry out enhanced due diligence to evaluate the bank’s internal AML/CFT and KYC policies before proceeding.
crmp.riskDescription: Partnering with an unregulated entity without strong internal controls could facilitate ML/TF/PF and result in regulatory sanctions or reputational harm.
crmp.primaryControl: Perform enhanced due diligence, including review of internal AML/CFT and KYC policies, governance framework, and effectiveness of controls

points.text: If the correspondent bank is unregulated, the bank must carry out enhanced due diligence to evaluate the bank's internal AML/CFT and KYC policies before proceeding.
points.content: If the correspondent bank is unregulated, the bank must carry out enhanced due diligence to evaluate the bank's internal AML/CFT and KYC policies before proceeding.

crmp.title: Correspondent Banking Relationship
crmp.description: (5) FIs shall maintain records and ensure that sufficient due diligence has been undertaken by the remitting bank on the underlying client and the origin of the funds in respect of the funds passed through their accounts.
crmp.plain: The bank must keep proper records and ensure that the remitting bank has verified both the identity of the customer and the source of the funds before accepting any transaction.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of processing illicit or unverified funds due to weak checks by the remitting institution, leading to AML/CFT breaches.
crmp.primaryControl: Require remitting bank to provide evidence of KYC and source of funds checks before processing; periodic audits

points.text: The bank must keep proper records and ensure that the remitting bank has verified both the identity of the customer and the source of the funds before accepting any transaction.
points.content: The bank must keep proper records and ensure that the remitting bank has verified both the identity of the customer and the source of the funds before accepting any transaction.

crmp.title: Correspondent Banking Relationship
crmp.description: (6) FIs shall guard against establishing correspondent relationships with high risk foreign banks such as shell banks or with correspondent banks that permit their accounts to be used by such banks.
crmp.plain: The bank must avoid establishing relationships with shell banks or any correspondent bank that allows access to shell banks or other high-risk institutions.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of being used as a conduit for money laundering or terrorist financing through relationships with non-transparent or unregulated entities.
crmp.primaryControl: Conduct thorough background checks; maintain a list of prohibited entities; update risk appetite criteria

points.text: The bank must avoid establishing relationships with shell banks or any correspondent bank that allows access to shell banks or other high-risk institutions.
points.content: The bank must avoid establishing relationships with shell banks or any correspondent bank that allows access to shell banks or other high-risk institutions.

crmp.title: Correspondent Banking Relationship
crmp.description: (7) Staff dealing with correspondent banking accounts shall be trained to recognize higher risk circumstances and be prepared to challenge the correspondents over irregular activity whether isolated transactions or trend and to submit a suspicious transaction report to the NFIU.
crmp.plain: Staff handling correspondent accounts must be trained to detect high-risk activity, challenge unusual transactions, and report suspicious activity to the NFIU when needed.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of undetected suspicious transactions due to untrained or unaware staff, leading to regulatory breaches or ML/TF exposure.
crmp.primaryControl: Targeted AML/CFT training for relevant staff; escalation procedures; STR reporting protocols

points.text: Staff handling correspondent accounts must be trained to detect high-risk activity, challenge unusual transactions, and report suspicious activity to the NFIU when needed.
points.content: Staff handling correspondent accounts must be trained to detect high-risk activity, challenge unusual transactions, and report suspicious activity to the NFIU when needed.

crmp.title: Correspondent Banking Relationship
crmp.description: (8) FIs shall terminate an account with a correspondent bank that fails to provide satisfactory answers to questions including confirming the identity of customers involved in unusual or suspicious circumstances.
crmp.plain: The bank must immediately terminate any correspondent relationship if the other bank fails to provide clear information or refuses to confirm customer identities in suspicious circumstances.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of continued exposure to ML/TF activity by maintaining relationships with non-cooperative or non-transparent banks.
crmp.primaryControl: Clear policy and procedure for termination of non-compliant correspondent relationships; escalation protocol

points.text: The bank must immediately terminate any correspondent relationship if the other bank fails to provide clear information or refuses to confirm customer identities in suspicious circumstances.
points.content: The bank must immediately terminate any correspondent relationship if the other bank fails to provide clear information or refuses to confirm customer identities in suspicious circumstances.

crmp.title: Trusts
crmp.description: Where the arrangement for a Foreign Trust or Foundation is opaque or information on the parties to the legal arrangements cannot be provided because it is incorporated in a jurisdiction (such as tax havens and off-shore financial centres) that makes it impractical to do so, the FI shall decline to open an account for the legal arrangement.
crmp.plain: The bank must not open an account for a foreign trust or foundation if the ownership or control structure is unclear or if required information about the parties involved cannot be obtained due to the trust being based in a secrecy jurisdiction.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of facilitating money laundering or tax evasion through untraceable legal arrangements or offshore secrecy structures.
crmp.primaryControl: Prohibit onboarding of opaque foreign trusts; require full disclosure and verification of UBOs before onboarding.

points.text: The bank must not open an account for a foreign trust or foundation if the ownership or control structure is unclear or if required information about the parties involved cannot be obtained due to the trust being based in a secrecy jurisdiction.

crmp.title: Foreign Intermediaries
crmp.description: Where business is introduced or received from a financial intermediary regulated for AML and CFT, who is outside Nigeria, the reliance that shall be placed on that intermediary to undertake the verification of identity-check shall be assessed by the Compliance Officer or some other competent persons within the FI, on a case-by-case basis based on the knowledge of the intermediary.
crmp.plain: If a foreign bank (outside Nigeria) introduces a customer and is regulated for AML/CFT, the bank must assess—on a case-by-case basis—whether it can rely on that intermediary for customer identity verification. This assessment must be done by the Compliance Officer or another qualified officer, based on how well the bank knows the intermediary.
crmp.riskDescription: Over-reliance on weak foreign institutions for KYC checks.

crmp.title: Corporate Group Introduction
crmp.description: (1) Where a customer is introduced by one part of a financial sector group to another, the customer’s identity shall be re-verified, and the records shall not be duplicated except— (a) the identity of the customer has not been verified by the introducing parent company, branch, subsidiary or associate in line with the money laundering requirements of equivalent standards and taking account of any specific requirements such as separate address verification; (b) no exemptions or concessions have been applied in the original verification procedures that may not be available to the new relationship; (c) a group introduction letter is obtained and placed with the customer’s account opening records; and (d) in respect of group introducers from outside Nigeria, in which case arrangements shall be put in place to ensure that identity is verified in accordance with requirements and that the underlying records of identity in respect of the introduced customers are retained for the required period.
crmp.plain: When a customer is referred by another part of the same financial group (like a parent, branch, or affiliate), the customer’s identity must be re-verified unless all of the following conditions are met:  (a) The previous verification was done properly, in line with equivalent anti-money laundering (AML) standards, including address checks if required. (b) The previous verification did not rely on exemptions or shortcuts that the new bank cannot apply. (c) A group introduction letter has been collected and filed with the new account documents. (d) If the introduction is from outside Nigeria, the FI must ensure that identity was verified correctly and that records will be kept for the required time.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of flawed onboarding from weak or exempted prior checks.
crmp.primaryControl: Verify each condition and retain letter; checklist.

crmp.source: INCLUSION OF INEC VOTER'S REGISTRATION CARD AS A MEANS OF CUSTOMER IDENTIFICATION, SEPTEMBER 2012
crmp.title: Uniform Account Opening Forms and Minimum KYC Requirements
crmp.description: Towards the effort to ensure that depositors in banks and other financial institutions provide necessary background information for effective Know Your Customer (KYC) due diligence,the CBN in collaboration with relevant stakeholders has developed Uniform Account Opening Forms. The uniformity is to ensure that Customer Due Diligence (CDD) is consistently and uniformly practiced in account opening process for prospective customers of financial institutions. Individual prospective customers are required to complete account opening FORM A(1), FORM A(2) and FORM A for accounts in Tier I, II and III respectively, while legal entities are to complete FORM B. Whereas prospective customers are required to provide the relevant information applicable to them as prescribed above, existing customers are to regularly update their records in line with the formats.
crmp.plain: The Bank must accept the INEC Voter’s Registration Card as a valid means of customer identification and use the CBN-approved Uniform Account Opening Forms for all new account openings. It must ensure that customers (individuals and legal entities) provide all required Know Your Customer (KYC) information based on their account type or tier, and that existing customers regularly update their records to align with the prescribed formats. This ensures consistent and effective Customer Due Diligence (CDD) across all financial institutions.
crmp.riskDescription: Risk of regulatory breach if non-standard forms or unapproved IDs are used; risk of onboarding unidentified or misrepresented customers.
crmp.primaryControl: Enforce use of approved forms and verify INEC Voter’s Card as ID; monitor for outdated records

crmp.source: National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) Act, 2007 (Access to Register Information in the National Identity Database Regulations, 2017)
crmp.title: Disclosure of Registered Information
crmp.description: (1) The Commission may provide any person other than designated persons stipulated under Regulations 5, 6 and 7 of these Regulations with the registered information of a registered individual where— (a) an application for the provision of the information to that person is made by or with the authority of that registered individual ; or (b) the registered individual consents to the provision of that information to that person by submitting his NIN or biometrics to the Commission. (2) The fingerprint and other biometric information shall be outside the purview of an application under sub-regulation (1) of this regulation. (3) The information that may be provided to a person under regulation 5 (3) of these Regulations shall be limited to— (b) any photograph of the registered individual recorded in the National identity database ; (c) the registered individual’s signature that is so recorded ; (d) information about whether the multipurpose identity card issued to the registered individual is active or inactive and if not active, the reason for it not being active ; (e) information in relation to confirmation whether or not information falling within sub-regulation (2) of this regulation submitted to the Commission corresponds with the information recorded in the registered individual’s entry in the National Identity Database ; and (f ) information in relation to confirmation that the registered individual’s entry in the National Identity Database does not contain information of a particular description falling within sub-regulation (2) of this regulation.
crmp.plain: The Bank may only request a customer’s registered information from the National Identity Database if the customer has either (a) authorized the request or (b) submitted their NIN or biometrics to the Commission. The Bank must not request access to fingerprints or biometric data. The Bank may only receive limited information: the customer’s photograph, signature, ID card status (and reason if inactive), and confirmation of whether the submitted identity data matches or that no biometric data is stored in the database.

crmp.source: National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) Act, 2007 (Access to Register Information in the National Identity Database Regulations, 2017)
crmp.title: Access by Licensed Private Agencies
crmp.description: (1) The Commission may, with the consent of a registered individual, grant access to licenced private sector agencies for the purpose of verification and authentication of the identity of that individual. (2) The disclosure of registered information about the registered individual to the licensed private agency shall be— (a) for the purpose connected with the carrying out of that agency’s function of verifying the registered individual for the provision of a requested service ; (b) upon the payment of applicable fees ; and (c) on the grant of licence to that agency by the Commission. (3) The Commission may, for the purposes of this regulation, provide secured access through various platforms to licensed private agencies. (4) The platforms referred to in sub-regulation (3) of this regulation, shall be password login-protected, have user accounts, access level rights, login credentials for proper auditing and have further security features in accordance with international best practices. (5) Registered information that may be disclosed to a licensed private agency pursuant to this regulation shall be limited to information listed under Regulation 4 (3) of these Regulations and subject to the terms and conditions of the licence issued to the agency.
crmp.plain: The Bank may only access a customer’s identity information in the National Identity Database for verification purposes if the customer consents, the Bank is licensed by the NIMC, and all applicable fees are paid. Access must be through secure, audited, login-protected platforms provided by NIMC. The Bank can only view limited data listed under Regulation 4(3), and only as allowed by its licence.

crmp.description: The signatories verification portal is expected to replace the printed signature booklets that banks distribute, such that instructions/documents received from other banks can be verified electronically (online). crmp.title: BPS/DIR/GEN/CIR/02/004
crmp.description: The Central Bank of Nigeria, in furtherance of its efforts at combating fraud within the Banking Industry, established the Nigeria Electronic Fraud Forum (NeFF) to proffer solutions towards addressing frauds arising from the increased adoption of electronic payments. Following submissions to the Bank by NeFF and consultations with DMBs and electronic payments service providers, it has become imperative that an effective mechanism for receiving and responding promptly to fraud alerts be set up within the Nigerian Banking industry, towards managing and reducing successful electronic payments fraud rate in the Nigerian Banking Industry.  To this end, all DMBs, MMOs, Switches and all payments service providers are hereby directed to maintain a dedicated Fraud Desk in their respective organisations. The Fraud Desk shall be appropriately staffed with personnel that have requisite training on emerging fraud trends on various electronic payments channels. The desk shall, at a minimum, offer the following services:  1. Provide support to customers on electronic frauds with a minimum of 10 dedicated phone lines, manned and available to customers at all times; 2. Make available the option for calls to contact centre, in respect of fraud alerts or complaints, to be redirected to fraud desk; 3. Block and/or Place No Debit restrictions on accounts upon receipt of fraud complaint; 4. Receive customers’ stop-transaction instructions to block their accounts through short codes service provided to customers by the banks; 5. Log all customer fraud alert and/or complain and escalate in line with internally predefined escalation path; 6. Submit reports to the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) Plc on fraud information logged by the fraud desk; 7. Honour “hold” instructions from NIBSS with respect to fraud matters and grant NIBSS permissions to view details on logged transactions; 8. Sensitise customers on e-Fraud and Fraud Desk services; 9. Manage/Resolve all intra-bank fraud issues leveraging an enterprise fraud management system; 10. Maintain a mail group mapped to members of the fraud desk team.  Further to the above: Banks shall implement across all electronic channels, an enterprise fraud monitoring system, which ensures behavioural monitoring, patterns and hold/block controls on transactions suspected to be fraudulent, etc. Banks may subscribe to NIBSS’ central anti-fraud solution for this purpose.
crmp.plain: The bank must: 1. Establish and maintain a dedicated Fraud Desk. 2. Staff the desk with trained personnel on emerging e-fraud trends. 3. Provide at least 10 dedicated phone lines available 24/7 to customers. 4. Redirect fraud-related calls from the contact center to the Fraud Desk. 5. Place No Debit restrictions or block accounts immediately upon receiving fraud complaints. 6. Enable customers to stop transactions via short code services. 7. Log and escalate all fraud alerts/complaints based on internal escalation procedures. 8. Report fraud cases to NIBSS. 9. Honour “hold” instructions from NIBSS and grant it access to logged transaction details. 10. Sensitize customers regularly about e-fraud and Fraud Desk services. 11. Resolve intra-bank frauds using an enterprise fraud management system (EFMS). 12. Maintain a functional email group for the fraud desk team. 13. Implement a centralized enterprise fraud monitoring system across all e-channels (or subscribe to NIBSS’ anti-fraud solution).
crmp.riskDescription: - May lead to financial losses, regulatory penalties, reputational damage, and loss of customer confidence. - Poor fraud escalation or failure to honour NIBSS instructions may be seen as regulatory non-compliance. - Lack of real-time fraud monitoring tools may allow fraudulent activities to go undetected.

esg.title: Financial Inclusion
esg.description: • Development of a financial inclusion policy, either as a standalone policy or integrated into the Sustainable Banking policy. The policy will be consistent with the CBN Financial Inclusion Strategy and will:   o Support SME development and growth.   o Define a financial literacy framework, promote inclusion of financial literacy curricula in primary, secondary and tertiary institutions of learning by 2020.    o Promote consumer protection: implement consumer protection framework as defined by the CBN by 2012.   o Develop products and services tailored to middle, low income and disadvantaged groups (e.g. female and youth clients) consistent with the CBN strategy including:   o For female client segments:  • Target of 60% of the micro SME development funds at women borrowers;   • Require a minimum level of female staff of 30% in microfinance banks;   • Encourage female management at retail agents;   • Offer specifically tailored women entrepreneurship development.   o For youth client segments:  • Ensure inclusion of 50% of youth that turn 18 every year;   • Develop and implement a framework for child and youth finance;   • Implement children and youth financial literacy initiatives in Nigerian education institutions.   o Drive innovation for improved financial system accessibility and usage (e.g. branchless banking, access to physically challenged persons).   • Development of implementation plan to initially establish and roll-out financial inclusion requirements; on-going implementation thereafter.
esg.plain: The Bank shall develop a financial inclusion policy, either as a standalone policy or integrated into its Sustainable Banking Policy, consistent with the CBN Financial Inclusion Strategy, to:  a) Support SME development and growth. b) Define a financial literacy framework and promote inclusion of financial literacy curricula in primary, secondary, and tertiary institutions of learning. c) Promote consumer protection by implementing the consumer protection framework as defined by the CBN. d) Develop products and services tailored to middle, low-income, and disadvantaged groups (e.g., female and youth clients) in line with the CBN strategy, including: e) For female clients: i. Allocate 60% of micro-SME development funds to women borrowers. ii. Maintain a minimum level of 30% female staff in microfinance operations. iii. Encourage female management at retail agents. iv. Offer specifically tailored women entrepreneurship development programs. f) For youth clients: i. Ensure inclusion of 50% of youth turning 18 every year. ii. Develop and implement a framework for child and youth finance. iii. Implement children and youth financial literacy initiatives in Nigerian educational institutions. g) Drive innovation for improved financial system accessibility and usage (e.g., branchless banking, access for physically challenged persons). h) The Bank shall also develop and implement an implementation plan to establish and roll out these financial inclusion requirements, with ongoing application thereafter.
esg.riskDescription: Failure to implement financial inclusion measures may lead to regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, exclusion from CBN incentives, and poor public perception.
esg.responsibility: Head of Strategy / Compliance / Retail Banking
esg.primaryControl: Internal policy and procedures; periodic compliance review; product development strategy aligned with CBN
esg.additionalControl: Internal audit monitoring; regulatory engagement; stakeholder training

esg.title: Climate Change Obligations of Private Entities
esg.description: (1) Any private entity with employees numbering 50 and above, shall — (a) put in place measures to achieve the annual carbon emission reduction targets in line with the Action Plan; and (b) designate a Climate Change Officer or an Environmental Sustainability Officer, who shall submit to the Secretariat, through the State Director, annual reports on the entity's efforts at meeting its carbon emission reduction and climate adaptation plan.  (2) A private entity that fails to meet its target, as specified under subsection (1) shall be liable to a fine to be determined by the Council, relying on a system of Environmental Economic Accounting with attention on the health impacts, impact on climate variation, and total damage to ecosystem services.
esg.plain: The Bank as an entity with 50 or more employees must: - Implement measures to achieve annual carbon emission reduction targets in line with Nigeria's National Action Plan. - Appoint a Climate Change Officer or Environmental Sustainability Officer. - Submit annual climate compliance reports to the Secretariat via the State Director, detailing progress on emission reduction and climate adaptation efforts.
esg.deadlineType: - Annually: Report submission. - Ongoing: Implementation of carbon reduction measures.
esg.riskDescription: - Regulatory penalties or fines for non-compliance. - Risk of reputational damage due to perceived environmental negligence. - Potential disqualification from public procurement or sustainability-driven funding. - Operational risk due to failure in adapting to regulatory climate reporting.
esg.owner: - Chief Sustainability Officer (CSO) - Head of ESG (Environmental, Social & Governance) - Facility/Operations Manager - Climate Change Officer
esg.responsibility: - Climate Change Officer - Head of Sustainability - Chief Risk Officer
esg.primaryControl: - Develop and implement an internal carbon emission tracking and reduction plan. - Appoint a qualified Climate or Sustainability Officer. - Submit annual environmental performance reports to regulatory bodies. - Embed climate change metrics into corporate KPIs and ESG reports.
esg.additionalControl: - Conduct third-party environmental audits to validate reports. - Integrate carbon management tools and emissions tracking software. - Join industry coalitions or alliances for climate best practices.

esg.source: The Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE) Sustainable Disclosure Guidelines
esg.title: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability
esg.description: 3.1 Principle 1: Businesses should conduct and govern themselves with Ethics, Transparency and Accountability.Core Elements:1. Develop governance structures, procedures and practices that ensure ethical conduct at all levels; and promote adoption across value chain.2. Communicate transparently and assure access to information about stakeholder-impacting decisions.3. Avoid abusive, corrupt, or anti-competitive practices.4. Discharge responsibility on financial and other mandatory disclosures truthfully.5. Report adoption status of these Guidelines as per recommendations.6. Avoid complicity with third parties violating these principles.
esg.plain: The Bank shall establish governance systems that ensure ethical behavior at all levels, ensure transparency in its decisions, avoid unethical practices, and report on compliance with these guidelines.
esg.riskDescription: Failure to uphold ethical standards or transparency could lead to loss of trust, legal action, or sanctions.
esg.primaryControl: Governance frameworks, transparency policies, code of ethics, disclosure protocols
esg.additionalControl: Regular training on ethics and transparency, independent compliance reviews

esg.title: Responsible Policy Advocacy
esg.description: 3.2 Principle 2: Businesses, when engaged in influencing public and regulatory policy, should do so in a responsible manner.Core Elements:1. While pursuing policy advocacy, businesses should ensure their advocacy positions align with the Principles and Core Elements of these Guidelines.2. To the extent possible, businesses should use trade, commerce, industry chambers, associations, or other collective platforms for policy advocacy.
esg.plain: The Bank shall ensure that any attempt to influence public policy or regulation aligns with ethical and responsible Bankprinciples and, where possible, be done through credible collective platforms.
esg.riskDescription: Irresponsible or unethical advocacy could damage the company’s public reputation, regulatory relationships, or result in penalties.
esg.primaryControl: Internal policy for advocacy conduct, stakeholder engagement protocols, executive approvals
esg.additionalControl: Periodic review of policy positions, industry association engagement, advocacy register

esg.source: The Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE) Sustainable Disclosure Guidelines
esg.title: Safe and Sustainable Products & Services
esg.description: 3.3 Principle 3: Businesses should provide products and services that are safe and contribute to sustainability throughout their life cycle.Core Elements:1. Assure safety and optimal resource use from design to disposal and ensure all connected parties are aware of responsibilities.2. Ensure proper labeling, accurate marketing, content transparency, and guidance on usage and disposal.3. Use resource-efficient and sustainable manufacturing processes.4. Continuously improve technology development with social, ethical, and environmental considerations.5. Respect rights of traditional knowledge and intellectual property holders.6. Promote sustainable consumption and recycling to avoid resource overuse.7. Maintain responsible procurement practices covering fairness, corruption, child/forced labour, support for SMEs/women-owned businesses, health & safety.
esg.plain: The Bank shall ensure its products and services are safe, resource-efficient, properly labeled, and sustainably managed across the full life cycle. It must engage in responsible procurement and uphold environmental and ethical standards in technology and sourcing.
esg.riskDescription: Unsafe or unsustainable products can result in consumer harm, legal action, reputational damage, and environmental degradation.
esg.primaryControl: Product life cycle analysis, labeling policies, sustainable sourcing guidelines, supplier code of conduct
esg.additionalControl: Environmental audits, R&D innovation reviews, supplier ESG assessments

esg.source: The Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE) Sustainable Disclosure Guidelines
esg.title: Responsible Customer & Consumer Engagement
esg.description: 3.4 Principle 4: Businesses should engage with and provide value to their customers and consumers in a responsible manner.Core Elements:1. Serve customer needs while considering their wellbeing and societal impact.2. Avoid restricting customer freedom or limiting fair competition.3. Disclose product information truthfully, including individual, societal, and environmental risks; educate customers on safe usage.4. Avoid misleading advertising and uphold transparency in promotions.5. Exercise caution in promoting products that could exploit resources or encourage excessive consumption.6. Establish proper customer grievance mechanisms to address complaints and feedback.
esg.plain: The Bank shall engage with customers responsibly by ensuring product transparency, ethical marketing, informed choice, and access to complaint resolution. It must avoid misleading promotions and protect the wellbeing of both consumers and society.
esg.riskDescription: Misleading advertising, inadequate disclosures, or poor grievance handling can lead to customer dissatisfaction, litigation, reputational loss, or regulatory fines.
esg.primaryControl: Product disclosure protocols, marketing review checklists, fair competition policies, customer service standards
esg.additionalControl: Customer education programs, periodic customer satisfaction surveys, independent ad review panels

esg.source: The Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE) Sustainable Disclosure Guidelines
esg.title: Employee Wellbeing
esg.description: 3.5 Principle 5: Businesses should promote the wellbeing of all employees.Core Elements:1. Respect freedom of association, collective bargaining, and access to grievance mechanisms.2. Ensure equal opportunity at hiring and during employment regardless of caste, creed, gender, race, religion, or disability.3. Prohibit use of child, forced, or involuntary labour.4. Consider work-life balance, especially for women.5. Provide welfare facilities, including for employees with special needs, and pay fair living wages.6. Maintain a safe, hygienic, and humane workplace environment that preserves employee dignity; communicate and train on these standards.7. Offer equal and non-discriminatory access to skills development, learning, and career growth.
esg.plain: The Bank shall promote the holistic wellbeing of employees by ensuring equal opportunity, fair wages, freedom of association, skill development, safe working conditions, and work-life balance.
esg.riskDescription: Poor labour practices, discrimination, unsafe work conditions, or inadequate development opportunities may result in employee disengagement, legal action, or reputational harm.
esg.primaryControl: Equal opportunity policy, health & safety policy, HR handbook, whistleblower and grievance redress system
esg.additionalControl: Staff training programs, diversity audits, periodic workplace condition assessments

esg.title: Stakeholder Engagement & Inclusion
esg.description: 3.6 Principle 6: Businesses should respect the interests of, and be responsive towards all stakeholders, especially those who are disadvantaged, vulnerable and marginalized.Core Elements:1. Identify stakeholders, understand their concerns, define engagement purpose and commit to engagement.2. Take responsibility and be transparent about the business’s impact on stakeholders.3. Give special attention to stakeholders in underdeveloped areas.4. Resolve stakeholder differences fairly and equitably.

esg.riskDescription: Lack of stakeholder engagement or disregard for vulnerable groups may lead to reputational damage, community unrest, or regulatory sanctions.
esg.primaryControl: Stakeholder mapping, ESG disclosure policies, grievance mechanisms, community engagement plans

esg.source: The Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE) Sustainable Disclosure Guidelines
esg.title: Respect and Promotion of Human Rights
esg.description: 3.7 Principle 7: Businesses should respect and promote human rights.Core Elements:1. Understand the human rights provisions of the Nigerian Constitution, relevant national laws, and international human rights instruments; recognize that human rights are inherent, universal, and interdependent.2. Integrate human rights into management systems by assessing and managing human rights impacts and ensuring access to grievance mechanisms.3. Respect the rights of all stakeholders—including employees, consumers, communities, and marginalized groups—within and beyond the workplace.4. Promote awareness and realization of human rights across the value chain.5. Avoid complicity in third-party human rights abuses.
esg.plain: The Bank shall respect and promote human rights in all operations by understanding legal and international obligations, embedding rights protections in management systems, and ensuring all stakeholders—especially the vulnerable—are protected from abuse and have access to redress.
esg.riskDescription: Violating or ignoring human rights can lead to legal liabilities, reputational damage, public protests, and investor withdrawal.
esg.primaryControl: Human rights due diligence, grievance redress systems, non-discrimination and fair treatment policies
esg.additionalControl: Human rights training, third-party audits, stakeholder engagement on rights awareness

esg.title: Inclusive Growth and Equitable Development
esg.description: 3.8 Principle 8: Businesses should support inclusive growth and equitable development.Core Elements:1. Understand the business’s impact on social and economic development and take action to minimize negative effects.2. Innovate and invest in products, technologies, and processes that enhance societal wellbeing.3. Support national and local development priorities and ensure fair resettlement and rehabilitation for displaced communities.4. Be especially sensitive to local concerns when operating in underdeveloped regions.

esg.riskDescription: Neglecting local community needs or causing displacement without proper rehabilitation can lead to conflicts, reputational harm, and legal penalties.
esg.primaryControl: Community impact assessments, CSR initiatives, rehabilitation and resettlement programs, stakeholder dialogue
esg.additionalControl: Continuous monitoring of community impact, third-party evaluations of CSR initiatives

esg.title: General Reporting Requirements
esg.description: 4.1 General Requirements: All listed companies should ensure that the sustainability report contains information relevant and meaningful to stakeholders. cybersecurity.title: Exceptions to Financial Institutions posting and authorized posting options.
cybersecurity.description: (1) From the commencement of this Act, no Financial Institution shall give posting and authorising access to any single employee. (3) Financial Institutions shall, as a duty to their customers, put in place effective counter-fraud measures to safeguard their sensitive information, where a security breach occurs the proof of negligence lies on the customer to prove the Financial Institution in question could have done more to safeguard its information integrity.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Not allow one employee to both initiate (post) and authorize financial transactions. 2. Ensure segregation of duties in financial operations. 3. Implement effective counter-fraud controls to protect customers’ sensitive information. 4. cybersecurity.title: Reporting Cyber Threats
cybersecurity.description: (1) Any person or institution, who operates a computer system or a network, whether public or private, must immediately inform the National Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) Coordination Centre through their respective sectoral CERTS or sectoral security operations centres (SOC) of any attacks, intrusions and other disruptions liable to hinder the functioning of another computer system or network, so that the National CERT can take the necessary measures to tackle the issues. (2) In such cases mentioned in subsection (1) above, and in order to protect computer systems and networks, the National CERT Coordination Center may propose the isolation of affected computer systems or network pending the resolution of the issues.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Immediately report any cyberattacks, intrusions, or disruptions that may affect other systems or networks to the National Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) through the bank's sectoral CERT or Security Operations Centre (SOC). 2. Cooperate with CERT recommendations, including isolating affected systems until the issue is resolved.
cybersecurity.riskDescription: - Failure to report threats could lead to non-compliance penalties. - Delay in reporting may worsen the impact of a cyberattack on the bank or other institutions. - Operational disruptions if systems are not properly isolated or handled per CERT guidelines. - Reputational risk for not acting swiftly during a cybersecurity incident.

cybersecurity.responsibility: - CISO- Compliance Officer- Head of IT- SOC Team Lead

cybersecurity.additionalControl: - Schedule periodic simulations and drills involving threat reporting to CERT. - Engage with industry CERT coordination workshops and updates. - Audit and review compliance with incident reporting SOPs. - Automate CERT notification triggers within the threat management system.

cybersecurity.title: Duties of Financial Institutions.
cybersecurity.description: (1) A Financial Institution shall— (a) verify the identity of its customers carrying out electronic financial transactions by requiring the customers to present National Identity Number issued by the National Identity Managment Commission and other valid documents bearing their names, addresses and other relevant information before issuance of ATM cards, credit cards, debit cards and other related electronic devices ; and (b) apply the principle of know your customer in documentation of customers preceding execution of customers electronic transfer, payment, debit and issuance orders.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall: (a) Verify customer identity before issuing any ATM card, debit/credit card, or electronic device, by collecting: – National Identity Number (NIN) from NIMC – Other valid documents with name, address, and other identifying information. (b) Apply Know Your Customer (KYC) principles before processing any: – Electronic transfers – Payments – Debit orders – Issuance orders

cybersecurity.riskDescription: - Violation of customer onboarding regulations. - Exposure to fraud and identity theft risks. - Regulatory sanctions from CBN, NIMC, or NDPC. - Reputational damage due to weak KYC practices. - Increased AML/CFT exposure if identities are not properly verified.

cybersecurity.additionalControl: - Periodic internal audits of account opening and KYC procedures. - Enable KYC review alerts for expiring documents or missing data. - Conduct staff training on identity verification and fraud prevention. - Implement data validation tools and 2FA for electronic transactions.

cybersecurity.title: Records Retention and Protection of Data
cybersecurity.description: (1) A service provider shall keep and protect specific traffic data and subscriber information in accordance with the provision of the Nigeria Data Protection Act and as may be prescribed by the relevant authority for the time being, responsible for the regulation of communication services in Nigeria, for a period of two years. (2) A Service Provider shall, at the request of the relevant authority referred to in subsection (1) of this section or any Law Enforcement Agency— (a) preserve, hold or retain any traffic data, subscriber information, non-content information, and content data ; or (b) release any information required to be kept under subsection (1) of this section.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Retain subscriber and traffic data securely for at least 2 years, in accordance with the Data Protection Act and relevant regulations. 2. Upon request by Law Enforcement Agencies or regulators, preserve, retain, and release traffic, subscriber, non-content, and content data as required by law.

cybersecurity.description: (1) Every Service Provider in Nigeria shall comply with all the provisions of this Act and disclose information requested by any Law Enforcement Agency or otherwise render assistance in any inquiry or proceeding under this Act. cybersecurity.title: Respinsibilities of the Board
cybersecurity.description: 1.0 Board Oversight and Cybersecurity Governance Responsibilities  The Board, through the Board Risk or Information Technology Committee, shall have oversight and responsibility for the cybersecurity programme of the Systemically Important Financial Institution (SFI). The Board shall provide leadership, direction, and resources for the effective implementation of cybersecurity processes and ensure that cybersecurity governance is integrated into the SFI’s organisational structure.  To this end, the Board shall be responsible for ensuring that:  i. At least two Non-Executive Directors (NEDs), one of whom shall be an Independent NED, possess requisite knowledge and experience in innovative financial technology, Information Communication Technology (ICT), and/or cybersecurity. ii. Cybersecurity is integrated with business functions and effectively managed across the SFI. iii. Cybersecurity governance aligns with Corporate and Information Technology (IT) governance and is driven by business objectives. iv. Cybersecurity management processes align with business requirements and applicable laws and regulations, while security targets are defined and met across the SFI. v. Senior Management provides central oversight for the cybersecurity programme, assigns responsibilities, and ensures the effectiveness of cybersecurity management processes. vi. The audit function remains independent and is staffed with skilled professionals who possess relevant qualifications and experience. vii. Cybersecurity governance documents (such as cybersecurity strategy, framework, and policies) are established and aligned with the SFI’s business goals and objectives. viii. Quarterly cybersecurity reports are presented by Senior Management to the Board. These reports shall include, at a minimum:  * a. Cyber risk assessment updates. * b. Status of security initiatives to address cyber risks. * c. Summary of incidents, including loss status and recovery efforts. * d. Vulnerability management and penetration testing reports, including remediation actions and compensating controls. * e. Compliance status with Board-approved cyber risk thresholds. * f. Status of implementation of recommendations from the CBN Cybersecurity Supervisory Review and Evaluation.  ix. A qualified individual is appointed as the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) on the recommendation of Senior Management. The CISO shall be responsible for overseeing and implementing the SFI’s cybersecurity programme.  x. In the case of banking groups, while SFIs may collaborate with the group-level CISO, a dedicated CISO shall still be appointed in accordance with Section 1.4 of this Framework.  xi. A stand-alone cybersecurity budget, distinct from the IT or Risk Management budget, is approved by the Board.  xii. The cybersecurity risk appetite is clearly defined and documented in the SFI’s Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework.  ---  ## **1.1.1 Cybersecurity Strategy and Framework**  The Board is responsible for the SFI’s cybersecurity strategy and shall ensure that:  i. The strategy defines how cybersecurity goals will be achieved, risks mitigated, and compliance with legal, regulatory, contractual, and statutory obligations ensured. ii. The cybersecurity framework aligns with business objectives and technology needs, and clearly defines key cybersecurity roles and responsibilities. iii. The cybersecurity policy clearly articulates the institution’s intent and approach toward achieving its cybersecurity objectives, including:  * Risk assessment * Security policy development * Incident response planning * Vulnerability management * Log monitoring   iv. The cybersecurity policy is reviewed at least annually, or upon significant changes to the SFI’s cyber risk exposure.  ---  ## **1.1.2 Cybersecurity Programme Requirements**  SFIs shall implement a comprehensive cybersecurity programme which shall, at a minimum, include:  * Data backup and recovery plans * Security awareness and training programmes * Initiatives to attain the target cybersecurity maturity level * Metrics to assess the effectiveness of the cybersecurity programme
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Ensure that at least two Non-Executive Directors (including one Independent Director) have relevant experience in financial technology, ICT, or cybersecurity.  2. Integrate cybersecurity into all business activities and manage it effectively.  3. Align its cybersecurity governance with overall business and IT goals.  4. Make sure cybersecurity processes follow legal requirements and business needs, and that defined security targets are met.  5. Assign central oversight of the cybersecurity programme to Senior Management, who shall ensure it runs effectively.  6. Maintain an independent audit function staffed with skilled and qualified professionals to review cybersecurity processes.  7. Establish and maintain cybersecurity strategy, framework, and policies that align with the Bank’s business goals.  8. Receive quarterly cybersecurity reports from Senior Management, which shall include:    - Cyber risk assessment updates      - Progress on key cybersecurity initiatives      - Summary of security incidents, including losses and recovery efforts      - Reports on system weaknesses and test results, including remedial actions      - Status of compliance with Board-approved cyber risk thresholds      - Implementation updates from CBN supervisory reviews  9. Appoint a qualified Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), based on Senior Management’s recommendation, to oversee and implement the cybersecurity programme.  10. Appoint a dedicated CISO even when operating as part of a larger banking group, in line with regulatory requirements.  11. Approve a separate and dedicated budget for cybersecurity, independent of the IT or Risk Management budget.  12. Define and document its cybersecurity risk appetite within the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework.  The Bank shall also ensure that its cybersecurity strategy:  - Clearly outlines how to meet cybersecurity goals and legal obligations   - Aligns with business and technology objectives   - Clearly defines cybersecurity responsibilities   - Covers areas such as risk assessments, security policies, incident response, vulnerability management, and activity monitoring   - Is reviewed at least annually or when there are major changes in cyber risk exposure  Furthermore, the Bank shall implement a cybersecurity programme that includes:  - A data backup and recovery plan   - Security awareness and training for staff   - Initiatives to reach target maturity levels in cybersecurity   - Clear metrics to measure how well the programme is working

cybersecurity.title: Responsibilities of senior management
cybersecurity.description: 1.2 Responsibilities of Senior Management**  Senior Management shall be responsible for the effective implementation of Board-approved cybersecurity policies, programmes, standards, and the clear assignment of cybersecurity responsibilities within the organisation.  To fulfill this responsibility, Senior Management shall:  i. Recommend to the Board the appointment of a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) who meets the applicable regulatory qualifications and standards. ii. Obtain the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) approval for the appointment of the CISO. iii. Provide periodic reports, at least quarterly, to the Board on the overall status of the cybersecurity programme, as specified in Section 1.1(viii). iv. Ensure that Information Security personnel undergo relevant and regular training programmes to maintain technical competence and awareness of emerging threats. v. Incorporate cybersecurity risk management into the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and governance structures to ensure consistent and holistic management of cyber risks across the SFI. vi. Drive cyber risk management processes to ensure effective adherence to the institution’s defined cybersecurity risk appetite.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall ensure that Senior Management:  1. Recommends to the Board the appointment of a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) who meets regulatory qualifications and standards.  2. Obtains approval from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) for the CISO’s appointment.  3. Submits regular cybersecurity status reports—at least quarterly—to the Board, covering progress and updates as required under Section 1.1(viii).  4. Ensures that Information Security staff receive ongoing, relevant training to maintain their skills and stay informed about current cyber threats.  5. Integrates cybersecurity risk management into the Bank’s overall Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and governance systems to ensure risks are consistently managed across all areas.  6. Leads the implementation of cybersecurity risk processes that ensure the Bank stays within its defined cyber risk appetite.

cybersecurity.title: Responsibilities of the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)
cybersecurity.description: 1.3 Responsibilities of the Chief Information Security Officer**  The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) shall be responsible for the day-to-day management of cybersecurity operations and the mitigation of cyber risks within the Specialized Financial Institution (SFI). The CISO shall ensure that the SFI’s information assets are adequately protected from internal and external threats.  Accordingly, the CISO shall:  i. Oversee and implement the Board-approved cybersecurity programme and strategy, ensuring alignment with the institution’s business objectives and risk appetite. ii. Develop and promote secure business and communication practices; define security objectives and performance metrics; and recommend the acquisition and deployment of appropriate cybersecurity tools and technologies to safeguard the SFI’s information assets. iii. Ensure the SFI maintains compliance with data privacy requirements and oversee the implementation of periodic cybersecurity awareness and training programmes for all employees.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall ensure that the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO):  1. Oversees and implements the cybersecurity programme and strategy approved by the Board, making sure it aligns with the Bank’s business goals and risk tolerance.  2. Establishes secure business and communication practices, sets cybersecurity goals and performance measures, and recommends suitable tools and technologies to protect the Bank’s information systems.  3. Ensures compliance with data privacy regulations and leads regular cybersecurity training and awareness programmes for all employees.

cybersecurity.title: Requirements for appointment as a Chief Information Security Officer
cybersecurity.description: 1.4. Requirements for appointment as a Chief Information Security Officer** The SFI shall appoint a CISO who meets the under-listed requirements subject to CBN approval:  i. The CISO shall possess adequate authority, experience, independence and shall be of appropriate grade to function effectively. The minimum grade of staff to be appointed as CISO shall be as specified below or as may be approved by the CBN from time to time: a. Commercial Bank with International Authorisation – Senior Manager b. Commercial Bank with National Authorisation – Senior Manager c. Non-Interest Bank with National Authorisation – Manager d. Commercial Bank with Regional Authorisation – Manager e. Merchant Bank – Manager f. Payment Service Bank – Manager g. Non-Interest Bank with Regional Authorisation – Manager  ii. The CISO shall report directly/functionally to the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer.  iii. To avoid conflict of interest, the CISO shall not report directly or indirectly to the Head of Information Technology (IT) operations or Chief Risk Officer.  iv. The Appointment of a CISO shall be in line with the provisions of the Revised Assessment Criteria for Approved Persons’ Regime for Financial Institutions, 2015 or any subsequent regulation.  v. Where the SFI is part of a Group that has a Group CISO charged with establishing and maintaining an enterprise vision, strategy and programme, the SFI’s CISO is required to replicate the responsibilities as required in Section 1.3 of this Framework.  vi. The CISO shall possess relevant qualifications with Information Security Certifications such as Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Certified Information Security Manager (CISM) and Certified Chief Information Security Officer (CCISO) among others and a minimum of ten year’s in-depth experience in any of the following roles: Cybersecurity, Information Technology, IT Risk Management, Information Security Risk Management or IT Audit.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall:  Appoint a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) who has enough authority, experience, and independence to perform the role effectively. The CISO must hold at least the position of Senior Manager for commercial banks with international or national licenses, and Manager for those with regional licenses, in line with CBN requirements.  Ensure that the CISO reports directly to the Managing Director or Chief Executive Officer, not through the Head of IT or Chief Risk Officer, to maintain independence.  Appoint the CISO in accordance with the CBN’s Approved Persons Regime guidelines or any updated regulation.  If the Bank is part of a larger banking group with a Group CISO, the Bank shall still have its own CISO who performs all required responsibilities as outlined in the cybersecurity governance framework.  Ensure that the CISO has the right qualifications, such as professional certifications like CISSP, CISM, or CCISO, and at least 10 years of strong experience in areas such as cybersecurity, IT, IT risk management, information security, or IT audit.

cybersecurity.description: 1.5. The Information Security Steering Committee** Every SFI shall establish an Information Security Steering Committee (ISSC) that shall be responsible for the governance of the cybersecurity programme. The committee shall meet the following requirements:  i. It shall comprise senior representatives of relevant departments within the SFI and be chaired by the MD/CEO, while the Executive Director in charge of Technology/Operations may serve as the alternate chairman. ii. The roles, responsibilities, scope and activities of the ISSC shall be as defined in the Terms of Reference. iii. The ISSC shall meet at least once in a quarter. iv. The agenda for the meeting shall include a presentation on the “State of cybersecurity” and address recent cyber events, vulnerabilities and proposals for controls to reduce cyber risks. The summary of the report shall be included in the reports to the Board referenced in Section 1.1(viii).  ---  **1.5.1. Terms of Reference of the ISSC**  The ISSC shall be responsible for:  i. ensuring that the SFI’s security policies and processes align with its business objectives. ii. evaluating, approving and sponsoring institution-wide security investment. iii. enforcing implementation of policies for investment prioritisation and security risk management. iv. providing strategic direction and cybersecurity governance for the SFI. v. recommend cybersecurity risk acceptance level to the Board for approval.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Set up an **Information Security Steering Committee (ISSC)** to oversee its cybersecurity programme.  2. Ensure the Committee is led by the **Managing Director/CEO**, and if unavailable, the **Executive Director responsible for Technology or Operations** may act as chair.  3. Include senior staff from key departments as members of the Committee.  4. Clearly define the Committee’s roles, responsibilities, and scope in a **Terms of Reference** document.  5. Hold Committee meetings **at least once every quarter**.  6. Ensure that each meeting covers the **current state of cybersecurity**, including recent threats, system weaknesses, and recommendations for improving controls. A summary of this discussion shall be included in quarterly cybersecurity reports to the Board.  ---  **The Bank shall ensure that the ISSC is responsible for:**  1. Making sure cybersecurity policies and processes support the Bank’s business goals.  2. Reviewing and approving major cybersecurity investments.  3. Enforcing policies that prioritize and manage cybersecurity risks.  4. Providing overall strategic guidance for the Bank’s cybersecurity programme.  5. Recommending the Bank’s level of acceptable cyber risk to the Board for approval.

cybersecurity.title: Other Risk Management Control Functions
cybersecurity.description: All SFIs shall ensure the effectiveness of their cybersecurity governance by reviewing their processes and controls annually. In this regard, these risk management control functions shall have the following responsibilities:  1.6.1. Risk Management i. The Risk Management function, internal or outsourced, shall independently and proactively evaluate all cybersecurity risks. This should be executed using appropriate tools and methodologies for risk identification, analysis and control. The assessment report shall be presented to Senior Management monthly and the Board Risk Management Committee quarterly. ii. Senior Management shall ensure that staff or external risk management professionals engaged to evaluate the institution’s cybersecurity posture possess the requisite qualifications and experience.  1.6.2. Audit i. The Audit function shall be independent and the scope of cybersecurity audits shall be clearly defined. ii. The SFI’s cybersecurity programme shall be reviewed by the Audit function, internal or external, to determine the effectiveness of the controls put in place and ascertain if they are adequate for the institution’s risk exposure. iii. Senior Management shall ensure that internal or outsourced audit staff engaged to review the institution’s cybersecurity posture, possess requisite qualifications and experience.  1.6.3. Compliance The Compliance function of SFIs shall periodically review the cybersecurity programmes and processes to ensure adherence to relevant CBN directives and extant regulations.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Review cybersecurity governance processes and controls at least annually. 2. Assign a Risk Management function (internal or external) to independently and proactively assess all cybersecurity risks using suitable tools and methodologies. 3. Present risk assessment reports to Senior Management monthly and to the Board Risk Management Committee quarterly. 4. Ensure Risk Management staff or external professionals have appropriate qualifications and experience. 5. Maintain an independent Audit function with a clearly defined scope for cybersecurity reviews. 6. Conduct cybersecurity audits to evaluate the effectiveness and adequacy of implemented controls. 7. Ensure Audit personnel (internal or external) possess the requisite qualifications and experience. 8. Assign the Compliance function to periodically review cybersecurity programmes for compliance with CBN directives and applicable regulations.

cybersecurity.title: The Risk Management System
cybersecurity.description: 2.1.1. Risk Identification SFIs shall identify associated threats and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of their information assets to determine their cyber risk exposure.  2.1.2. Risk assessment SFIs are required to evaluate risks to their operations, probability of occurrence, impact of risk crystallisation, and security controls to mitigate identified risks. This process should be carried out annually and whenever major changes occur within the institution such as an acquisition, merger or when new technology is deployed to handle key business processes. The outcome of this process should be documented in a Cybersecurity Risk Control Self-Assessment. An independent Audit function shall be responsible for ensuring that the methodology used in risk assessment is reviewed periodically.  2.1.4. Risk mitigation/Risk treatment SFIs should implement risk mitigation and control measures consistent with the criticality of information assets. Risk treatment options such as risk reduction, acceptance, avoidance, transfer and management of residual risk should be selected based on the outcome of the risk assessment. Risk acceptance criteria should be as defined and approved by the Board. In cases where the SFI chooses to transfer risk, a detailed risk assessment for outsourcing or cyber risk insurance should be documented.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Identify all threats and vulnerabilities that may affect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of their information assets (2.1.1). 2. Assess risks to operations, evaluate likelihood and potential impact, and review current security controls (2.1.2). 3. Conduct these assessments annually and during major changes like acquisitions, mergers, or implementation of new technologies. 4. Document the result of each assessment in a Cybersecurity Risk Control Self-Assessment. 5. Ensure the Audit function periodically reviews the risk assessment methodology for adequacy (2.1.2). 6. Apply risk mitigation and control measures based on the criticality of affected assets (2.1.4). 7. Choose and document appropriate risk treatment options—such as risk reduction, acceptance, avoidance, or transfer. 8. Define and get Board approval for risk acceptance criteria (2.1.4). 9. For risk transfers (e.g., outsourcing or insurance), conduct and document a detailed risk assessment (2.1.4).

cybersecurity.riskDescription: - Failure to properly identify, assess, and treat cyber risks may lead to data breaches, financial losses, regulatory penalties, and reputational damage.

cybersecurity.responsibility: - CISO - CRO - Head of Audit - Risk Management Unit - Board Risk Management Committee
cybersecurity.primaryControl: - Maintain a risk register identifying threats and vulnerabilities. - Perform and document Cybersecurity Risk Control Self-Assessments. - Ensure annual and change-triggered risk assessments. - Establish Board-approved risk acceptance criteria. - Maintain audit-reviewed risk assessment methodology. - Maintain documentation for risk treatment decisions (e.g., acceptance, transfer).
cybersecurity.additionalControl: - Use automated risk assessment tools. - Implement scenario-based testing and simulation exercises. - Conduct quarterly mini-risk reviews in addition to annual assessments. - Train all relevant staff on enterprise risk management and treatment strategies. - Link risk treatment plans directly to the SFI’s cybersecurity roadmap and business continuity plans.

cybersecurity.title: Third party risk management
cybersecurity.description: i. SFIs shall implement a third-party risk management framework to assess and mitigate the risks associated with such relationships. The third-party risk management framework should include processes for vendor selection, due diligence, contract negotiations, ongoing monitoring and incident response. ii. Third-party cybersecurity awareness programme shall be conducted at least annually to inform stakeholders about their roles and responsibilities around cybersecurity. iii. Contracts with third parties shall be used to implement appropriate measures designed to meet the objectives of the SFI’s cybersecurity programme. iv. Third parties shall be routinely assessed using audits, test results, or other forms of evaluations to confirm that contractual obligations are fulfilled. vii. Business continuity response and recovery planning and testing shall be conducted with third-party providers. viii. SFIs shall implement Insurance cover for various insurable technology risks to mitigate financial losses.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Implement a Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM) Framework covering vendor selection, due diligence, contract terms, monitoring, and incident response. 2. Conduct annual cybersecurity awareness programs for third-party stakeholders. 3. Ensure contracts with vendors reflect cybersecurity expectations aligned with internal policies. 4. Perform regular evaluations or audits to verify vendor compliance with contractual and cybersecurity obligations. 7. Include third-party vendors in business continuity and recovery testing. 8. Obtain insurance cover for insurable technology-related risks to reduce financial exposure.
cybersecurity.deadlineType: - Annually: Cybersecurity awareness training, BCP testing with vendors, insurance review - Ongoing: Vendor due diligence, performance reviews, contract monitoring
cybersecurity.riskDescription: Weak vendor management may expose the bank to cybersecurity breaches, non-compliance fines, data leaks, service disruption, and reputational damage due to third-party failures.
cybersecurity.owner: - Head, Procurement - Head, IT Risk & Information Security - Legal & Compliance Unit

cybersecurity.primaryControl: - Implement formal TPRM framework with documented procedures. - Enforce due diligence checklists and third-party risk ratings. - Maintain central register of all contracts and SLAs. - Schedule periodic vendor performance reviews and audits. - Conduct annual cybersecurity training for critical third parties. - Include business continuity clauses in vendor agreements. - Review insurance policies annually for adequacy.
cybersecurity.additionalControl: - Include right-to-audit and breach notification clauses in all contracts. - Automate third-party onboarding and monitoring via TPRM tools. - Report third-party risk trends to the Risk Management Committee.

cybersecurity.title: Cybersecurity Maturity Assessment
cybersecurity.description: An SFI shall conduct annual evaluation using the CBN Cybersecurity Self-Assessment tool (CSAT) to determine its maturity level.  2.4.1. Determining the Current Cybersecurity Profile (current state) To determine its current state, an SFI shall carry out the following: i. Identify its Inherent Cyber risks. ii. Assess existing Cybersecurity mitigants.  2.4.2. Establishing a Target Cybersecurity Profile (desired state) An SFI shall determine its desired state of cybersecurity maturity. The information security function shall ensure that a roadmap towards achieving the target cybersecurity profile is included in the SFI’s corporate strategy.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall:  1. Conduct a yearly self-assessment using the CBN Cybersecurity Self-Assessment Tool (CSAT). 2. Identify their inherent cybersecurity risks and assess existing cybersecurity controls (to determine current state). 3. Define their target cybersecurity maturity level (desired state). 4. Develop a roadmap, aligned with corporate strategy, to close gaps between current and target maturity levels.
cybersecurity.riskDescription: Without a clear understanding of cybersecurity maturity and gaps, the bank may leave critical risks unaddressed, resulting in exposure to cyber threats and possible regulatory sanctions.

cybersecurity.title: Enhancing Cybersecurity Resilience
cybersecurity.description: Cyber resilience is the SFI’s ability to prevent, withstand and recover from cyber incidents. SFIs are required to establish procedures to enhance their cyber resilience. This will ultimately strengthen the financial industry’s cybersecurity posture. The following are the minimum controls that an SFI shall put in place to ensure the confidentiality, integrity and availability of critical information assets among others. 3.1 Know Your Environment An SFI shall proactively familiarise itself with its business environment and identify its critical assets. To ensure effective security measures, an SFI shall establish mechanisms for maintaining up-to-date inventory of authorised software, hardware as well as internal and external network connections. Additionally, an SFI shall identify and document its data, assets and capabilities. Also, potential threats and vulnerabilities associated with its assets shall be monitored. Employees and contractors providing information technology and cybersecurity services shall also be identified and documented. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix II. 3.2 Implement Preventive Controls An SFI shall implement appropriate measures/controls/safeguards for IT systems, processes and people to mitigate cyber risks. These can be administrative, logical or physical controls. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix III. 3.3 Monitor and Detect An SFI shall establish capability for ongoing (24/7) monitoring of its IT systems, infrastructure, applications, services, and other relevant components to promptly detect anomalies or cyber incidents. This capability may be managed internally or outsourced to a third-party provider. Notwithstanding the approach chosen, monitoring should be adequate to detect cyber threats. 3.4 Respond and Remediate An SFI shall ensure that the capability for responding to cyber incidents is available in-house or, if outsourced, can be accessed at short notice. Details on specific controls are contained in Appendix III. 3.5 Restore Service Operations An SFI shall aim at recovering its operations timeously to reduce the overall impact of cyber incidents. 3.6 Cyber-Threat Intelligence An SFI is expected to possess knowledge of emerging threats, cyber-attacks, attack vectors, mechanisms and indicators of attack/compromise that may impact its information assets. 3.7 Sector-specific Cyber Resilience An SFI is required to participate in industry cyber exercises and programmes to evaluate its level of preparedness to recover from cyber incidents. These exercises may include cyber drills, war games or as defined by the CBN from time to time. SFIs shall avoid creating single points of failure in the industry and proactively define plans to mitigate such risks.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall establish, implement, and maintain a cybersecurity resilience framework to prevent, withstand, and recover from cyber incidents, as follows:  1. Identify and document its critical assets, including data, hardware, software, networks, and capabilities. It shall maintain an up-to-date inventory of these assets and their associated threats and vulnerabilities. Employees and contractors involved in IT and cybersecurity services shall also be documented.  2.  Apply appropriate administrative, logical, or physical safeguards to protect its IT systems, processes, and people against cyber risks.  3. Maintain continuous (24/7) monitoring capabilities across its IT systems, infrastructure, and applications to promptly detect anomalies or cyber incidents, whether through internal resources or qualified third-party providers.  4.  Ensure that adequate resources and plans for responding to cyber incidents are available in-house or can be accessed at short notice if outsourced.  5. Recover operations promptly to minimize the overall impact of cyber incidents.  6. Maintain knowledge of emerging threats, attack methods, indicators of compromise, and other cyber risks relevant to its information assets.  7. Participate in industry-wide cyber exercises, drills, and programs to test its preparedness for recovering from cyber incidents, and shall develop plans to avoid industry-wide single points of failure.

cybersecurity.title: Open Banking
cybersecurity.description: Open Banking refers to the practice of sharing financial data, such as account and transaction information, products and services with other financial institutions and third parties through API connections. The Regulatory Framework for Open Banking in Nigeria establishes principles for data sharing across the banking and payments system to promote innovation and broaden the range of financial products and services available to bank customers. Cyber-risks associated with open banking include data privacy, fraud, identity theft and API compromise. SFIs shall ensure compliance with the provisions of the Regulatory Framework for Open Banking in Nigeria and Operational Guidelines for Open Banking in Nigeria.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Comply with the Regulatory Framework for Open Banking in Nigeria and the Operational Guidelines for Open Banking in Nigeria. 2. Ensure that data sharing via APIs is secure, transparent, and consent-based. 3. Put controls in place to address cyber risks such as data privacy breaches, fraud, identity theft, and API compromise.

cybersecurity.title: Adoption of Emerging Technology
cybersecurity.description: SFIs are required to comply with the following regulations in the use of emerging technologies: 1. obtain CBN approval before deploying emerging technologies or products. 2. ensure products and services are not provided by parties or countries on sanction lists. 3. refrain from establishing API connections or granting access to organisations not licensed by the CBN without prior regulatory approvals. 4. maintain professional due diligence and care in the adoption of emerging/evolving technologies.
cybersecurity.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Obtain CBN approval before deploying any new or emerging technology or product. 2. Ensure that no product or service is provided to or through parties or countries listed on sanction lists. 3. Do not integrate with or grant API access to organizations not licensed by the CBN without prior CBN approval. 4. Conduct professional due diligence and risk assessments before adopting any new or evolving technology.
cybersecurity.deadlineType: - Immediate for existing and upcoming tech rollouts - Sanction screenings and API vetting: Ongoing per engagement - Quarterly audit of compliance with this section
cybersecurity.riskDescription: - Unauthorized deployment of emerging tech can lead to regulatory sanctions. - Engaging with blacklisted entities could result in reputational, legal, and financial damage. - Improper API integration with unlicensed parties may expose systems to cyber-attacks. - Poorly vetted technologies could result in operational disruptions, data loss, or fraud.

cybersecurity.additionalControl: - Integrate automated sanction list screening tools. - Schedule compliance reviews for all ongoing tech partnerships. - Maintain audit trails of regulatory approvals and API access permissions. - Implement emerging tech sandbox/testing environments to assess risks before full deployment.
