amlcft.plain: 1)The Bank shall treat any transaction as suspicious and report it immediately to the appropriate authority if it: happens too frequently or without a clear reason, is unusually complicated or lacks justification, seems to have no clear legal or economic purpose, does not match the customer’s typical transaction pattern, or appears to involve money from crime, unlawful activity, money laundering, or terrorist financing.  2)The bank must within 24 hours of identifying a suspicious transaction:  (a) Prepare a written report with all relevant details of the transaction, including the reasons for suspicion and the identities of the principal and beneficiaries.  (b) Take necessary preventive actions to stop possible laundering of criminal proceeds.  (c) Report the suspicious transaction and actions taken to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU).
amlcft.deadlineType: Within 24 hours of identifying the suspicious transaction
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to detect and report suspicious transactions may result in:  - Regulatory sanctions by CBN or NFIU  - Legal liability  - The bank being used for money laundering or terrorist financing  - Loss of reputation and trust
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Transaction Monitoring Team, Branch/Operations Staff
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Officer (primary), Operations Head (transaction review), Internal Control (oversight)
amlcft.primaryControl: - Automated suspicious transaction monitoring systems (rules/AI-based) - Internal STR checklist and red flag indicators - Escalation protocol to compliance unit - Centralized STR logging and approval workflow
amlcft.additionalControl: - Periodic review of STR quality by internal audit - Training for front-line and back-office staff - 24-hour internal escalation matrix for urgent STRs - Testing of reporting timelines to NFIU

amlcft.title: Suspicious transaction reporting
amlcft.description: (10) A financial institution or designated non-financial business and profession which fails to comply with the provisions of subsections (1) and (2) commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of ₦1,000,000 for each day during which the offence continues.  (11) The directors, officers and employees of financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions who carry out their duties under this Act in good faith shall not be liable to any civil or criminal liability or have any criminal or civil proceedings brought against them by their customers.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall:  Ensure full compliance with required due diligence rules. If it fails to comply, it may be fined ₦1,000,000 for every day the violation continues.  Ensure that its staff, officers, and directors are protected from lawsuits or criminal charges by customers if they perform their compliance duties honestly and in good faith.
amlcft.deadlineType: Ongoing
amlcft.riskDescription: If the Bank fails to comply with due diligence rules, it faces financial penalties of ₦1,000,000 per day. However, employees who act in good faith are protected from legal consequences. Non-compliance poses serious financial, legal, and reputational risks.
amlcft.owner: Compliance, AML Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Head of Compliance, AML Reporting Officer
amlcft.primaryControl: Suspicious Transaction Reporting (STR) policy; staff training; whistleblower protection framework
amlcft.additionalControl: Conduct quarterly STR compliance audits; refresh staff training annually

amlcft.title: Preservation of Records
amlcft.description: (1) Financial institution and designated non-financial business and profession shall preserve and keep at the disposal of the authorities specified in section 9 of this Act— (a) all necessary records on transactions, both domestic and international, for at least five years following completion of the transaction; and (b) all records obtained under section 4 of this Act, including account files and business correspondence, and results of any analysis undertaken, for at least five years following the termination of the business relationship or after the date of the occasional transaction.  (2) The records referred to in subsection (1) shall be— (a) sufficient to permit individual transactions to be readily reconstructed at any time by the competent authorities; and (b) made swiftly available to the competent authorities.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall: 1(a) Keep all transaction records (domestic and international) for at least 5 years after the transaction is completed. (b) Retain customer identification records, account files, business correspondence, and results of analysis for 5 years after the end of the business relationship or occasional transaction. (2) These records must be: (a) Detailed enough to allow authorities to reconstruct the transaction. (b) Swiftly retrievable when requested by competent authorities.
amlcft.deadlineType: Continuous obligation; retention: 5 years post-transaction or relationship termination
amlcft.riskDescription: Inadequate record preservation may lead to: - Failure to support investigations by law enforcement - Regulatory breaches and sanctions - Inability to trace transaction trails or confirm customer due diligence - Loss of credibility and trust with regulators
amlcft.owner: Records Management Team, Compliance Department, IT/Data Storage Team
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Officer (oversight), Head of Operations/Records, IT Manager (for digital records)
amlcft.primaryControl: Inadequate record preservation may lead to: - Failure to support investigations by law enforcement - Regulatory breaches and sanctions - Inability to trace transaction trails or confirm customer due diligence - Loss of credibility and trust with regulators
amlcft.additionalControl: - Document retention policies aligned with AML laws - Secure archiving systems (physical and digital) - Role-based access to archived data - Periodic audits of records management processes

amlcft.title: Coomunication of Information
amlcft.description: The records referred to in section 8 of this Act shall be communicated on demand to a competent authority and such other regulatory authorities or judicial persons as the Unit or Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering may specify by order published in the Federal Government Gazette.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall promptly communicate any customer or transaction records (as specified in Section 8) upon request to: - Any competent authority (e.g., CBN, NFIU) - Regulatory/judicial authorities designated by the Unit (SCUML or NFIU), as published in the Federal Government Gazette.
amlcft.deadlineType: On-demand by competent authority
amlcft.riskDescription: - Regulatory penalties for failure to share requested records. - Obstruction of justice or Regulatory investigation. - Reputational damage and legal liabilities. - Potential suspicion of collusion or concealment.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Legal Department, Records Management Team
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Officer (primary), Legal Advisor (oversight), Records Officer (execution)
amlcft.primaryControl: - Maintain up-to-date communication protocols with relevant authorities. - Ensure authorized access to records for rapid compliance. - Assign a team for regulatory liaison and urgent document handling. - Maintain log of all requests and responses.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Test response readiness via mock regulatory requests. - Staff training on information disclosure protocols. - Legal review before release to unauthorized bodies.

amlcft.title: Internal procedures, policies and controls
amlcft.description: (1) Every financial institution and designated non-financial business and profession shall develop programmes to combat the laundering of the proceeds of a crime or other unlawful acts, and these shall include— (a) the designation of compliance officers at management level at its headquarters and at every branch and local office; (b) regular training programmes for its employees; (c) the centralisation of the information collected; and (d) the establishment of an internal audit unit to ensure compliance with and effectiveness of the measures taken to enforce the provisions of this Act.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall: (a) Appoint Compliance Officers at management level at both the headquarters and all branches/local offices. (b) Provide regular AML/CFT/CPF training to all employees. (c) Ensure centralized data and information collection related to AML/CFT/CPF efforts. (d) Establish an Internal Audit Unit to monitor and verify the effectiveness and enforcement of AML/CFT/CPF measures.
amlcft.deadlineType: Immediate and ongoing (continuous requirement)
amlcft.riskDescription: - Risk of regulatory breach due to poor internal controls. - Operational risk from fragmented compliance oversight. - Failure to detect/report suspicious activity. - High exposure to money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing.
amlcft.owner: Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), Head of HR (for training), Head of Internal Audit, Branch Managers
amlcft.responsibility: CCO (primary oversight), Internal Audit Lead, HR Director, IT/Data Governance Lead (for centralisation)
amlcft.primaryControl: - Appoint trained compliance officers across all operational units. - Maintain a centralized AML system for data/information. - Schedule regular and role-specific AML/CFT training. - Set up and empower internal audit with AML-specific scope.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Independent external AML compliance review annually. - Quarterly reports from internal audit to executive management. - HR to track training compliance metrics.

amlcft.title: Mandatory disclosure by financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions
amlcft.description: (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law or regulation, a financial institution or designated non-financial business and profession shall report to the Unit in the case of a financial institution and to Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering in the case of a designated non-financial business and profession in writing within seven days, any single transaction, lodgment or transfer of funds in excess of— (a) N5,000,000 or its equivalent, in the case of an individual; or (b) N10,000,000 or its equivalent, in the case of a body corporate.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall report in writing to the NFIU within 7 days any single transaction, lodgment, or transfer exceeding: (a) ₦5,000,000 (for individuals); or (b) ₦10,000,000 (for corporate entities).
amlcft.deadlineType: Within 7 days of the transaction
amlcft.riskDescription: - Regulatory breach for non-disclosure of high-value transactions. - Potential reputational damage or sanctions. - Opportunity for criminals to launder money through large, unreported transactions.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Transaction Monitoring Unit, Operations Manager
amlcft.responsibility: Chief Compliance Officer (overall oversight), NFIU Liaison Officer, Head of Operations
amlcft.primaryControl: - Automated transaction monitoring system with value thresholds. - Daily exception reports for high-value transactions. - Internal escalation and approval workflow for report submission.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Periodic reconciliation of reported transactions with system records. - Independent audit of high-value transaction reporting compliance. - Continuous staff training on reporting obligations.

amlcft.title: Prohibition of numbered or anonymous accounts, accounts in fictitious names and shell banks
amlcft.description: (1) The opening or maintaining of numbered or anonymous accounts by any person, financial institution or body corporate is prohibited. (2) A person shall not establish or operate a shell bank in Nigeria. (3) A financial institution shall— (a) not enter into or continue correspondent banking relationships with shell banks; and (b) satisfy itself that a respondent financial institution in a foreign country does not permit its accounts to be used by shell banks.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall:  1.Not allow the opening or use of anonymous or numbered accounts. 2.Not set up or operate any shell bank in Nigeria. 3.Not do business with shell banks, and must also confirm that any foreign bank it works with does not allow shell banks to use its accounts.
amlcft.deadlineType: Ongoing at account opening and during periodic reviews
amlcft.riskDescription: Allowing anonymous accounts or doing business with shell banks may expose the Bank to serious financial crime risks, including money laundering, regulatory violations, and reputational damage. Strict adherence to these rules protects the Bank from facilitating illicit activities.
amlcft.owner: Chief Compliance Officer, Head of International Banking, Legal & Risk Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Unit, Correspondent Banking Relationship Team, Legal Department
amlcft.primaryControl: - Perform Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) on all correspondent banking relationships. - Require written confirmation from foreign respondent banks that they do not deal with shell banks. - Periodic audits of international correspondent relationships.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Maintain a blacklist of identified shell banks. - Subscribe to updated international watchlists and FATF advisories. - Include shell bank checks in onboarding and periodic review checklists.

amlcft.title: New products, business practices and technologies
amlcft.description: (1) Financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions shall identify and assess the money laundering and terrorism financing risks that may arise in relation to the development of new products and new business practices, including new delivery mechanisms, and the use of new or developing technologies for both new and pre-existing products in accordance with the requirements specified by the regulatory authorities.  (2) Pursuant to the provisions of subsection (1), financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions shall— (a) undertake the risk assessments prior to the launch or use of such products, business practices and technologies; and (b) take appropriate measures to manage and mitigate the risks.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Identify and assess ML/TF risks linked to new products, services, delivery channels, and technologies (whether new or existing). (2) Conduct risk assessments before launching or using such products or technologies. (3) Implement appropriate risk mitigation measures.
amlcft.deadlineType: Before product launch and on an ongoing basis thereafter
amlcft.riskDescription: - New delivery channels (e.g., mobile apps, online banking) may facilitate undetected money laundering or terrorism financing. - Failure to assess or mitigate such risks could result in regulatory sanctions, customer fraud, and reputational harm.
amlcft.owner: Chief Risk Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, Product Development/Innovation Teams
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Unit, Product Teams, Internal Audit
amlcft.primaryControl: - Conduct pre-launch ML/TF risk assessment on all new products/technologies. - Use risk-based controls, including enhanced due diligence and transaction monitoring for tech-driven products. - Maintain a risk register for new technology-enabled services.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Involve Compliance in product development lifecycle (design to launch). - Periodic post-launch risk reviews of new products. - Incorporate AI/ML tools for enhanced anomaly detection.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: CUSTOMER IDENTIFICATION AND VERIFICATION PROCEDURES FOR PEPS
amlcft.description: FIs are required to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) for the purpose of establishing that a customer is a PEP, as provided by the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations. FIs are expected to identify and verify the identities of PEPs before providing them with financial services, or as soon as possible afterwards. The identification should also cover legal persons and legal arrangements that have at least one beneficial owner who is a PEP.  3.1 New Customers 3.1.1 Self-declaration by customers of their PEP status will guide the FIs in determining whether a customer is a PEP (i.e. by disclosing present or former employment or principal occupation clearly recognizable as a PEP). FIs may obtain verbal or written declarations from customers. 3.1.2 Information may be obtained directly from the customer in response to questions posed in the application or on-boarding form. FIs may also develop questionnaires with specific reference to criteria that identify PEPs, including family members and persons known to be their close associates. Such questionnaire would be required to be completed and signed by the customer and the beneficial owner, where applicable. 3.1.3 FIs should apply risk-based procedures in determining whether a customer is a PEP, either before the relationship is established or shortly thereafter. Once a new customer is established to be a PEP the FI should assess the risk on the customer and apply appropriate due diligence measures in a timely manner.  3.2 Existing Customers: where the FI becomes aware that an individual or beneficial owner has become a PEP it should re-classify the customer as such and apply risk-based due diligence and controls.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Conduct CDD to determine if a customer or beneficial owner is a PEP, both at onboarding and during ongoing relationships. (2) Obtain PEP status through self-declaration, questionnaires, and onboarding forms. (3) Apply risk-based due diligence to PEPs, both new and existing. (4) Reclassify existing customers as PEPs if new information surfaces.
amlcft.deadlineType: At onboarding and periodically thereafter (e.g., annually or as risk dictates)
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to properly identify PEPs can expose the bank to money laundering, corruption-related offenses, and regulatory sanctions. It may also lead to relationships with high-risk clients without proper controls.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Onboarding/KYC Teams, Relationship Managers
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Department, Risk Management, Internal Audit
amlcft.primaryControl: - Embed PEP screening in onboarding forms. - Use PEP identification checklists/questionnaires. - Automate screening with PEP databases. - Implement enhanced due diligence (EDD) for confirmed PEPs. - Periodically re-screen existing customers.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Integrate PEP identification into customer risk scoring system. - Conduct periodic compliance audits. - Train staff on identifying and handling PEP relationships.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: Customer Due Diligence
amlcft.description: 4.1 Financial Institutions (FIs) are expected to carry out Customer Due Diligence (CDD) measures proportionate to the risks posed by customers. When dealing with Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), their family members, or known close associates, additional measures in the form of Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) are to be applied by the FIs to mitigate the higher Money Laundering/Terrorist Financing/Proliferation Financing (ML/TF/PF) risks. FIs are, however, not to turn away a prospective customer or close a business relationship simply on the basis that the customer, or beneficial owner, is a PEP (or a family member or person known to be their close associate).  4.2 When considering whether to establish or continue a business relationship with a PEP, the focus should be on the level of ML/TF/PF risk posed by the PEP, and whether the FI has adequate controls in place to mitigate such risks. This is to prevent the FI from being used for illicit purposes should the PEP be involved in criminal activities.  4.3 Once it has been established that a new or existing customer is a PEP, the FI should undertake a risk assessment to determine the level of risk posed by that customer and the proportionate levels of due diligence and monitoring required.  4.4 The FI should use its customer risk assessment policy/process, considering risk factors such as geography, product, business type, and delivery channel. For geographical risk, FIs should consider information available from reliable and independent sources as to the levels of systemic ML/TF risk in the country of political exposure.  4.5 When assessing the ML/TF/PF risk level of a relationship with a domestic/international organization PEP, FIs should take into account factors such as whether the PEP:  a) Has business interests related to his/her public functions (i.e., conflict of interest);  b) Is involved in public procurement processes; or holds several (related or unrelated) prominent public functions that may enable influence to be exerted at key decision-making processes.  c) Is from a country identified by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) or others as having strategic AML/CFT/CPF regime deficiencies or is known to have a high level of corruption.  d) Holds a prominent public function in sectors exposed to higher corruption levels (e.g., oil and gas, mining, construction, natural resources, defense industries, sports, gaming, gambling).  e) Holds a prominent public function that could enable him/her to negatively impact the effective implementation of FATF Recommendations in his/her country.  4.6 For medium or low-risk domestic PEPs or international organization PEPs who are customers or beneficial owners, FIs must, at a minimum, apply the customer identification procedures.  4.7 Where a board member, senior management, or corporate officer of the following types of organizations is a PEP, an FI may be exposed to lower risk and may apply commensurate due diligence accordingly:  a) A publicly quoted company listed on a recognized exchange, subject to appropriate listing rules, good corporate governance, and transparent reporting.  b) Well-regulated organizations subject to independent supervision (e.g., banks and other FIs).  c) Private or state-owned organizations (including Central Banks, sovereign wealth funds), except those from designated high-risk countries, subject to good governance and transparent reporting.  4.8 For high-risk PEPs and foreign PEPs who are customers or beneficial owners, FIs must apply customer identification procedures for individuals and undertake Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD).  4.9 When assessing whether adequate controls are in place to mitigate the risk of doing business with a particular PEP, consideration should be given to the level, frequency, and extent of ongoing monitoring and (enhanced) due diligence required. FIs must ensure their systems are appropriate and efficient based on the risks posed.  4.10 Where a customer’s circumstances change, FIs must reassess the risk posed by that change, conduct EDD if the PEP is high-risk or foreign, and adjust transaction monitoring processes to account for the higher risk associated with the customer.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall: (1) Apply CDD proportional to the risk level of each customer. (2) Conduct Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) for PEPs, their close associates, or family members. (3) Not automatically reject or exit relationships solely due to PEP status. (4) Use a risk-based approach in establishing or continuing relationships with PEPs. (5) Undertake a risk assessment once PEP status is confirmed. (6) Apply customer risk assessment across geography, sector, product, delivery channels, and political exposure. (7) Apply full identification and EDD for high-risk or foreign PEPs. (8) Monitor transactions and customer behavior regularly and adjust controls when the customer's circumstances change.
amlcft.deadlineType: At onboarding, annually (or more frequently based on risk triggers or regulatory changes)
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to identify and manage PEP risks may result in the bank being used for corruption, money laundering, or terrorist financing, attracting regulatory sanctions, reputational damage, and possible criminal liability.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, KYC Unit, Relationship Managers, Risk Management Team
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Department, Risk/AML Unit, Internal Audit for oversight
amlcft.primaryControl: - Conduct PEP screening at onboarding and periodically. - Use automated watchlists and questionnaires. - Perform EDD for high-risk/foreign PEPs. - Maintain a PEP Risk Register. - Monitor transactions linked to PEPs continuously. - Reassess risks when customer status or circumstances change.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Integrate EDD triggers into core banking system. - Assign senior management approval before onboarding high-risk/foreign PEPs. - Conduct annual reviews of PEP profiles. - Implement geo-political risk analytics tools.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: SOURCES OF INFORMATION FOR THE DETERMINATION OF PEPS, THEIR FAMILY MEMBERS & CLOSE ASSOCIATES
amlcft.description: There are several sources of information that can be used by FIs in determining whether a customer is a PEP. In determining whether the customer or a beneficial owner is a PEP, FI may consider the following:  5.1. Periodic review of customer database FIs are required to ensure that CDD information is up-to-date as provided by the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations. Existing customers may become PEPs after they enter a business relationship, so it is essential that FIs monitor non-PEP accounts for a change in the PEP status, customer profile or account activity and update customer information. Such ongoing monitoring should be on a risk basis.  5.2 conduct internet and media searches FIs may use the internet and media as sources of information for the determination, monitoring, verification of information in relation to PEPs, although it should be noted that such information may not be comprehensive or reliable.  5.3. conduct searches using commercial databases 5.3.1 There are a variety of commercial databases available which may assist in the detection of PEPs, FIs may acquire access to such databases. 5.3.2 The use of these databases should never replace traditional CDD processes as contained in the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations 2022. 5.3.3 FIs using such databases as a support tool should ensure that they are fit for the purpose and are not simply outsourcing their risk assessment. 5.3.4 FIs should also determine whether the use of commercial databases, to confirm the information provided by the customer, is necessary. Prior to making use of any commercial databases, FIs should understand how commercial databases are populated and how these are able to detect and flag PEPs, family members and persons known to be close associates of PEPs.  5.4. create in-house databases and share information within financial groups or countries 5.4.1. FIs may choose to develop in-house databases as tools to assist in determining PEPs, and such database should be kept up-to-date. 5.4.2. In line with provisions of the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations, Financial Groups are required to implement procedures for sharing information with the Group for AML/CFT/CPF purposes. In relation to foreign PEPs, it is best practice for institutions within Financial Groups to share information on PEPs for AML purposes.  5.5. customer questionnaire/self-declaration Information obtained directly from the customer may be obtained in response to questionnaires and/or on-boarding forms. FIs may develop questionnaires with specific reference to criteria that identify PEPs including family members and persons known to be close associates of the PEP. Such a questionnaire would be required to be completed and signed by the customer and the beneficial owner, where applicable. Information obtained directly from the customer may be obtained in response to the questionnaire and/or on-boarding form.  5.6 information sharing by competent authorities FIs may rely on the information shared by competent authorities which is helpful in determining whether a particular customer is a PEP or the PEP is trying to abuse the financial system (e.g., the level of corruption in the country, the level of income for certain types of positions, etcetera) or specific information about particular persons which would facilitate the detection of foreign PEPs. Both general information concerning the country from which a foreign PEP originates and more specific information (e.g., about particular persons) are useful tools for verifying CDD information.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall: 1. Periodically review its customer database to detect any status changes to PEPs. 2. Conduct internet and media searches to aid in identifying or verifying PEP information. 3. Use commercial databases for screening and detection but not as a substitute for CDD processes. 4. Maintain and update in-house PEP databases and share PEP-related information within the financial group. 5. Use self-declaration and customer questionnaires to detect PEPs and their close associates. 6. Rely on information from competent authorities, especially when identifying foreign PEPs and assessing country risk.
amlcft.deadlineType: Continuous – with checks at onboarding, every 6–12 months, or when red flags/events occur
amlcft.riskDescription: Inadequate identification of PEPs increases exposure to corruption, money laundering, and terrorist financing. Reliance on unreliable sources or failure to monitor PEP status may lead to non-compliance and regulatory sanctions.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Customer Onboarding Team, AML Monitoring Unit, Relationship Managers
amlcft.responsibility: AML Compliance Unit, IT/Database Admin (for tool updates), Internal Audit (oversight)
amlcft.primaryControl: - Maintain an up-to-date PEP screening tool. - Conduct scheduled PEP status reviews. - Perform multi-source checks (internet, media, commercial databases, customer declarations, competent authority info). - Enable group-wide information sharing mechanisms. - Integrate PEP detection questions into onboarding forms.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Use automated PEP screening software with AI-based alerts. - Conduct regular training on PEP detection for front-line and compliance staff. - Audit trail of all PEP status checks and updates.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: RISK MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
amlcft.description: FIs should in addition to performing CDD measures, establish appropriate risk management systems to determine whether a potential customer or existing customer or the beneficial owner is a PEP.  6.1 PEPs Screening The conduct of PEP screening in each FI will depend on the size and complexity of each institution and the inherent risk of PEPs using the FI’s products and services to launder the proceeds of crime. FI should conduct onboarding screening and ongoing screening on all customers. Where appropriate, PEP screening should be automated. However, manual screening may be acceptable depending on the size of the institution and the materiality of the inherent risk posed by PEPs. PEP screening should be carried out in accordance with FI’s risk appetite while applying RBA and take place at least: a) During onboarding process; b) at periodic customer review; c) when there is a trigger event which warrants a customer due diligence review. d) Upon notification/tip-off from reliable sources. It should be noted that, in many instances, PEP screening is not the primary control for identifying PEPs.  6.2 Customer Risk Assessment 6.2.1 FIs should understand their customer’s risk profiles in order to apply appropriate procedures and processes to manage and mitigate risk. FIs should be consistent with a risk-based approach, the level and type of CDD should be commensurate with the risks presented by the customer relationship. 6.2.2 FIs must have appropriate risk-based procedures for conducting ongoing CDD to understand the nature and purpose of customer relationships, and to develop a customer risk profile. It must be consistent with a risk-based approach for conducting ongoing CDD, FI should obtain more customer information for those customers with higher risk profile and ensure ongoing monitoring. 6.2.3 The information collected to create a customer risk profile should also assist FIs in conducting ongoing monitoring to identify and report suspicious transactions and activity. Furthermore, conducting appropriate level of ongoing CDD commensurate with the customer’s risk profile will assist the FI in determining whether a customer’s transactions or activities are suspicious. 6.2.4 Based on the customer risk profile, the FI may consider obtaining, at account opening (and throughout the relationship), more customer information and updates in order to understand the nature and purpose of the customer relationship. 6.2.5 The following information may be useful to FI in understanding the nature and purpose of the customer relationship and in determining the ML/TF/PF and other illicit financial activity risk profile of its identified PEP customers: a) The type of products and services used. b) The volume and nature of transactions. c) Geographies associated with the customer’s activity and domicile. d) The customer’s official government responsibilities. e) The level and nature of the customer’s authority or influence over government activities or officials. f) The customer’s access to significant government assets or funds. 6.2.6 FIs may leverage existing processes for assessing geographically specific ML/TF/PF and other illicit financial activity risks when developing the customer risk profile. Existing processes may also take into account the legal and enforcement frameworks, including ethical reporting and oversight requirements. 6.2.7 When developing customer risk profiles and determining when to collect additional customer information, and what to collect, FIs may take into account such factors as the customer’s public office or position of public trust (or that of the customer’s family members or close associates), as well as any indication that the identified PEP misuses or might misuse his or her authority or influence for personal gain.  6.3 Approval For Relationship With PEP FIs are required to obtain senior management approval for establishing (or continuing, for existing customers) business relationships with PEPs as provided by the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations.  6.4 Enhanced Monitoring For PEP Relationships/Accounts Higher risk PEPs require enhanced ongoing monitoring of the business relationship. FIs should implement electronic and/or manual monitoring systems to constantly monitor the business relationship and detect unusual and potential suspicious transactions and activities. This process should include: a) Understanding and documenting the circumstances that warrant the classification of the customer as a PEP (such as the title or position and country in which the PEP holds/held political exposure and duration of appointment). If the individual customer is a close family member or close associate, the relationship of the person to the PEP must be documented. b) Understanding and documenting the nature and intended purpose of the relationship/account, the source of the initial funds (where appropriate) and the anticipated levels of account activity. c) Understanding and documenting the customer’s source of funds and source of wealth (e.g. salary and compensation from official duties and wealth derived from other sources). d) When the due diligence on an immediate family member or close associate of a PEP indicates that the source of funds originates from the PEP, the FI should determine and document the PEP’s sources of funds and wealth. e) Conduct searches including internet and media searches to screen customers for adverse reports/news.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall: 6.1 – PEP Screening: - Conduct PEP screening during onboarding, at periodic reviews, upon trigger events or tip-offs. - Choose manual or automated screening based on institution size and PEP risk.  6.2 – Customer Risk Assessment: - Build risk profiles using CDD info. - Apply risk-based approach to determine level of due diligence. - Collect more data for higher-risk customers.  6.3 – Approval for PEP Relationships: - Obtain senior management approval before entering/continuing a business relationship with a PEP.  6.4 – Enhanced Monitoring: - Conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring of higher-risk PEPs. - Document source of funds, wealth, political exposure, and perform adverse media searches.
amlcft.deadlineType: At onboarding, periodic reviews (quarterly/annually), and upon trigger events
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to detect or monitor PEPs may expose the bank to ML/TF/PF risks, reputational damage, and regulatory sanctions.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Risk Management Unit, Relationship Managers, IT (screening systems)
amlcft.responsibility: Head of Compliance, Head of Risk, Internal Audit (oversight), Relationship Managers (first line detection)
amlcft.primaryControl: - Implement automated/manual PEP screening systems. - Use customer questionnaires and onboarding checks. - Maintain a structured customer risk profiling process. - Require senior management approval for all PEPs. - Monitor PEP accounts regularly using risk triggers.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Integrate AI or rule-based alert systems for unusual activity. - Conduct periodic compliance audits focused on PEPs. - Maintain a PEP Watchlist and update frequently. - Provide regular staff training on handling high-risk PEPs.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: RISK MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
amlcft.description: 6.5 Time Limit For PEP Status It is often stated that once a PEP will always remain a PEP, however the handling of a client who is no longer entrusted with a prominent public function should be based on an assessment of risk and not on prescribed time limits. The risk-based approach requires that FIs assess the ML/TF risk of a PEP who is no longer entrusted with a prominent public function or has lost such power and influence (such as the case of deceased) and take effective action to mitigate this risk. However, where the corruption risk remains even if a PEP has been out of office for a certain time, the FI may continue to treat a customer as a PEP. Possible factors to consider in determining whether the customer is no longer a PEP include:  the level of (formal and informal) influence or control that the individual could still exercise; the seniority of the position that the individual held as a PEP; or whether the individual’s previous and current function are linked in any way (e.g., formally by appointment of the PEPs successor, or informally by the fact that the PEP continues to deal with the same substantive matters);  the corruption risks or links to any industries that are high risk for corruption; and  How politically connected they remain once they have left office.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall:  1.Not automatically stop treating someone as a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) just because they’ve left public office.  2.Assess the customer’s risk level based on their current influence, past position, and possible links to corruption or high-risk industries.  3.Continue to treat a former PEP as high-risk if they still have power, connections, or are involved in related business matters.  4.Use a risk-based approach to decide whether the person still poses a money laundering or terrorism financing risk, instead of relying on fixed timelines.
amlcft.deadlineType: Ongoing
amlcft.riskDescription: If the Bank automatically removes a former PEP from enhanced monitoring without a proper risk assessment, it may overlook ongoing corruption risks. This could expose the Bank to money laundering, reputational damage, regulatory breaches, and penalties. Continued influence or industry ties may still pose high-risk factors.
amlcft.owner: Compliance, AML Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Head of Compliance, AML Officer
amlcft.primaryControl: PEP risk assessment policy; enhanced due diligence on high-risk customers
amlcft.additionalControl: Implement periodic review of former PEP status; update PEP screening system to flag ongoing influence factors

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: PEPs AS BENEFICIAL OWNERS
amlcft.description: When conducting CDD, FIs are required to identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable measures to verify the identity of the beneficial owner. If there are reasonable grounds to believe that a beneficial owner is a PEP EDD shall be mandatory.
amlcft.plain: When conducting Customer Due Diligence (CDD), the Bank shall: - Identify and verify the identity of all beneficial owners. - If there is reasonable ground to believe that the beneficial owner is a PEP, the bank must apply Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD).
amlcft.deadlineType: At onboarding and during periodic KYC updates or trigger events
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to identify PEPs as beneficial owners may result in undetected exposure to ML/TF/PF risks, reputational harm, regulatory penalties, and misuse of the financial system.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Customer Onboarding Unit, KYC/CDD Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Head of Compliance, Relationship Manager, Internal Audit (for assurance), Legal Unit (for complex ownership verification)
amlcft.primaryControl: - Mandatory verification of all beneficial owners. - Risk-based screening to flag PEPs among beneficial owners. - Automated checks against internal and external PEP lists. - Escalation for EDD if beneficial owner is a PEP.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Conduct periodic reviews and reassessment of beneficial owners. - Use adverse media and commercial PEP databases. - Staff training on identifying complex ownership structures. - Legal review for layered ownership schemes.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: DOMESTIC/INTERNATIONAL ORGANISATION PEPS WHEN NOT HIGHER RISK
amlcft.description: When the risk assessment established that the business relationship with a domestic/international organization PEP does not present a higher risk, the PEP in question can be treated like any other normal customer, i.e. the FI should apply normal customer due diligence measures and monitoring as required under the CBN-AML/CFT/CPF Regulations.
amlcft.plain: When a PEP is assessed not to pose a higher risk, the bank must treat them as a normal customer, applying standard CDD and ongoing monitoring in line with the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations.
amlcft.deadlineType: At onboarding, and during scheduled KYC review cycles
amlcft.riskDescription: Misclassification of a low-risk PEP who later engages in illicit activity may result in regulatory scrutiny or reputational damage due to perceived negligence in risk categorization.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Customer Due Diligence (CDD) Team
amlcft.responsibility: Risk Management Unit, Compliance Department, Relationship Manager
amlcft.primaryControl: - Perform risk assessments to determine the correct PEP risk level. - Apply standard CDD measures for low/medium-risk PEPs. - Document justification for risk classification. - Ensure consistent application of procedures across branches.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Include the customer in periodic PEP re-screenings. - Provide guidance for reassessing risk if new information emerges (e.g. adverse media, career changes).

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: PERIODIC REVIEW FOR PEP CUSTOMERS
amlcft.description: 9.1 CDD should continue after establishing a relationship with the customer. On a regular basis, transactions and account activities should be monitored and scrutinized for ML/TF/PF risks. The behavior of the customer, transactions and accounts should be in line with the expected level of activity. Ongoing monitoring is crucial as a customer risk profile may change over time. 9.2 PEP accounts should be subject to periodic reviews as may be determined by the FI in line with risk assessment. Frequency of the periodic reviews should be determined by the risk of the customer and documented appropriately. FIs should also review their PEP database frequently.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall conduct ongoing monitoring and periodic reviews of PEP accounts based on their risk level. The frequency and depth of the reviews must align with the risk assessment, and any changes in customer behavior or risk profile must be addressed.
amlcft.deadlineType: As defined by FI’s risk-based review cycle (e.g., quarterly, semi-annually, annually based on risk level)
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to perform ongoing or risk-based reviews of PEP accounts could result in undetected ML/TF/PF activities, leading to regulatory penalties and reputational damage.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Relationship Managers, Risk Management Team
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Department, Internal Audit, and Business Units managing PEP relationships
amlcft.primaryControl: - Establish a risk-based schedule for reviewing PEP accounts. - Update PEP risk profiles periodically. - Flag and investigate deviations in expected account behavior. - Review PEP database regularly to capture status changes.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Implement automated alerts for unusual activity. - Use PEP re-screening tools to capture updated statuses. - Escalate high-risk findings to senior management.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: Record Keeping
amlcft.description: Financial Institutions (FIs) should ensure that the records maintained are as provided in extant laws and Regulations. The records should be readily available in a timely and appropriate format to competent authorities upon request.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall maintain records in line with existing AML/CFT laws and regulations. These records must be easily retrievable and available promptly in a proper format when requested.
amlcft.deadlineType: - Immediately on record generation- Ongoing throughout record retention period (typically 5 years or more as required by law)
amlcft.riskDescription: - Inability to provide records promptly may result in regulatory penalties, loss of critical evidence, investigation delays, and non-compliance with AML/CFT laws.
amlcft.owner: - Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)- Records & Information Management Unit- IT/Database Administrators
amlcft.responsibility: - Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)- Head of Data Management- Internal Audit Unit
amlcft.primaryControl: - Centralized digital archiving system- Documented Record Retention Policy- Access control logs- Retrieval SLA for regulatory data requests
amlcft.additionalControl: - Regular audits of record storage systems- Compliance drills (simulated requests)- Data integrity and backup validation routines- Defined escalation matrix for record-related requests

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: Reporting
amlcft.description: 11.1 FIs should closely monitor the transactions of all foreign PEPs and high-risk domestic or international organization PEPs. If there is a suspicion that a transaction involves funds linked to any form of criminal activity, a Suspicious Transaction/Activity Report (STR) must be filed with the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU).
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall closely monitor all transactions involving foreign PEPs and high-risk domestic/international PEPs. If there is any suspicion that a transaction is linked to criminal activity, the bank must file a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with the NFIU without delay.
amlcft.deadlineType: Immediately upon suspicion, within the regulatory timeframe
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to identify and report suspicious activities linked to PEPs may lead to regulatory sanctions, financial penalties, and exposure to ML/TF/PF risk, including loss of reputation.
amlcft.owner: Compliance Officer, Transaction Monitoring Unit, Operations Department
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Department (STR Filing), Risk Monitoring Unit, Internal Audit
amlcft.primaryControl: - Implement real-time transaction monitoring systems for PEP accounts. - Establish PEP-specific monitoring rules. - Train staff to escalate suspicious behavior for PEPs. - Maintain a PEP activity watchlist.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Conduct automated adverse media screening. - Periodically audit STR filings related to PEPs.  - Escalate alerts involving high-value or unusual cross-border transactions.

amlcft.source: Guidance Note on Politically Exposed Persons (PEP)
amlcft.title: Training and Education
amlcft.description: AML/CFT/CPF training policies of FIs should include ongoing employee training programmes. These training programmes need to address effective ways of determining whether clients are PEPs, and understanding, assessing and handling the potential risks associated with PEPs. Training should also incorporate real-life case studies and examples to make it up to date. Emphasis should be placed on human input and analysis from experienced and trained employees rather than on automated software programmed for detecting and handling the risks associated with PEPs.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall implement ongoing AML/CFT/CPF training for all employees. Training must include how to identify PEPs, assess related risks, and handle such risks effectively. It should include real-life case studies and emphasize human judgment alongside system automation.
amlcft.deadlineType: Quarterly (minimum), with refresher sessions annually
amlcft.riskDescription: Inadequate training may result in failure to detect PEPs, missed STRs, and regulatory non-compliance, potentially leading to fines, sanctions, or reputational damage.
amlcft.owner: Human Resources (Training), Compliance Officer, Departmental Heads
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Department (content), HR (delivery), Internal Audit (validation)
amlcft.primaryControl: - Develop a structured AML/CFT/CPF training plan. - Include PEP risk handling modules. - Use case-based learning. - Mandate periodic assessments to ensure knowledge retention.
amlcft.additionalControl: - Maintain training logs and attendance records. - Conduct periodic competency tests. - Engage external experts for advanced PEP training.

amlcft.source: Guidelines on Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism and Terrorism Financing
amlcft.title: Obligations on Financial Institutions to Implement TFS
amlcft.description: FIs shall undertake TFS measures in relation to terrorism and terrorism financing as provided for under TPPA and Regulations.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall freeze funds and block any transactions involving listed terrorists or terrorist groups and must not give them access to financial services.
amlcft.deadlineType: Ongoing and immediate upon updates
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to block or freeze terrorist-related assets can lead to financial support for terrorism, regulatory penalties, and reputational harm.
amlcft.owner: Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), Compliance Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), IT/Monitoring Team
amlcft.primaryControl: Use of sanctions screening tools, regular watchlist checks, automated alerts, staff training
amlcft.additionalControl: Real-time monitoring, auto-flagging of listed names, instant sanctions list updates

amlcft.source: Guidelines on Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism and Terrorism Financing
amlcft.title: Alert System
amlcft.description: All FIs shall subscribe to the alert system for receiving automated email notifications of the sanction lists through the following links: https://www.un.org/securitycouncil/content/un-sc-consolidated-list and https://www.nigsac.gov.ng
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall subscribe to email alerts from the UN and NIGSAC websites to receive updates when new names are added to terrorism-related sanction lists.
amlcft.deadlineType: Immediately upon setup and ongoing monitoring
amlcft.riskDescription: Missing updates to sanction lists may result in failing to freeze assets of designated persons or entities, leading to non-compliance and penalties.
amlcft.owner: Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), IT Department
amlcft.responsibility: IT Support Team, Compliance Officer
amlcft.primaryControl: Subscription to automated email alerts from UN and NIGSAC platforms; regular compliance checks
amlcft.additionalControl: Set up a monitoring calendar to verify list updates and email alerts weekly

amlcft.source: Guidelines on Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism and Terrorism Financing
amlcft.title: Screening
amlcft.description: FIs are required to carry out regular and ongoing screening against the latest updates of Sanction Lists prior to conducting any transaction or undertaking any financial Services to ascertain whether or not the name of such a person or entity is on the Lists. Specifically, screening should be conducted during the following:  a) Onboarding a new customer; b) Facilitating an occasional transaction; c) Establishing any relationship with any person or entity; d) Before carrying out any transaction; and e) Upon review of Know Your Customer (KYC) or changes to a customer’s information.  Screening must be conducted immediately and without delay to ensure compliance with implementing freezing measures without delay (within 24 hours). FIs are required to screen their entire customer base to prevent dissipation of funds of the designated persons or entities.  FIs (including those operating in free trade zones) must constantly screen their customers, potential customers, beneficial owners, and transactions to identify possible matches to the UN Consolidated Lists.  4.2.1 Screening of Customers – Related and Third Parties FIs shall undertake further screening and analysis on designated persons or entities whose properties or accounts are jointly owned and/or indirectly controlled by the designated persons or entities.  FIs shall conduct further CDD on parties related to frozen accounts including checking on the control and conduct of the frozen accounts and other related or third parties accounts connected to designated persons or entities.  The requirements for CDD on legal persons and legal arrangements and beneficial owners in the respective provisions under the CBN AML/CFT/CPF Regulations and Guidelines should be applied in determining the funds are directly or indirectly owned or controlled.  FIs are also advised to screen the names of the beneficiary of wire transfers and make an assessment whether such transaction should be blocked or rejected.  FIs are also advised to search, examine and analyse past financial activities of the designated persons or entities, related or third parties.  4.2.2 Confirmed Match A confirmed match is when an individual, entity, or group matches all the key identifiers published on the Sanctions Lists. The range of information that constitute identifiers of designated individuals, entities, or groups are as follows:  For natural person:  ✓ Name  ✓ Aliases/also known as/formerly known as  ✓ Date of birth  ✓ Nationality  ✓ ID or passport information  ✓ Last known address  For legal persons:  ✓ Name(s)  ✓ Aliases also known as/formerly known as  ✓ Certificate of Registration (RC No.)  ✓ Registered Address  ✓ Address of branches  ✓ Other information  Where the individual, entity, or group matches all the key identifiers published on the Sanctions Lists, the result is considered a ‘confirmed match’. In case the confirmed match is an existing customer, FIs are required to immediately, identify and freeze, without delay and without prior notice, all funds and assets owned or controlled by the designated person or entity in their possession.  Where the confirmed match is a potential customer, the FIs are required to reject the transaction immediately and report to the NSC. However, before rejecting the transaction, FIs are required to search their records to confirm whether the potential customer is a BO and where the search is positive, FIs are required to immediately identify and freeze, without delay and without prior notice, all funds and assets owned or controlled by the BO in their possession.  In cases of confirmed matches (for either existing or potential customer and closed/dormant relationships), FIs are required to report to the NSC, within 24 hours, any assets frozen or actions taken in compliance with the prohibition requirements of the relevant UNSCRs including attempted transactions.  In addition, FIs are required to immediately file STR to the NFIU, including all cases of name matching in financial transactions prior to or after publication or update of the lists for further analysis.  4.2.3 False Positive A false positive is a potential match to listed individuals, entities, or groups, either due to the common nature of the name or due to ambiguous identifying data, which on examination proves not to be a confirmed match.  FIs are required to obtain additional information and identification documents from the customer or a third party to ascertain whether a customer is a designated person or entity in the case of similar names.  FIs are required to forward queries to NSC to ascertain whether or not the customer is a designated person or entity in the case of similar names. Any query submitted to NSC is to be accompanied by additional information, copies of identification documents and the FIs assessments.  Where FIs are satisfied that the customer (potential or BO) is not a designated individual, entity, or group, i.e. a ‘False Positive Result’, FIs do not need to implement any TFS measures. FIs may allow the transaction or business to continue its normal course, and are required to maintain evidence of this process in their records.  Where FIs’ customers feel that their accounts have been mistakenly frozen or transactions have been mistakenly rejected or blocked, the FIs may advise their customers to contact the NSC to verify the false positive match. The contact details for the NSC in relation to TFS on TF is: https://nigsac.gov.ng/  4.2.4 Potential Match A potential match is when there is a partial match between identifiers in the Sanctions Lists with any information in FIs databases, and the FIs are unable to conclude a false positive or a confirmed match.  Due to prevalence of some names, FIs may find various potential matches. However, it does not necessarily mean that the individual, entity, or group they are dealing with is subject to TFS. FIs are required to cross-check their customers’ database with the identifiers published on the Sanctions Lists when identifying the potential match, by taking into consideration their knowledge of the customer (potential and BO) or transaction, through CDD and/or other sources of information.  Where FIs are unable to internally verify whether the ‘potential match’ is a false positive result or a confirmed match, they transaction should be suspended and the case reported to the NSC. The reported transaction should remain suspended until a response is received on the status of the potential match.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall screen all customers, beneficial owners, and transactions against updated sanction lists before any financial service or transaction. This must happen during onboarding, transactions, changes in customer data, and periodically. If a match is found, funds must be frozen immediately and NSC and NFIU notified. False positives and potential matches must be investigated and verified before action.
amlcft.deadlineType: Ongoing
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to conduct proper and timely screening can lead to dealing with sanctioned individuals or entities, resulting in regulatory penalties and reputational damage.
amlcft.owner: Chief Compliance Officer, AML/CFT Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Officer, IT & Risk Management Teams
amlcft.primaryControl: Automated sanction screening tools; real-time transaction screening; trained compliance team; periodic full customer base screening; documented procedures for potential and confirmed matches.
amlcft.additionalControl: Daily watchlist updates; periodic audits of screening logs; enhanced training on match escalation protocol; integrated alerts with onboarding and transaction platforms.

amlcft.source: Guidelines on Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism and Terrorism Financing
amlcft.title: Application of targeted financial sanctions
amlcft.description: FIs are required to immediately implement TFS by identifying and freezing, without delay and without prior notice, all funds and assets owned or controlled by the designated person or entity in their possession.  The following are the TFS measures that must be implemented if a match with the Sanctions Lists is identified.  i. Freeze all funds or other assets without delay: freeze without delay (immediately or in any case within 24 hours) and without prior notice to the designated individual, entity, or group, all the funds or other assets: a) Owned or controlled, wholly or jointly, directly, or indirectly, by an individual, entity, or group designated in the Sanctions Lists; b) Derived or generated from funds or other assets under item (a); or c) Any individual or entity acting on behalf of or at the direction of any designated individual, entity, or group.  ii. Prohibition of making funds or other assets or services available: FIs are prohibited from providing funds or other assets to or rendering financial services or other services related to, whether in whole or in part, directly or indirectly, or for the benefit of any designated individual, entity, or group on the Sanctions Lists.
amlcft.plain: The Bank shall freeze all funds and assets of designated persons or entities immediately (within 24 hours) and without giving notice. They must not provide funds, services, or access to assets—directly or indirectly—to anyone on the Sanctions List.
amlcft.deadlineType: Immediate and ongoing
amlcft.riskDescription: Delay or failure to freeze assets or continuing business with designated individuals or entities may result in regulatory sanctions, criminal liability, or reputational damage.
amlcft.owner: Chief Compliance Officer, Sanctions Compliance Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Officer, Sanctions Monitoring Team, IT Security Department
amlcft.primaryControl: Real-time sanctions screening system; immediate transaction freeze protocols; periodic staff training; access to updated Sanctions Lists; defined escalation procedures.
amlcft.additionalControl: Automated freeze triggers in transaction processing systems; daily reconciliation of sanctioned accounts; internal audit testing of freeze timelines; escalation matrix for sanction matches.

amlcft.source: Guidelines on Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism and Terrorism Financing
amlcft.title: Categories of Funds Subject to Freezing Obligations
amlcft.description: All types of funds or other assets are subject to freezing measures. The funds or other assets that can be subject to freezing measure includes the following:  i. Cash, cheques, claims on money, drafts, money orders, bearer instruments, internet-based and other electronic or digital payment instruments, including virtual currencies.  ii. Deposits with FIs or other entities and balances on accounts, including but not limited to: fixed or term deposit accounts, balances on share trading accounts with banks, or other investment trading accounts.  iii. Debts and debt obligations, including trade debts.  iv. Other accounts receivable, notes receivable, and other claims of money on others.  v. Other financial interest in a sole trader or partnership.  vi. Publicly and privately traded securities and debt instruments, including stocks and shares, certificates representing securities, bonds, notes, warrants, debentures, and derivatives contracts.  vii. Interest, dividends, or other income on or value accruing from or generated by assets.  viii. Credit, right of set-off, guarantees, performance bonds or other financial commitments.  ix. Letters of credit, bills of lading, bills of sale; notes receivable and other documents evidencing an interest in funds or financial resources and any other instruments of export-financing.  x. Insurance and reinsurance.
amlcft.plain: All types of financial instruments—cash, deposits, securities, digital currencies, and related income—shall be frozen if linked to a designated person or entity.
amlcft.deadlineType: Immediate and continuous
amlcft.riskDescription: Failure to identify and freeze all forms of financial assets may lead to partial compliance, regulatory penalties, or misuse of financial systems by sanctioned individuals/entities.
amlcft.owner: Chief Compliance Officer, Treasury Department, Asset Management Unit
amlcft.responsibility: Compliance Officer, Asset Management Lead, Treasury Operations, IT Systems Monitoring
amlcft.primaryControl: Comprehensive sanctions screening across all asset classes; internal asset classification register; digital currency monitoring; asset freeze procedures; cross-functional verification with finance, operations, and IT units.
amlcft.additionalControl: Integration of screening tools with asset registers; periodic review of asset holdings; automated detection and flagging of asset categories linked to sanctioned persons; refresher training for treasury and investment staff on new asset types (e.g., virtual currencies).

points.content: Other financial interest in a sole trader or partnership is subject to freezing.
